questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: For a language L over a finite alphabet, which of the following statements are TRUE?
questions.question_html: For a language L over a finite alphabet, which of the following statements are TRUE?
options: If L and L̄ are both recursively enumerable, then L is recursive.
If L is recursive, then L is recursively enumerable.
If L is r.e. but not recursive, then L̄ is not r.e.
If L is not r.e., then L̄ is r.e.
options_html: If L and L̄ are both recursively enumerable, then L is recursive.
If L is recursive, then L is recursively enumerable.
If L is r.e. but not recursive, then L̄ is not r.e.
If L is not r.e., then L̄ is r.e.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Three facts organise this question: recursive ⊂ r.e.; "both r.e." ⟺ recursive; and a language that is r.e. but not recursive has a complement that is not r.e. Statement (D) is the only one that goes wrong, because a language can be neither r.e. nor co-r.e.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true. Dovetail the two recognisers: exactly one of them accepts w, so the combined machine always halts. That is a decider for L.
  2. (B) true. A decider is a recogniser that happens to halt on every input, so every recursive language is r.e.
  3. (C) true. If L̄ were also r.e. then (A) would make L recursive, contradicting the hypothesis. So L̄ is not r.e.
  4. (D) false. Take the join J = {0x : x ∈ K} ∪ {1x : x ∉ K}, where K is the halting set. The join is r.e. exactly when K is, so J is not r.e.; and its complement is not r.e. either. Hence "not r.e." does not force the complement to be r.e.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Why (D) fails. The four possibilities are: recursive (both r.e.), r.e. only (like K), co-r.e. only (like K̄), and neither (like the join above). "Not r.e." covers the last two, and only in the co-r.e. case is the complement r.e.

Common misconception. Believing every language is either r.e. or co-r.e. Most languages are neither: there are uncountably many languages but only countably many Turing machines.

Takeaway. "Recursive" is a decision procedure; "r.e." is a recognition procedure. Everything in this unit is a consequence of that one distinction.

questions.question: Consider the following five languages, where M ranges over all Turing machines, G over all context-free grammars and w over all strings.(i) {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w within 100 steps}(ii) {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = ∅}(iii) {⟨G⟩ : G is a context-free grammar and L(G) = ∅}(iv) {⟨M⟩ : M accepts ε}(v) {⟨M⟩ : M halts on every input}How many of these five languages are recursive?
questions.question_html:
Consider the following five languages, where M ranges over all Turing machines, G over all context-free grammars and w over all strings.
(i) {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w within 100 steps}
(ii) {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = ∅}
(iii) {⟨G⟩ : G is a context-free grammar and L(G) = ∅}
(iv) {⟨M⟩ : M accepts ε}
(v) {⟨M⟩ : M halts on every input}
How many of these five languages are recursive?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A language is recursive when a total algorithm decides it. A bounded simulation or a finite fixed-point computation is total; anything that needs to know how a machine behaves on all inputs is not.

Step by step.

  1. (i) recursive. Simulate M on w for exactly 100 steps and report whether it halted. The simulation is bounded, so the procedure always halts — this is the standard "bounded halting is decidable" fact.
  2. (ii) not recursive. L(M) = ∅ is a non-trivial property of L(M), so Rice's theorem applies. Intuitively, to say yes you would have to prove that no input is ever accepted, which needs unbounded search.
  3. (iii) recursive. Emptiness of a context-free language is decidable: compute the set of productive nonterminals by a fixed-point iteration, or test whether the start symbol can derive any terminal string. Always terminates.
  4. (iv) not recursive. It is r.e. — just run M on ε — but not recursive: deciding whether M accepts ε is undecidable by reduction from the halting problem.
  5. (v) not recursive. M halts on every input is a non-trivial property of L(M), undecidable by Rice's theorem; it is not even r.e.
  6. Counting: exactly (i) and (iii) are recursive, so the answer is 2.

Answer: 2

How the answer was checked. Each of the five is settled by a known result rather than by intuition: bounded halting is decidable by the 100-step clock; CFG emptiness is decidable by the productivity fixed point; (ii), (iv) and (v) are three different undecidable problems, two of them by Rice's theorem and one by reduction from halting.

Common misconception. Marking (i) undecidable "because halting is undecidable". The undecidability of halting concerns unbounded running time; once the time budget is fixed the problem becomes a finite simulation. Conversely, marking (iv) decidable because it looks like a single test on one string — the test may not terminate.

Takeaway. Bounded questions are decidable; unbounded questions about the whole behaviour of a machine are not. That single criterion answers most questions in this unit.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let A and B be recursively enumerable languages over Σ such that A ∪ B = Σ* and A ∩ B = ∅. Which one of the following must hold?
questions.question_html: Let A and B be recursively enumerable languages over Σ such that A ∪ B = Σ* and A ∩ B = ∅. Which one of the following must hold?
options: A and B are both recursive.
A is regular.
A is recursively enumerable but need not be recursive.
At least one of A and B is finite.
options_html: A and B are both recursive.
A is regular.
A is recursively enumerable but need not be recursive.
At least one of A and B is finite.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Disjointness together with A ∪ B = Σ* makes the two languages exact complements of each other. A language whose complement is also r.e. is recursive — so both parts are recursive, whatever they look like.

Step by step.

  1. Since A ∪ B = Σ*, every string is in A or in B.
  2. Since A ∩ B = ∅, no string is in both. Together the two facts give B = Σ* \ A = Ā.
  3. So A is r.e. (given) and Ā is r.e. (given). Dovetail the two recognisers: on any w exactly one of them accepts, so the combined procedure always halts.
  4. Hence A is recursive, and B, being its complement, is recursive as well.
  5. No regularity and no finiteness follows: take A to be any recursive non-regular language, for instance {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0}, and B its complement.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) fails with A = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0}, which is recursive but not regular.
  • (C) fails because the extra hypothesis "the complement is r.e." is exactly what rules out the r.e.-but-not-recursive case.
  • (D) fails with the same example: both A and B are infinite.

Common misconception. Using only A ∪ B = Σ* and concluding "one of them must be the whole thing". Disjointness and covering together are much stronger than either alone: they say the two languages split Σ* into a decidable pair.

Takeaway. A partition of Σ* into two r.e. parts is automatically a partition into two recursive parts. This is the standard route for showing that a language is recursive: exhibit recognisers for both it and its complement.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following languages is recursive (decidable)?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following languages is recursive (decidable)?
options: {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w}
{⟨M⟩ : M halts on every input}
{⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w within 1000 steps}
options_html: {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w}
{⟨M⟩ : L(M) = Σ*}
{⟨M⟩ : M halts on every input}
{⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w within 1000 steps}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A language is decidable when there is a procedure that always halts. The only option with a built-in clock is (D): once the number of steps is bounded, the simulation is a finite, terminating computation.

Step by step.

  1. Decider for (D): on input ⟨M, w⟩, decode the pair, then simulate M on w for at most 1000 steps. If the machine halts inside the budget, accept; otherwise reject.
  2. The simulation takes at most 1000 steps of work, so the decider halts on every input. Hence (D) is recursive.
  3. Option (A) is the halting problem itself, undecidable by the diagonal argument.
  4. Option (C) asks whether a machine halts on all inputs, a non-trivial property of L(M), undecidable by Rice's theorem (indeed not even r.e.).
  5. Option (B) is also a non-trivial property of L(M), undecidable by Rice's theorem.

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is the canonical undecidable problem: the diagonal machine differs from every machine on its own code.
  • (B) and (C) are semantic properties of L(M) that hold for some machines and fail for others, so Rice's theorem applies.

Common misconception. Reading "halts on w within 1000 steps" as a special case of "halts on w". The bound is what makes the difference: with a bound the search space is finite, without one it is not.

Takeaway. Bounded simulation is always decidable. Undecidability enters only when a procedure would have to run an unbounded computation to answer "no".

questions.question: To prove that a language L is undecidable by reduction from the halting problem HALT = {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w}, which one of the following must be constructed?
questions.question_html: To prove that a language L is undecidable by reduction from the halting problem HALT = {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w}, which one of the following must be constructed?
options: A computable function f such that ⟨M, w⟩ ∈ HALT ⟺ f(⟨M, w⟩) ∈ L for every pair (M, w).
A computable function f such that x ∈ L ⟺ f(x) ∈ HALT for every string x.
A Turing machine that decides L.
An enumeration of all the strings in L.
options_html: A computable function f such that ⟨M, w⟩ ∈ HALT ⟺ f(⟨M, w⟩) ∈ L for every pair (M, w).
A computable function f such that x ∈ L ⟺ f(x) ∈ HALT for every string x.
A Turing machine that decides L.
An enumeration of all the strings in L.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A reduction from HALT to L is a computable map that translates questions about halting into questions about L, preserving the answer. If such a map exists and L were decidable, halting would be decidable too — a contradiction.

Step by step.

  1. What must be built: a computable f with ⟨M, w⟩ ∈ HALT ⟺ f(⟨M, w⟩) ∈ L. Then a decider for L composed with f would decide HALT, which is impossible.
  2. In practice f is described by a construction: on input ⟨M, w⟩, build the description of a new machine M′ that behaves as required, and output ⟨M′⟩.
  3. This direction — from the known-undecidable problem to the new one — is what transfers undecidability.
  4. Option (B) is the opposite direction, L ≤m HALT. It only shows that L is no harder than halting, i.e. that L is r.e.; every decidable language reduces to HALT in that direction, so nothing is proved.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) is the classic direction error: L ≤m HALT shows only L ∈ RE.
  • (C) would prove L decidable, the opposite of the goal — and it cannot exist.
  • (D) shows only that L is r.e., which is far weaker than decidability.

Common misconception. Getting the arrow backwards. Remember the mnemonic: to prove L hard, reduce a known hard problem to L, so that solving L would solve the hard one.

Takeaway. A ≤m B means "A is at most as hard as B". Reductions therefore flow from the problem already known to be hard to the problem to be proved hard.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which of the following problems are undecidable?
questions.question_html: Which of the following problems are undecidable?
options: Given a Turing machine M, does M halt on the empty string?
Given a Turing machine M and a state q of M, does M ever enter the state q when started on the empty string?
Given a DFA A, does A accept at least one string?
Given a Turing machine M, does M ever write the symbol 1 on its tape when started on the empty string?
options_html: Given a Turing machine M, does M halt on the empty string?
Given a Turing machine M and a state q of M, does M ever enter the state q when started on the empty string?
Given a DFA A, does A accept at least one string?
Given a Turing machine M, does M ever write the symbol 1 on its tape when started on the empty string?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Each option asks about the unbounded behaviour of a machine, except (C), which asks about a finite automaton — and finite automata can be decided by graph search. The three Turing-machine questions are undecidable, each by a small reduction from halting.

Step by step.

  1. (A) undecidable. HALT reduces to it: given ⟨M, w⟩, build M′ that first writes w on its tape and then simulates M. Then M′ halts on ε iff M halts on w.
  2. (B) undecidable. Given ⟨M, w⟩, build M′ that simulates M and enters a fresh state q only when that simulation halts. Then M′ enters q iff M halts on w.
  3. (C) decidable. Do a reachability search from the start state of A over its finitely many states, and accept iff some final state is reachable. The graph is finite, so the search terminates.
  4. (D) undecidable. Given ⟨M, w⟩, build M′ that simulates M and writes 1 only when the simulation halts. Then M′ ever writes 1 iff M halts on w.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Why (C) survives. A DFA has finitely many states, so "is a final state reachable?" is a finite graph question with a terminating algorithm. Emptiness, finiteness and universality of a DFA are decidable for the same reason.

Common misconception. Believing that a "simple" question about a Turing machine must be decidable. "Does it ever enter state q?" and "does it ever write 1?" look local, but the answer may depend on an unbounded computation, and unbounded is what makes it undecidable.

Takeaway. Undecidability is about the quantifier structure: a question of the form "does there exist a time t at which ..." over an unbounded t is undecidable, while the same question over a finite object is decidable.

questions.question: Consider the deterministic Turing machine with states q₀, q₁, q₂, q₃, q_f, tape alphabet {0, 1, X, Y, ␣} (␣ is the blank) and the transition function below. X and Y are "crossed-off" marks; every pair not listed sends the machine to the halting reject state q_r.δ(q₀,0)=(q₁,X,R) δ(q₀,Y)=(q₃,Y,R) δ(q₁,0)=(q₁,0,R) δ(q₁,Y)=(q₁,Y,R) δ(q₁,1)=(q₂,Y,L)δ(q₂,0)=(q₂,0,L) δ(q₂,Y)=(q₂,Y,L) δ(q₂,X)=(q₀,X,R) δ(q₃,Y)=(q₃,Y,R) δ(q₃,␣)=(q_f,␣,R)The head starts on the leftmost cell, which holds the first input symbol. Started on the input 0011, how many transitions (applications of δ) does the machine make before it halts?
questions.question_html:
Consider the deterministic Turing machine with states q₀, q₁, q₂, q₃, q_f, tape alphabet {0, 1, X, Y, ␣} (␣ is the blank) and the transition function below. X and Y are "crossed-off" marks; every pair not listed sends the machine to the halting reject state q_r.
δ(q₀,0)=(q₁,X,R)   δ(q₀,Y)=(q₃,Y,R)   δ(q₁,0)=(q₁,0,R)   δ(q₁,Y)=(q₁,Y,R)   δ(q₁,1)=(q₂,Y,L)
δ(q₂,0)=(q₂,0,L)   δ(q₂,Y)=(q₂,Y,L)   δ(q₂,X)=(q₀,X,R)   δ(q₃,Y)=(q₃,Y,R)   δ(q₃,␣)=(q_f,␣,R)
The head starts on the leftmost cell, which holds the first input symbol. Started on the input 0011, how many transitions (applications of δ) does the machine make before it halts?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The machine is the standard "cross off one 0 at the left and one 1 at the right" decider for {0ⁿ1ⁿ : n ≥ 1}. Counting its moves is a matter of walking the head across the tape; nothing has to be guessed.

Step by step.

  1. Write the tape as 0 0 1 1 ␣ ␣ … with the head on the first cell, and run the table literally.
  2. Moves 1–3: (q₀,0)→(q₁,X,R) crosses the first 0; (q₁,0)→(q₁,0,R) skips the second 0; (q₁,1)→(q₂,Y,L) crosses the second 1 and turns left. Tape: X 0 Y 1.
  3. Moves 4–5: the head walks left over the 0 and the X — (q₂,0)→(q₂,0,L) then (q₂,X)→(q₀,X,R) — so q₀ now faces the first uncrossed 0.
  4. Moves 6–10: the second pass crosses the remaining 0 (move 6), skips the crossed Y (move 7), crosses the last 1 (move 8), then walks left over Y and X (moves 9–10). Tape: X X Y Y.
  5. Moves 11–13: (q₀,Y)→(q₃,Y,R) moves to the check phase, (q₃,Y)→(q₃,Y,R) skips the second Y, and (q₃,␣)→(q_f,␣,R) reads the blank and halts. Total: 13 transitions.
  6. Cross-check with the closed form: this machine needs 2n² + 2n + 1 moves on 0ⁿ1ⁿ, giving 5, 13 and 25 for n = 1, 2, 3, and the trace above reproduces 13 exactly.

Answer: 13 transitions.

How the answer was checked. The machine was executed step by step and the transition count recorded at each move; the 13 moves above are the complete computation, ending when δ(q₃,␣) is applied to the blank. The same run on 000111 gives 25 moves and on 01 gives 5, both matching 2n² + 2n + 1, which confirms the trace is not an off-by-one.

Common misconception. Counting cells visited or passes instead of applications of δ, or forgetting the final transition that reads the blank and enters q_f. Every application of δ counts as one move, including the one that halts the machine.

Takeaway. A Turing machine is a completely explicit object: given the table, the computation and its length are determined. This is why "does it halt within k steps" is decidable — the trace is computable — while "does it halt at all" is not.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let ≤m denote mapping reducibility. Which one of the following statements is TRUE for all languages A and B?
questions.question_html: Let ≤m denote mapping reducibility. Which one of the following statements is TRUE for all languages A and B?
options: If A ≤m B and B is undecidable, then A is undecidable.
If A ≤m B and A is r.e., then B is r.e.
If A ≤m B and B is decidable, then A is undecidable.
If A ≤m B and A is undecidable, then B is undecidable.
options_html: If A ≤m B and B is undecidable, then A is undecidable.
If A ≤m B and A is r.e., then B is r.e.
If A ≤m B and B is decidable, then A is undecidable.
If A ≤m B and A is undecidable, then B is undecidable.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A ≤m B means: there is a computable f with x ∈ A ⟺ f(x) ∈ B. So A is at most as hard as B. Hardness therefore flows backwards along the arrow, and decidability flows forwards.

Step by step.

  1. Assume A ≤m B via f.
  2. If B were decidable with decider N, then N ∘ f would decide A: compute f(x), then run N. Since f is computable and N always halts, the composite always halts.
  3. So decidability of B gives decidability of A. In contrapositive form: if A is undecidable then B is undecidable. That is statement (D).
  4. The same argument with "recognisable" in place of "decidable" shows: if A is r.e. then B is r.e.
  5. The converses all fail, because an easy language reduces to a hard one: ∅ reduces to every language, including the undecidable ones.

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) reverses the arrow. A ≤m B says nothing about A when B is the hard one: ∅ reduces to any language, yet ∅ is decidable.
  • (B) has the same defect: r.e.-ness of the left side does not transfer to the right side.
  • (C) contradicts the transfer of decidability proved above.

Common misconception. Reading A ≤m B as "equally hard". It is a one-way statement: the left side is no harder than the right. Hardness of B says nothing about A.

Takeaway. To prove B undecidable, reduce a known undecidable language to B. To prove A decidable, reduce A to a known decidable language. Both are applications of the single composition rule above.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: By Rice's theorem, which one of the following languages is undecidable?
questions.question_html: By Rice's theorem, which one of the following languages is undecidable?
options: {⟨M⟩ : M has at least three states}
{⟨M⟩ : the transition table of M contains the symbol 0}
{⟨M⟩ : L(M) is regular}
{⟨M⟩ : M halts on ε within 100 steps}
options_html: {⟨M⟩ : M has at least three states}
{⟨M⟩ : the transition table of M contains the symbol 0}
{⟨M⟩ : L(M) is regular}
{⟨M⟩ : M halts on ε within 100 steps}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Rice's theorem: every non-trivial semantic property of L(M) is undecidable. Non-trivial means some r.e. language has the property and some does not; semantic means the property depends only on which strings the machine accepts, not on how the machine is built.

Step by step.

  1. Check the four options against the two conditions.
  2. (A) and (B) are syntactic: they are decided by inspecting the description of M — count its states, scan its table. Both are decidable.
  3. (D) is bounded: simulate for 100 steps and report. Decidable.
  4. (C) is semantic — it speaks only of L(M) — and non-trivial: ∅ is regular, while {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0} is not. Rice's theorem therefore makes it undecidable.
  5. So exactly one option is undecidable.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are decidable. Each is answered by a finite inspection: count the states, search the transition table, or run a clocked simulation. None requires knowing the language the machine accepts.

Common misconception. Applying Rice's theorem to any question about Turing machines. It applies only to properties of L(M). "Has three states" and "contains the symbol 0" are properties of the program text, and program text is a finite string that can be examined directly.

Takeaway. The test is always: does the property change if I replace M by an equivalent machine? If yes, it is semantic; if it is also non-trivial, it is undecidable.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Rice's theorem applies only to properties of the language L(M), and only to non-trivial ones. To which one of the following languages does Rice's theorem NOT apply?
questions.question_html: Rice's theorem applies only to properties of the language L(M), and only to non-trivial ones. To which one of the following languages does Rice's theorem NOT apply?
options: {⟨M⟩ : M has an even number of states}
{⟨M⟩ : L(M) is infinite}
{⟨M⟩ : L(M) contains at least one palindrome}
options_html: {⟨M⟩ : M has an even number of states}
{⟨M⟩ : L(M) = ∅}
{⟨M⟩ : L(M) is infinite}
{⟨M⟩ : L(M) contains at least one palindrome}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Rice's theorem is a statement about properties of L(M). A property of the machine's description — its number of states, its alphabet, the length of its encoding — is outside its scope, and such properties are usually decidable outright.

Step by step.

  1. Option (A) counts the states of M. Two machines accepting the same language may have different state counts, and an equivalent machine can always be padded with unreachable states. So the property is not semantic, and Rice's theorem says nothing about it.
  2. In fact (A) is decidable: read the description, count the states, test parity.
  3. Options (B), (C) and (D) are each properties of L(M) alone, and each is non-trivial: ∅ satisfies (B) but not (C); Σ* satisfies (C) but not (B); and Σ* satisfies (D) while {ab} does not.
  4. So Rice's theorem applies to (B), (C) and (D) and makes them undecidable, and it does not apply to (A).

Answer: Option (A).

Why the others are covered. Emptiness, infiniteness and "contains a palindrome" all speak only about which strings are accepted. Each holds for some machines and fails for others, so each is a non-trivial semantic property and Rice's theorem applies.

Common misconception. Thinking a syntactic property must be trivial. Syntactic properties can be interesting — "uses more than 10 states", "has a transition on the blank" — but because the description is a finite string they are all decidable by inspection. Rice's theorem is silent about them, not permissive.

Takeaway. Semantic properties are undecidable by Rice; syntactic properties are decidable by inspection. When a question mixes the two, split them before reaching for the theorem.

questions.question: Which of the following are non-trivial properties of the language L(M), and therefore undecidable by Rice's theorem?
questions.question_html: Which of the following are non-trivial properties of the language L(M), and therefore undecidable by Rice's theorem?
options: L(M) is finite.
L(M) contains at least one string of length 5.
M uses at most 50 tape cells on every input.
options_html: L(M) is finite.
L(M) = Σ*.
L(M) contains at least one string of length 5.
M uses at most 50 tape cells on every input.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A property qualifies for Rice's theorem when (i) it is decided by L(M) alone and (ii) it is neither always true nor always false over the r.e. languages. The first three pass both tests; the fourth speaks about the machine's space usage.

Step by step.

  1. (A) qualifies. Finiteness depends only on L(M). Non-trivial: ∅ is finite, Σ* is infinite.
  2. (B) qualifies. Non-trivial: Σ* has L(M) = Σ* while ∅ has not. Undecidable by Rice's theorem.
  3. (C) qualifies. The set Σ⁵ is fixed and finite (32 strings over a binary alphabet), so "does M accept one of them" is a property of L(M). Non-trivial: ∅ accepts none, Σ* accepts all.
  4. (D) does not qualify. Space usage is a property of the computation, not of the accepted language: two machines accepting the same language can use very different space. It is still undecidable — by a reduction from halting — but not by Rice's theorem.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Why (D) is excluded. Rice's theorem is about the extensional object L(M). Whether a machine stays within 50 cells is intensional: a wasteful machine and a frugal one may accept exactly the same language. The theorem has no purchase on it.

Common misconception. Treating "undecidable" and "undecidable by Rice's theorem" as the same thing. (D) is undecidable, yet Rice's theorem is not the reason; the correct tool is a direct reduction, since a halting computation can be encoded by making the machine write far out on the tape.

Takeaway. Read the property literally: if it mentions cells, steps, states or tape usage, Rice does not apply. If it mentions only the set of accepted strings, and some language has it while another does not, it does.

questions.question: The standard reduction proving that NE = {⟨M⟩ : L(M) ≠ ∅} is undecidable maps ⟨M, w⟩ to ⟨M′⟩, where M′ on input x ignores x, simulates M on w and accepts if that simulation halts. Which one of the following statements about this construction is correct?
questions.question_html: The standard reduction proving that NE = {⟨M⟩ : L(M) ≠ ∅} is undecidable maps ⟨M, w⟩ to ⟨M′⟩, where M′ on input x ignores x, simulates M on w and accepts if that simulation halts. Which one of the following statements about this construction is correct?
options: It is not a valid reduction, because M′ ignores its input x.
⟨M, w⟩ ∈ HALT ⟺ L(M′) ≠ ∅, so HALT ≤m NE and NE is undecidable.
⟨M, w⟩ ∈ HALT ⟺ L(M′) = ∅, so HALT ≤m NE.
It shows only that NE is r.e., not that it is undecidable.
options_html: It is not a valid reduction, because M′ ignores its input x.
⟨M, w⟩ ∈ HALT ⟺ L(M′) ≠ ∅, so HALT ≤m NE and NE is undecidable.
⟨M, w⟩ ∈ HALT ⟺ L(M′) = ∅, so HALT ≤m NE.
It shows only that NE is r.e., not that it is undecidable.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The construction makes M′ a "witness machine": it accepts every input if M halts on w, and no input otherwise. That turns a question about one computation into a question about emptiness of a language.

Step by step.

  1. Case 1: M halts on w. Then M′ accepts every x it is given, so L(M′) = Σ*, in particular L(M′) ≠ ∅.
  2. Case 2: M does not halt on w. Then M′ loops on every input and accepts nothing, so L(M′) = ∅.
  3. Hence ⟨M, w⟩ ∈ HALT ⟺ L(M′) ≠ ∅, which is exactly the biconditional a reduction from HALT to NE requires. The map is computable: from the descriptions of M and w one writes down the description of M′ mechanically.
  4. If NE were decidable, composing its decider with this map would decide HALT, which is impossible. So NE is undecidable.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) misreads the technique. Ignoring the input is the whole point: it makes acceptance independent of x, so the only remaining question is whether the simulation of M on w halts.
  • (C) has the biconditional inverted. If M halts on w then M′ accepts everything, so L(M′) is not empty.
  • (D) understates the result. The reduction transfers undecidability, not merely r.e.-ness — though NE does happen to be r.e. as well.

Common misconception. Forgetting to check both directions of the biconditional. A reduction must map yes-instances to yes-instances and no-instances to no-instances; case 2 supplies the second half.

Takeaway. The "ignore the input, simulate, then accept" gadget is the workhorse of undecidability proofs. Rice's theorem packages it once and for all: any non-trivial property of L(M) can be forced to hold or fail by choosing whether the simulated computation halts.

questions.question: Consider the following six properties of L(M).(i) L(M) = ∅(ii) L(M) is regular(iii) 0101 ∈ L(M)(iv) L(M) is co-finite, that is Σ* \ L(M) is finite(v) L(M) ⊆ Σ*(vi) |L(M)| ≤ 3How many of these six are undecidable by Rice's theorem?
questions.question_html:
Consider the following six properties of L(M).
(i) L(M) = ∅
(ii) L(M) is regular
(iii) 0101 ∈ L(M)
(iv) L(M) is co-finite, that is Σ* \ L(M) is finite
(v) L(M) ⊆ Σ*
(vi) |L(M)| ≤ 3
How many of these six are undecidable by Rice's theorem?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Rice's theorem needs two things of a property: it must be a property of L(M), and it must be non-trivial — true for at least one r.e. language and false for at least one. Five of the six pass both tests; the exception is trivially true.

Step by step.

  1. (i) undecidable. Non-trivial (∅ has it, Σ* does not) and semantic. Rice applies.
  2. (ii) undecidable. Regularity depends only on L(M); ∅ is regular and {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0} is not. Rice applies.
  3. (iii) undecidable. Membership of one fixed string is a semantic property; Σ* contains 0101, ∅ does not. Rice applies.
  4. (iv) undecidable. Co-finiteness is semantic and non-trivial: Σ* is co-finite, ∅ is not. Rice applies.
  5. (v) decidable. Every language over Σ satisfies L(M) ⊆ Σ*, so the property is trivial and the language in question is all of Σ*; a decider simply accepts everything. Rice's theorem requires non-triviality and therefore does not apply.
  6. (vi) undecidable. Bounded cardinality is semantic and non-trivial: ∅ satisfies it, Σ* does not. Rice applies.
  7. Counting: (i), (ii), (iii), (iv) and (vi) are undecidable by Rice's theorem, and (v) is not. The answer is 5.

Answer: 5

How the answer was checked. Each of the six was tested against the two conditions rather than judged by feel. For every one of (i), (ii), (iii), (iv) and (vi) a witness pair was produced — a language with the property and a language without it — which is exactly the non-triviality certificate Rice's theorem needs. Property (v) has no such pair, because it holds for every language over Σ.

Common misconception. Assuming every property of L(M) is undecidable by Rice. The theorem excludes the two trivial properties — always true and always false — and those are decidable precisely because a decider can ignore its input. It also excludes properties of the machine rather than of its language.

Takeaway. Before invoking Rice, ask: can I name a language with the property and a language without it? If yes, the property is non-trivial and undecidable. If no, it is trivial, and trivially decidable.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements about the classes of the Chomsky hierarchy is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following statements about the classes of the Chomsky hierarchy is TRUE?
options: Every recursive language is context-sensitive.
Every context-sensitive language is recursive.
Every recursively enumerable language is context-sensitive.
The class of context-free languages equals the class of context-sensitive languages.
options_html: Every recursive language is context-sensitive.
Every context-sensitive language is recursive.
Every recursively enumerable language is context-sensitive.
The class of context-free languages equals the class of context-sensitive languages.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The Chomsky hierarchy is a chain of strict inclusions: Regular ⊂ CFL ⊂ CSL ⊂ RE. Each step up adds a more powerful machine, and each step up keeps everything the level below can do.

Step by step.

  1. A context-sensitive language is accepted by a linear-bounded automaton, whose tape is bounded by the input length n. With |Q| states and n cells there are only |Q| · n · |Γ|ⁿ configurations — finitely many — so a brute-force search of the configuration graph decides membership.
  2. A total decision procedure therefore exists, so every CSL is recursive. Option (B) is true.
  3. The inclusion is strict at the top: the halting set K is r.e. and not recursive, hence not context-sensitive. Option (C) is false.
  4. The inclusion is strict at the bottom too: there are recursive languages that no non-contracting grammar generates, so some recursive languages are not context-sensitive. Option (A) is false.
  5. And {aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 1} is context-sensitive but not context-free, so the two classes differ. Option (D) is false.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) reverses a strict inclusion: recursion is above context-sensitivity, not below it.
  • (C) ignores the top of the hierarchy; Type 0 is strictly larger than Type 1.
  • (D) contradicts the standard witness {aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 1}, which an LBA accepts but no PDA does.

Common misconception. Reading the hierarchy as "bigger type number, bigger class" and then assuming every level is decidable. Only Type 0 escapes decidability: Types 1, 2 and 3 are all recursive.

Takeaway. Type 3 ⊂ Type 2 ⊂ Type 1 ⊂ Type 0. Decidability is lost exactly once, between Type 1 and Type 0, when the tape bound is removed.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: The class of languages accepted by a linear-bounded automaton is exactly the class of:
questions.question_html: The class of languages accepted by a linear-bounded automaton is exactly the class of:
options: regular languages
context-free languages
recursive languages
context-sensitive languages
options_html: regular languages
context-free languages
recursive languages
context-sensitive languages
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The Chomsky hierarchy pairs each language class with a machine: finite automaton with regular, pushdown automaton with context-free, linear-bounded automaton with context-sensitive, Turing machine with recursively enumerable.

Step by step.

  1. A linear-bounded automaton is a Turing machine whose tape is confined to the input cells. That restriction is exactly what a non-contracting grammar describes: every production either keeps the length or increases it, never shrinks it.
  2. By the standard equivalence, a language is context-sensitive iff some LBA accepts it — the tape bound on the machine matches the non-shrinking condition on the grammar.
  3. The class is strictly larger than the context-free languages ({aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 1} is accepted by an LBA but by no PDA) and strictly smaller than the recursive languages.
  4. So the answer is the context-sensitive class.

Answer: Option (D) — the context-sensitive languages.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) belongs to the one-way finite automaton and (B) to the pushdown automaton; both machines have strictly less storage than an LBA.
  • (C) is the class of languages decided by a Turing machine with no tape bound; every CSL is recursive, but not conversely.

Common misconception. Confusing "bounded tape" with "no tape". An LBA can still scan and rewrite its whole input many times; it simply cannot run off the end. That is why it reaches beyond the context-free languages.

Takeaway. Machine to language class: DFA gives regular, PDA gives context-free, LBA gives context-sensitive, TM gives recursively enumerable.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the Chomsky hierarchy and its machine models are TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about the Chomsky hierarchy and its machine models are TRUE?
options: Every regular language is context-free.
Every context-free language is recursive.
The membership problem for context-sensitive languages is decidable.
Every recursively enumerable language is recursive.
options_html: Every regular language is context-free.
Every context-free language is recursive.
The membership problem for context-sensitive languages is decidable.
Every recursively enumerable language is recursive.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Climbing the hierarchy never loses a language, and the first three levels are decidable. Only Type 0 is undecidable.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true. A DFA is a pushdown automaton that never uses its stack, so every regular language has a PDA and hence a context-free grammar.
  2. (B) true. The CYK algorithm decides membership in a context-free language in O(n³) time given the grammar in Chomsky normal form, and it always halts.
  3. (C) true. An LBA has finitely many configurations — at most |Q| · n · |Γ|ⁿ — so membership is decided by exploring the configuration graph and testing whether an accepting configuration is reachable. The search is finite, hence terminating.
  4. (D) false. The halting set is r.e. and not recursive; the inclusion Recursive ⊂ RE is strict.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Why (D) fails. If every r.e. language were recursive, the halting problem would be decidable, which the diagonal argument rules out. R.e. means recognisable, not decidable.

Common misconception. Believing context-sensitive membership is undecidable because the grammar is complicated. Complexity is not the issue: the configuration space of an LBA is finite, so even a crude search terminates. It may take exponential time, but decidability asks only for termination.

Takeaway. Types 1, 2 and 3 are decidable; Type 0 is not. The dividing line is the tape bound: bounded space makes the configuration graph finite.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following languages is context-sensitive but NOT context-free?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following languages is context-sensitive but NOT context-free?
options: {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1}
{w wᴿ : w ∈ {a, b}*}
{aⁿbᵐ : n ≠ m}
{aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 1}
options_html: {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1}
{w wᴿ : w ∈ {a, b}*}
{aⁿbᵐ : n ≠ m}
{aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 1}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A context-free language is recognised by a pushdown automaton, whose single stack can match one nested pair of counts. Three counts that must all agree need two independent comparisons, which one stack cannot make.

Step by step.

  1. Option (A) is context-free: S → aSb | ab generates it, and the stack counts the a's and matches them with the b's.
  2. Option (B) is context-free: guess the midpoint nondeterministically, then match the second half against the stack in reverse.
  3. Option (C) is context-free: it is the union {aⁿbᵐ : n > m} ∪ {aⁿbᵐ : n < m}, and context-free languages are closed under union.
  4. Option (D) is not context-free. By the pumping lemma, pumping any sufficiently long string of {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} produces a string that must still be in the language; but pumping changes one block while leaving the others fixed, so the three counts disagree.
  5. It is context-sensitive: the grammar with S → aSBC | aBC, CB → BC, aB → ab, bB → bb, bC → bc, cC → cc is non-contracting, so an LBA accepts the language.

Answer: Option (D) — {aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 1}.

Why the others are context-free. Each of (A), (B) and (C) can be recognised with one stack: (A) and (B) by matching symbols against the stack, (C) by a nondeterministic union of two one-stack machines.

Common misconception. Assuming {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} is context-free because it "looks like" {aⁿbⁿ}. Adding a third block that must equal the first two is exactly what one stack cannot do — the stack is popped while reading the b's, so no record of n remains to check the c's against.

Takeaway. One stack handles one nesting depth. {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} is the standard witness separating context-free from context-sensitive, exactly as {aⁿbⁿ} separates regular from context-free.

How many of these six are context-free?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A pushdown automaton has one stack, so it can enforce one "counted" equality. Languages demanding two independent equalities among three or more blocks are outside the class; languages that are a union of two one-equality conditions are inside it, because context-free languages are closed under union.

Step by step.

  1. (i) not context-free. Three blocks must agree; one stack cannot remember n while checking b's against it and also check c's. This is the standard pumping-lemma counterexample.
  2. (ii) context-free. Generated by S → aSb | ab.
  3. (iii) not context-free. Copy languages need to compare two halves without a marker at the midpoint; a PDA must guess where the middle is, and a wrong guess cannot be recovered from because the stack has been consumed. The pumping lemma confirms it.
  4. (iv) context-free. Generated by S → aSa | bSb | ε: guess the midpoint nondeterministically and match the second half against the stack in reverse. The reversal is what makes it fit one stack.
  5. (v) not context-free. Four blocks and three independent equalities — even further outside the class.
  6. (vi) context-free. It is {aⁱbʲcᵏ : i = j} ∪ {aⁱbʲcᵏ : j = k}, a union of two context-free languages, and context-free languages are closed under union.
  7. Counting: (ii), (iv) and (vi) are context-free, so the answer is 3.

Answer: 3

How the answer was checked. The three members were exhibited by grammar or construction, not merely asserted: S → aSb | ab for (ii), S → aSa | bSb | ε for (iv), and the union decomposition for (vi). The three non-members each require two independent equalities — (i) and (v) directly, (iii) through the midpoint argument — which one stack cannot supply.

Common misconception. Counting (iii) {w w} as context-free because {w wᴿ} is. The reversal in (iv) is what a stack can do; plain copying is not, since the machine would have to remember the first half in order and compare it forwards, but a stack returns symbols in reverse.

Takeaway. Context-free means "one counted comparison". Unions of such conditions stay context-free; conjunctions of two independent ones generally do not.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: In the standard formulation a Turing machine has a unique start state q₀ and two halting states, q accept and q reject , for which no transition is defined. Which one of the following statements about the behaviour of such a machine is TRUE ?
questions.question_html: In the standard formulation a Turing machine has a unique start state q₀ and two halting states, qaccept and qreject, for which no transition is defined. Which one of the following statements about the behaviour of such a machine is TRUE?
options: Entering q reject does not stop the machine; it keeps moving its head to the right until it reads a blank cell.
The computation stops as soon as q accept or q reject is entered; a computation that never enters either of them is said to loop on that input.
A machine that has entered q accept may leave it again if a transition happens to be defined there.
Every computation that loops must eventually enter q reject , because that is the state that records failure.
options_html: Entering qreject does not stop the machine; it keeps moving its head to the right until it reads a blank cell.
The computation stops as soon as qaccept or qreject is entered; a computation that never enters either of them is said to loop on that input.
A machine that has entered qaccept may leave it again if a transition happens to be defined there.
Every computation that loops must eventually enter qreject, because that is the state that records failure.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A halting state is a state in which the transition function is undefined. Reaching it ends the computation, and the outcome is read off from which halting state was reached. A computation that never reaches a halting state simply never ends: that is what “loops” means for a Turing machine.

Step by step.

  1. Both qaccept and qreject are halting states, so δ has no entry for any pair whose first component is one of them. The machine stops on entry, and accepts exactly when the state is qaccept.
  2. There is no third outcome. A machine either accepts, rejects, or runs forever; “running forever” is not a rejection, it is the absence of an answer.
  3. Option (A) is false because rejection is a halt, not a scan for a blank.
  4. Option (C) is false because qaccept is halting: nothing is defined there to take.
  5. Option (D) is false because a loop is precisely a computation that never enters a halting state.

Answer: Option (B) — entering either halting state ends the computation, and a computation that enters neither loops.

Common misconception. Reading a non-halting computation as a rejection. A machine that loops on w gives no answer at all; that is why the halting problem is not the same as the acceptance problem, and why an unbounded simulation of a machine can never be turned into a decision procedure.

Takeaway. Undefined transitions are not errors — they are the mechanism by which a Turing machine stops. Everything about decidability rests on this: a decider is a machine whose transitions are undefined only after it has produced a yes or a no.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: A universal Turing machine U takes a pair ⟨M, w⟩ and simulates the machine M on the string w . Which one of the following statements is TRUE ?
questions.question_html: A universal Turing machine U takes a pair ⟨M, w⟩ and simulates the machine M on the string w. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: U cannot exist, because a Turing machine cannot read the encoding of another machine.
U exists, and therefore the halting problem is decidable: run U on ⟨M, w⟩ and see whether it stops.
U exists only for machines that have a fixed, finite number of states, so it is not really universal.
U exists and is an ordinary Turing machine; its existence does not decide the halting problem, because U itself may run forever on inputs for which M does.
options_html: U cannot exist, because a Turing machine cannot read the encoding of another machine.
U exists, and therefore the halting problem is decidable: run U on ⟨M, w⟩ and see whether it stops.
U exists only for machines that have a fixed, finite number of states, so it is not really universal.
U exists and is an ordinary Turing machine; its existence does not decide the halting problem, because U itself may run forever on inputs for which M does.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Machines can be encoded as strings, and one machine can decode and step another. That is the universal machine. Simulation preserves the halting behaviour of the simulated machine, but it does not bound it: a simulator that faithfully follows a looping machine loops too.

Step by step.

  1. Encoding. Every tuple (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q₀, qaccept, qreject) is a finite object, so it can be written as a binary string ⟨M⟩. The pair ⟨M, w⟩ is likewise a string.
  2. Simulation. U keeps the encoding ⟨M⟩ on one part of its tape and the simulated tape on another, and repeats: read the current simulated state and symbol, look up the entry in the encoded table, update. Each simulated move costs a bounded number of moves of U.
  3. Consequence for halting. If M halts on w then U halts on ⟨M, w⟩; if M loops then U loops. So U is a recogniser for the halting problem, not a decider.
  4. Option (B) is false: a decider must halt on every input, and U does not.
  5. Option (C) is false because the encoding is just a string; nothing in the definition restricts what a machine may read.
  6. Option (D) is false because U is a single fixed machine, and its own state set is finite whatever the simulated machine is.

Answer: Option (D) — a universal machine exists and simulates any other, but simulating is not deciding.

Common misconception. The most common error is to conclude that universality solves the halting problem. A simulator inherits the loop of the machine it simulates, so “run U and watch” is exactly the semi-decision procedure that is known to be incomplete.

Takeaway. Universality is the reason one machine can run another program, and it is also the reason the diagonal argument works: a machine that could decide halting would decide it for U itself, and that leads straight to a contradiction.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following is an equivalent characterisation of the class of recursively enumerable languages over a finite alphabet Σ ?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following is an equivalent characterisation of the class of recursively enumerable languages over a finite alphabet Σ?
options: Exactly the languages that are the range of some total computable function f : Σ* → Σ* .
Exactly the finite languages.
Exactly the languages whose complement is recursive.
Exactly the languages that are the domain of some Turing machine that halts on every input.
options_html: Exactly the languages that are the range of some total computable function f : Σ* → Σ*.
Exactly the finite languages.
Exactly the languages whose complement is recursive.
Exactly the languages that are the domain of some Turing machine that halts on every input.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Three descriptions of the same class: recognised by a machine that halts on members, enumerated by a printer, and equal to the range of a total computable function. The third is the least familiar and the most useful, because it removes the machine from the picture.

Step by step.

  1. Let L be the range of a total computable f. To recognise L, on input w compute f(0), f(1), f(2), … in a dovetail and accept when w appears. Every member appears at some finite index, so every member is accepted.
  2. Conversely, let M recognise L. Enumerate the pairs (i, k) in order of i + k; for each pair run M on the i-th string for k steps and print that string if M has accepted it. Define f to return the string printed at step n (or a fixed string if nothing is printed then). This f is total and its range is L.
  3. Option (B) is false: Σ* is r.e. and infinite.
  4. Option (C) is false: that describes the recursive languages, a strict subclass.
  5. Option (D) is false: the domain of a machine that halts on every input is decided by that machine, so it is recursive, not merely r.e.

Answer: Option (A) — the r.e. languages are exactly the ranges of total computable functions.

Common misconception. Confusing “domain of a machine that always halts” with “r.e.”. Requiring the machine to halt on every input builds a decider, which yields only the recursive languages; for the r.e. class the machine may be undefined outside the language.

Takeaway. Range, domain of a partial computable function, and recognition are three faces of one class. When a question phrases an r.e. set as a range, the dovetail enumeration is almost always the proof to use.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: An enumerator is a Turing machine with a printer that writes out strings, one after another. Which of the following statements are TRUE ? Select all that apply.
questions.question_html: An enumerator is a Turing machine with a printer that writes out strings, one after another. Which of the following statements are TRUE? Select all that apply.
options: A language is recursively enumerable exactly when some enumerator prints precisely its members.
An enumerator for an infinite r.e. language must print its members in increasing order of length.
If L is recursive, then some enumerator prints the members of L in lexicographic order.
An enumerator for L also decides L , because it can be asked whether a given string is eventually printed.
options_html: A language is recursively enumerable exactly when some enumerator prints precisely its members.
An enumerator for an infinite r.e. language must print its members in increasing order of length.
If L is recursive, then some enumerator prints the members of L in lexicographic order.
An enumerator for L also decides L, because it can be asked whether a given string is eventually printed.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An enumerator converts “is recognised” into “is printed”. The two are equivalent for r.e. languages, but printing is weaker than deciding: an enumerator that never prints w never tells you so.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true. From an enumerator build a recogniser: run it and accept when w is printed. From a recogniser build an enumerator by dovetailing M over all strings and all step counts, printing a string whenever some computation accepts it.
  2. (B) false. Nothing in the definition constrains the order. The standard enumerator derived from a recogniser prints in whatever order the dovetail produces, which is by i + k and not by length.
  3. (C) true. A decider for L can test strings one at a time in lexicographic order (shorter strings first, alphabetically within a length) and print those it accepts. Lexicographic order is a well-order with finitely many predecessors of each string, so the printing runs through the whole list.
  4. (D) false. An enumerator gives a semi-decision: if w ∈ L it prints w eventually, but if w ∉ L it runs forever and the question is never answered. Deciding needs a machine that halts either way.

Answer: Options (A) and (C).

Common misconception. Assuming that an enumerator decides, or that enumeration must be tidy. The order is free; what a decider additionally needs is a bound on when to stop, which an enumerator never supplies.

Takeaway. Enumerability is recognition with the input removed. That is why the two notions coincide for r.e. languages and why neither of them coincides with decidability.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Consider the four levels of the Chomsky hierarchy: Type 3 (regular), Type 2 (context-free), Type 1 (context-sensitive) and Type 0 (recursively enumerable). For how many of these four classes is the union of any two languages of the class always again a language of the same class?
questions.question_html: Consider the four levels of the Chomsky hierarchy: Type 3 (regular), Type 2 (context-free), Type 1 (context-sensitive) and Type 0 (recursively enumerable). For how many of these four classes is the union of any two languages of the class always again a language of the same class?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A class is closed under union when a machine for L₁ ∪ L₂ can be built from machines for L₁ and L₂ without leaving the class. Each level of the hierarchy has such a construction, because each level has a machine model that can guess which side to follow.

Step by step.

  1. Regular. Take the two DFAs, form the product automaton and make a state final when either coordinate is final. Closed.
  2. Context-free. Take grammars G₁ = (V₁, Σ, P₁, S₁) and G₂ with disjoint nonterminal sets, add a fresh start symbol S and the productions S → S₁ | S₂. Closed.
  3. Context-sensitive. Take the non-contracting grammars, rename nonterminals apart, add S → S₁ | S₂. Every production still satisfies |α| ≤ |β|. Closed.
  4. Recursively enumerable. Run two recognisers in parallel (dovetail) and accept when either accepts. Closed.
  5. So all four levels are closed under union: the count is 4.

Answer: 4 — all four classes are closed under union.

Common misconception. Carrying the failure of one closure property over to another. The context-free languages are not closed under intersection or complementation, and that fact is often misremembered as a failure of union closure as well.

Takeaway. Union closure is nearly universal in the hierarchy; intersection and complementation are the properties that separate the levels. When a question asks which level breaks a closure property, expect the answer to be intersection or complement, not union.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let HALT = {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on the input w} . Which one of the following statements is TRUE ?
questions.question_html: Let HALT = {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on the input w}. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: HALT is recursive but not recursively enumerable.
HALT is not recursively enumerable.
HALT is recursively enumerable but not recursive.
HALT and its complement are both recursively enumerable.
options_html: HALT is recursive but not recursively enumerable.
HALT is not recursively enumerable.
HALT is recursively enumerable but not recursive.
HALT and its complement are both recursively enumerable.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Recognising is easy and deciding is impossible. A recogniser for HALT is the universal machine; a decider would have to answer no for a machine that loops, and no finite amount of simulation can establish that a computation will never end.

Step by step.

  1. Recognisable. On input ⟨M, w⟩, simulate M on w. Accept as soon as the simulation halts. Every halting pair is accepted, so HALT is r.e.
  2. Not decidable. Suppose a decider D existed. Build N which on input ⟨M⟩ runs D on ⟨M, ⟨M⟩⟩ and then does the opposite of what M does. Then N on ⟨N⟩ halts exactly when it does not — a contradiction.
  3. Hence HALT is r.e. and not recursive.
  4. Option (D) is false: if both a set and its complement were r.e., running the two recognisers in parallel would decide the set, contradicting the previous step.

Answer: Option (C) — recursively enumerable but not recursive.

Common misconception. Believing that a long simulation is evidence of non-halting. No finite run can rule out a halt on the next step, so simulation yields a recogniser and never a decider.

Takeaway. The halting problem is the canonical r.e.-but-not-recursive set. Any question that asks for its status should be answered on the two axes separately: recognisable (yes) and decidable (no).

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Rice’s theorem speaks of non-trivial properties of the language L(M) . Which one of the following is a trivial property of L(M) , that is, a property that every recursively enumerable language has?
questions.question_html: Rice’s theorem speaks of non-trivial properties of the language L(M). Which one of the following is a trivial property of L(M), that is, a property that every recursively enumerable language has?
options: L(M) ⊆ Σ*
L(M) is finite
ε ∈ L(M)
options_html: L(M) = ∅
L(M) ⊆ Σ*
L(M) is finite
ε ∈ L(M)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A property is trivial when it holds for every r.e. language or for none. Rice’s theorem needs non-triviality, because a trivial property is decided by a machine that ignores its input and always answers the same way.

Step by step.

  1. Every language is a subset of Σ* by definition, so L(M) ⊆ Σ* holds for every machine. The property is trivial and the language of encodings satisfying it is Σ* itself, which is decidable.
  2. The other three are true of some r.e. languages and false of others, so each is non-trivial: ∅ = ∅ but Σ* ≠ ∅; {ε} is finite but Σ* is not; ε ∈ Σ* but ε ∉ ∅.
  3. By Rice’s theorem all three of those are undecidable.

Answer: Option (B) — L(M) ⊆ Σ* is true of every machine, so it is trivial.

Common misconception. Treating “trivial” as “easy to check”. Triviality is about the truth set: a property is trivial when it is satisfied by all r.e. languages or by none, not when it looks simple.

Takeaway. Rice’s theorem has two hypotheses: the property must be semantic (about L(M)) and non-trivial (neither always true nor always false). A question that offers a universally true property is testing the second hypothesis.

Every language is a subset of Σ* by definition, so L(M) ⊆ Σ* holds for every machine. The property is trivial and the language of encodings satisfying it is Σ* itself, which is decidable. The other three are true of some r.e. languages and false of others, so each is non-trivial: ∅ = ∅ but Σ* ≠ ∅ ; {ε} is finite but Σ* is not; ε ∈ Σ* but ε ∉ ∅ . By Rice’s theorem all three of those are undecidable. Answer: Option (B) — L(M) ⊆ Σ* is true of every machine, so it is trivial. Common misconception. Treating “trivial” as “easy to check”. Triviality is about the truth set: a property is trivial when it is satisfied by all r.e. languages or by none, not when it looks simple. Takeaway. Rice’s theorem has two hypotheses: the property must be semantic (about L(M) ) and non-trivial (neither always true nor always false). A question that offers a universally true property is testing the second hypothesis.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following statements is FALSE ?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following statements is FALSE?
options: Every regular language is context-sensitive.
The class of context-sensitive languages is closed under complementation.
Membership of a string in a context-free language can be decided in polynomial time in the length of the string.
Every context-sensitive language is context-free.
options_html: Every regular language is context-sensitive.
The class of context-sensitive languages is closed under complementation.
Membership of a string in a context-free language can be decided in polynomial time in the length of the string.
Every context-sensitive language is context-free.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The hierarchy is a chain of strict inclusions Regular ⊂ CFL ⊂ CSL ⊂ RE. Each level is contained in the next, so a statement that reverses one of the inclusions is the false one.

Step by step.

  1. Regular languages are accepted by DFAs, which are linear-bounded automata with no tape use, so Regular ⊆ CSL. (A) is true.
  2. Context-sensitive languages are closed under complement: this is the Immerman–Szelepcsényi theorem, proved by counting reachable configurations of the linear-bounded automaton. (B) is true.
  3. Membership in a context-free language is decided by the CYK algorithm in O(n³) time, polynomial in n. (C) is true.
  4. The inclusion CFL ⊂ CSL is strict: {aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 1} is context-sensitive and not context-free. So (D) is false.

Answer: Option (D) — context-sensitive languages strictly contain the context-free ones.

Common misconception. Reversing the direction of an inclusion. Every context-free language is context-sensitive, but the converse fails; the witness {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} needs a tape that can compare three counts, which a pushdown store cannot do.

Takeaway. Keep the chain in one direction: Regular ⊂ CFL ⊂ CSL ⊂ RE. Any option that asserts the opposite inclusion is the false one, whatever else it says.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which of the following languages are undecidable by Rice’s theorem ? Select all that apply.
questions.question_html: Which of the following languages are undecidable by Rice’s theorem? Select all that apply.
options: {⟨M⟩ : M has exactly seven states}
{⟨M⟩ : L(M) is a finite set}
{⟨M⟩ : the encoding of M contains the substring 101}
{⟨M⟩ : L(M) contains every string of length at most 5}
options_html: {⟨M⟩ : M has exactly seven states}
{⟨M⟩ : L(M) is a finite set}
{⟨M⟩ : the encoding of M contains the substring 101}
{⟨M⟩ : L(M) contains every string of length at most 5}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Rice’s theorem needs the property to be about L(M) and to be non-trivial. A property of the encoding — how many states, which symbols appear — is not a property of L(M) at all, and is usually decidable by inspection.

Step by step.

  1. (A) false. The number of states is written into the encoding. Decode and count; no simulation is needed. The property is syntactic, so Rice’s theorem does not apply, and the language is decidable.
  2. (B) true. Finiteness is a property of L(M). It is non-trivial: ∅ is finite, Σ* is not. Both are r.e. languages, so the property is neither always true nor always false, and Rice’s theorem applies.
  3. (C) false. Containing the substring 101 is a property of the encoding string. It is checked by scanning that string.
  4. (D) true. Containing all strings of length at most 5 is a property of L(M). It is non-trivial: Σ* has it, ∅ does not. Rice’s theorem applies.

Answer: Options (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Applying Rice’s theorem to the machine instead of its language. “Has seven states” and “contains 101 in its encoding” are facts about the description, and the description is a finite object that can be read directly.

Takeaway. Before invoking Rice, ask two questions: is the property about L(M), and does some r.e. language have it while another does not? If either answer is no, Rice gives nothing.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let L₁ be a recursive language, let L₂ be recursively enumerable but not recursive, and set L₃ = L̄₂ (the complement of L₂ in Σ* ) and L₄ = L₂ ∪ L₃ . How many of the four languages L₁, L₂, L₃, L₄ are recursive?
questions.question_html: Let L₁ be a recursive language, let L₂ be recursively enumerable but not recursive, and set L₃ = L̄₂ (the complement of L₂ in Σ*) and L₄ = L₂ ∪ L₃. How many of the four languages L₁, L₂, L₃, L₄ are recursive?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The class of recursive languages is closed under complement, union and intersection; the class of r.e. languages is not closed under complement. That single asymmetry settles every one of the four cases.

Step by step.

  1. L₁ is recursive by hypothesis. That is one.
  2. L₂ is r.e. and not recursive by hypothesis. That is not one.
  3. L₃ = L̄₂. If L₃ were recursive, its complement L₂ would also be recursive, because the recursive languages are closed under complement. So L₃ is not recursive. (Equivalently: L₂ r.e. and not recursive means L̄₂ is not even r.e.)
  4. L₄ = L₂ ∪ L̄₂ = Σ*, and Σ* is decided by the machine that accepts everything. That is one.
  5. The count is therefore 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 = 2.

Answer: 2 — only L₁ and L₄ are recursive.

Common misconception. Expecting the complement of a non-recursive language to be non-recursive for the same reason, or counting L₄ as non-recursive because it is built from L₂. The union of a set and its complement is the whole alphabet, which is trivially decidable.

Takeaway. A set and its complement are recursive together or not at all. The moment you see L ∪ L̄ or L ∩ L̄, evaluate it: the first is Σ* and the second is ∅, and both are decidable whatever L is.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: A grammar is context-sensitive when every production α → β satisfies |α| ≤ |β| , with the single usual exception that S → ε is allowed when S is the start symbol and does not appear on any right-hand side. Which one of the following productions is allowed in a context-sensitive grammar?
questions.question_html: A grammar is context-sensitive when every production α → β satisfies |α| ≤ |β|, with the single usual exception that S → ε is allowed when S is the start symbol and does not appear on any right-hand side. Which one of the following productions is allowed in a context-sensitive grammar?
options: ABC → AB
A → ε
AB → BA
AB → A
options_html: ABC → AB
A → ε
AB → BA
AB → A
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The condition is purely length-based: no production may shorten the sentential form. A production with two symbols on the left needs at least two on the right, and the special empty production is reserved for the start symbol.

Step by step.

  1. Option (A): |ABC| = 3 and |AB| = 2. The form shrinks, so it is not allowed.
  2. Option (B): |A| = 1 and |ε| = 0. It shrinks, and A is not declared to be the start symbol, so it is not allowed.
  3. Option (C): |AB| = 2 and |BA| = 2. The lengths are equal, so the production is allowed. It is a genuine context-sensitive production: it swaps two adjacent nonterminals, which is how a context-sensitive grammar sorts a string without ever shortening it.
  4. Option (D): |AB| = 2 and |A| = 1. It shrinks, so it is not allowed.
  5. Exactly one option satisfies |α| ≤ |β|.

Answer: Option (C) — AB → BA keeps the length at 2, so it is allowed.

Common misconception. Reading the definition as a requirement on the form of the left side, for example insisting on αAβ → αγβ with γ ≠ ε. The length condition is the operational test, and it is the one that makes the language class decidable: no derivation ever shortens the string, so only finitely many sentential forms of each length exist.

Takeaway. Context-sensitive means non-shortening. Whenever a production is offered for inspection, compare the lengths of the two sides first.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: A machine with k tapes, where k is a fixed constant, runs in time t(n) on inputs of length n . The standard simulation of this machine by a single-tape Turing machine runs in time:
questions.question_html: A machine with k tapes, where k is a fixed constant, runs in time t(n) on inputs of length n. The standard simulation of this machine by a single-tape Turing machine runs in time:
options: O(t(n))
O(t(n) log t(n))
O(t(n)²)
options_html: O(t(n))
O(t(n) log t(n))
O(t(n)²)
O(2^{t(n)})
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The single-tape simulation stores all k tapes on one tape, separated by markers, with a mark under each simulated head. Every simulated move must first bring the real head to the relevant marked cell and then bring it back, and the distance travelled is bounded by the number of tape cells that have been used, which is at most O(t(n)).

Step by step.

  1. After t(n) simulated moves no tape can hold more than t(n) + 1 non-blank cells, because the head writes at most one cell per move.
  2. A single simulated move requires a walk of length O(t(n)) along the packed tape, so it costs O(t(n)) real moves.
  3. There are t(n) simulated moves, so the total is O(t(n)) · O(t(n)) = O(t(n)²).
  4. The quadratic factor is the price of the packing, and it is the reason the single-tape model is used for definitions rather than for complexity results.
  5. Option (D) is the cost of removing nondeterminism, not of removing extra tapes.

Answer: Option (C) — O(t(n)²).

Common misconception. Assuming that extra tapes are free because a constant number of them is used. The constant hides a factor that depends on the length of the tape, and the tape length grows with the running time.

Takeaway. Multitape and single-tape machines accept the same languages and differ by a square in time. The pair (same class, polynomial difference) is what makes the model robust for computability and fragile for fine-grained complexity.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let HALT ε = {⟨M⟩ : M halts when started on the empty string} . Which one of the following statements is TRUE ?
questions.question_html: Let HALTε = {⟨M⟩ : M halts when started on the empty string}. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: HALT ε is decidable, because the input to M is fixed and very short.
HALT ε is recursively enumerable but not recursive, and HALT ≤ m HALT ε .
HALT ε is co-recursively enumerable but not recursively enumerable.
HALT ε is neither recursively enumerable nor co-recursively enumerable.
options_html: HALTε is decidable, because the input to M is fixed and very short.
HALTε is recursively enumerable but not recursive, and HALT ≤m HALTε.
HALTε is co-recursively enumerable but not recursively enumerable.
HALTε is neither recursively enumerable nor co-recursively enumerable.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Fixing the input does not bound the computation. HALTε is the halting problem with the second component frozen, and the freezing is undone by a one-line construction.

Step by step.

  1. Reduction. Given ⟨M, w⟩, build Mw which on any input erases that input, writes w on the tape and then runs M. The construction is computable and Mw halts on ε exactly when M halts on w. Hence HALT ≤m HALTε.
  2. Consequence. If HALTε were decidable then HALT would be, so HALTε is undecidable.
  3. Recognisable. Simulating M on ε accepts every machine that halts, so HALTε is r.e.
  4. Option (A) fails because a short input can drive a very long computation; length of input is not a bound on running time.
  5. Options (C) and (D) fail because the set is r.e.

Answer: Option (B) — r.e. but not recursive, with HALT ≤m HALTε.

Common misconception. Assuming that a short input makes a problem easy. Decidability depends on whether the computation can be bounded, not on the size of the input string; a machine on ε can run for any number of steps.

Takeaway. Restricting the input is a reduction, not a simplification. Every “does M do X on ε” question is a candidate for undecidability, and the way to settle it is to encode an arbitrary ⟨M, w⟩ into a machine that ignores its input.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which of the following problems are decidable ? Select all that apply.
questions.question_html: Which of the following problems are decidable? Select all that apply.
options: Given a Turing machine M and an integer n , does M halt on ε within n steps?
Given a Turing machine M , does M , started on ε , ever move its head to the left of the cell on which it started?
Given a Turing machine M , is L(M) finite?
Given a deterministic Turing machine M and a string w , does M halt on w within 2^{|w|} steps?
options_html: Given a Turing machine M and an integer n, does M halt on ε within n steps?
Given a Turing machine M, does M, started on ε, ever move its head to the left of the cell on which it started?
Given a Turing machine M, is L(M) finite?
Given a deterministic Turing machine M and a string w, does M halt on w within 2^{|w|} steps?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A bounded question is decidable because the simulation has a clock. An unbounded question about behaviour or about the language is not, and the standard reductions apply.

Step by step.

  1. (A) decidable. Simulate M on ε for at most n steps. If it has not halted by then, answer no. The simulation terminates by construction.
  2. (B) undecidable. Reduce HALT to it: given ⟨M, w⟩, build M′ that simulates M on w and, once that halts, moves its head left. Then M′ moves left exactly when M halts on w. There is no bound on when the move happens, so simulation cannot answer no.
  3. (C) undecidable. Finiteness of L(M) is a non-trivial semantic property, so Rice’s theorem applies.
  4. (D) decidable. The bound is a function of the input: simulate M on w for at most 2^{|w|} steps and answer no if it has not halted. Determinism matters only for the step count; the simulation is still finite.

Answer: Options (A) and (D).

Common misconception. Treating a bound written in terms of |w| as if it were no bound at all. A function of the input length is computable from the input, so it serves as a clock exactly like a constant does.

Takeaway. Ask where the clock comes from. If the number of steps is fixed in advance, or computable from the input, the problem is decidable by brute simulation; if it is not, expect a reduction from HALT.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: A Turing machine has |Q| = 5 states and tape alphabet Γ = {␣, 1} , so |Γ| = 2 . Count a configuration as the triple (state, head position, tape contents), where the tape contents is the string held in the first six cells of the tape, blank cells included, and the head stands on one of those six cells. How many distinct configurations of this shape are there?
questions.question_html: A Turing machine has |Q| = 5 states and tape alphabet Γ = {␣, 1}, so |Γ| = 2. Count a configuration as the triple (state, head position, tape contents), where the tape contents is the string held in the first six cells of the tape, blank cells included, and the head stands on one of those six cells. How many distinct configurations of this shape are there?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A configuration is fixed independently by three facts: the state, the head position and what each cell holds. When all three ranges are finite the count is a product, and that product is what bounds the running time of a machine whose space is bounded.

Step by step.

  1. States: |Q| = 5 choices.
  2. Head positions: 6 choices, one for each of the six cells.
  3. Tape contents: each of the 6 cells independently holds one of the 2 tape symbols, giving 2⁶ = 64 strings. The blank is a legal cell content, so blank-filled strings are counted too.
  4. Multiply the independent choices: 5 × 6 × 64 = 1920.
  5. Sanity check on the shape of the formula: with n cells it is |Q| · n · |Γ|ⁿ, which grows without bound as n grows — the tape is not bounded here, only the window that is being counted.

Answer: 1920 configurations.

Common misconception. Forgetting that a cell may be blank, which reduces the content factor to 2⁵ and gives 960. The blank is a symbol of Γ, so it is one of the 2 choices for every one of the 6 cells.

Takeaway. Bounded space plus finite control gives finitely many configurations, and the count is |Q| · (cells) · |Γ|^{cells}. That product is the engine behind the decidability of LBA acceptance and of context-sensitive membership.
