questions.question: Which one of the following statements about the class of recursively enumerable languages is TRUE ?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following statements about the class of recursively enumerable languages is TRUE?
options: It is closed under union and under intersection, but not under complementation.
It is closed under complementation.
It is closed under union but not under intersection.
It is closed under neither union nor intersection.
options_html: It is closed under union and under intersection, but not under complementation.
It is closed under complementation.
It is closed under union but not under intersection.
It is closed under neither union nor intersection.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Two recognisers combine for union by running in parallel, and for intersection by running in sequence. Complementation is the operation that fails, because recognising a set gives no way to recognise its complement.

Step by step.

  1. Union. Dovetail the recognisers for L₁ and L₂ on the input and accept if either accepts.
  2. Intersection. Run the recogniser for L₁ to acceptance, then the recogniser for L₂. Both must accept, and both halt when they do, so the composite halts on every member of the intersection.
  3. Complementation fails. HALT is r.e. while its complement is not; if the class were closed under complement, both would be r.e. and HALT would be decidable.
  4. Option (C) is false because intersection closure holds; options (B) and (D) contradict the two facts above.

Answer: Option (A) — closed under union and intersection, not under complementation.

Common misconception. Believing that intersection is the operation that breaks, because intersection “feels” stricter. For recognition, strictness is cheap: a sequential run of two recognisers still halts on members.

Takeaway. Union and intersection are easy for recognisers; complement is the hard one, and it is exactly the operation that separates r.e. from recursive.

questions.question: To prove that INF = {⟨M⟩ : L(M) is infinite} is undecidable, the standard reduction from HALT maps ⟨M, w⟩ to ⟨M′⟩ , where M′ on input x simulates M on w for exactly |x| steps and accepts x if the simulation has halted by then. Why does the bound |x| , rather than a fixed constant, matter?
questions.question_html: To prove that INF = {⟨M⟩ : L(M) is infinite} is undecidable, the standard reduction from HALT maps ⟨M, w⟩ to ⟨M′⟩, where M′ on input x simulates M on w for exactly |x| steps and accepts x if the simulation has halted by then. Why does the bound |x|, rather than a fixed constant, matter?
options: Because it guarantees that M′ halts on every input.
Because it bounds the running time of M′ by a polynomial in |x| .
Because without a bound M′ would not be a legal Turing machine.
Because with it L(M′) is infinite exactly when M halts on w , so ⟨M, w⟩ ∈ HALT ⇔ ⟨M′⟩ ∈ INF .
options_html: Because it guarantees that M′ halts on every input.
Because it bounds the running time of M′ by a polynomial in |x|.
Because without a bound M′ would not be a legal Turing machine.
Because with it L(M′) is infinite exactly when M halts on w, so ⟨M, w⟩ ∈ HALT ⇔ ⟨M′⟩ ∈ INF.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The reduction must convert a question about one machine halting into a question about another machine having an infinite language. A threshold that grows with the input is what turns “halts in t steps” into “accepts infinitely many inputs”.

Step by step.

  1. If M halts on w after t steps, then for every x with |x| ≥ t the simulation finishes inside the budget, so x is accepted. There are infinitely many such x, so L(M′) is infinite.
  2. If M does not halt on w, the simulation never finishes inside any budget, so no x is accepted and L(M′) is empty, hence finite.
  3. Therefore ⟨M, w⟩ ∈ HALT ⇔ ⟨M′⟩ ∈ INF, which is exactly a mapping reduction HALT ≤m INF. With a fixed constant bound c the accepted set would be all x or nothing, and it would no longer track halting.
  4. Option (A) is false: M′ always halts, because its simulation is bounded. Halting is not what is being tested.
  5. Options (B) and (C) are irrelevant to the correctness of the reduction.

Answer: Option (D) — the growing bound makes L(M′) infinite exactly when M halts on w.

Common misconception. Thinking the bound is there to make M′ terminate. M′ terminates for any bound; the point of |x| is that it creates a threshold, so that a single halting time t controls infinitely many inputs.

Takeaway. In reductions to INF, FIN or REG, the gadget is always the same: a budget that grows with the input. The budget is the bridge between a finite event and an infinite language.

questions.question: The language L = {w ∈ {a, b}* : w contains the same number of a’s as b’s} belongs to which of the following classes, taking the smallest class that contains it?
questions.question_html: The language L = {w ∈ {a, b}* : w contains the same number of a’s as b’s} belongs to which of the following classes, taking the smallest class that contains it?
options: The regular languages
The context-free languages, but not the regular languages
The context-sensitive languages, but not the context-free languages
None of the four Chomsky classes
options_html: The regular languages
The context-free languages, but not the regular languages
The context-sensitive languages, but not the context-free languages
None of the four Chomsky classes
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A pushdown store can count a difference but a finite automaton cannot, and a single counter suffices here. So the language sits at Type 2 and no lower.

Step by step.

  1. Context-free. Use the grammar S → aSb | bSa | SS | ε. Each production adds one a and one b together, or nests a balanced block inside another, so every generated string has equal counts.
  2. Not regular. Intersect with a*b*, which is regular. The result is {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0}, which is not regular by the pumping lemma. Regular languages are closed under intersection with a regular language, so L cannot be regular.
  3. Since L is context-free, it is also context-sensitive and r.e., so options (C) and (D) are wrong: (C) claims it is not context-free and (D) claims it is in none of the classes.

Answer: Option (B) — context-free but not regular.

Common misconception. Confusing this language with {aⁿbⁿ} or assuming that any counting language must be context-sensitive. Equal counts of two symbols need one counter; equal counts of three symbols need two, and that is where context-freeness ends.

Takeaway. For a two-letter alphabet, “equal counts” is context-free: one stack holds the running difference. For three letters, the same idea needs a second stack, and the language becomes context-sensitive only.

questions.question: Consider Rice’s theorem and the properties of Turing machines listed below. Which of the following statements are TRUE ? Select all that apply.
questions.question_html: Consider Rice’s theorem and the properties of Turing machines listed below. Which of the following statements are TRUE? Select all that apply.
options: Rice’s theorem shows that {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = Σ*} is undecidable.
Rice’s theorem applies to the property “ L(M) contains the string 0101”.
Rice’s theorem applies to the property “ M has an odd number of states”.
Rice’s theorem shows that {⟨M⟩ : M uses more than 100 tape cells on some input} is undecidable.
options_html: Rice’s theorem shows that {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = Σ*} is undecidable.
Rice’s theorem applies to the property “L(M) contains the string 0101”.
Rice’s theorem applies to the property “M has an odd number of states”.
Rice’s theorem shows that {⟨M⟩ : M uses more than 100 tape cells on some input} is undecidable.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Rice’s theorem is about the set of strings a machine accepts, never about how the machine is built or how much space it uses. Semantic and non-trivial are the two conditions; everything else is outside the theorem.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true. “L(M) = Σ*” is a property of L(M). It is non-trivial: Σ* has it and ∅ does not. Rice applies, so the set is undecidable.
  2. (B) true. Containing a particular string is a property of L(M), and it is non-trivial: Σ* contains 0101 and ∅ does not. Rice applies.
  3. (C) false. The number of states is read off the encoding; it is a syntactic property, so Rice’s theorem says nothing about it, and the language is in fact decidable.
  4. (D) false. Space usage is a property of the machine’s behaviour, not of L(M): two machines accepting the same language can use very different amounts of tape. Rice does not apply. (The problem is undecidable, but for other reasons.)

Answer: Options (A) and (B).

Common misconception. Assuming that any undecidable problem about machines is undecidable “by Rice’s theorem”. Many are — space usage, for instance — but the theorem covers only properties of L(M).

Takeaway. Two tests, both required: is the property a fact about L(M), and is it true of some r.e. language while false of another? Rice’s theorem is a one-line proof when both answers are yes, and silent otherwise.

questions.question: How many of the following five languages are recursively enumerable? (i) {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = ∅} (ii) {⟨M⟩ : L(M) ≠ ∅} (iii) {⟨M⟩ : M halts on ε} (iv) {⟨M⟩ : M does not halt on ε} (v) {⟨M⟩ : M halts on ε within 10 steps}
questions.question_html:
How many of the following five languages are recursively enumerable?
(i) {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = ∅} (ii) {⟨M⟩ : L(M) ≠ ∅} (iii) {⟨M⟩ : M halts on ε} (iv) {⟨M⟩ : M does not halt on ε} (v) {⟨M⟩ : M halts on ε within 10 steps}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A language is r.e. when membership can be confirmed by a finite computation. A question whose yes-answer requires proving that something never happens is generally not r.e., even when it is decidable in a bounded form.

Step by step.

  1. (i) not r.e. “L(M) = ∅” is the complement of the r.e. set {⟨M⟩ : L(M) ≠ ∅}, and it is not itself r.e. Confirming emptiness would require showing that no input is ever accepted, which is an infinite check.
  2. (ii) r.e. Dovetail M over all inputs; accept as soon as some computation accepts.
  3. (iii) r.e. Simulate M on ε and accept when it halts.
  4. (iv) not r.e. This is the complement of (iii), and (iii) is r.e. without being recursive, so its complement is not r.e.
  5. (v) r.e. It is in fact recursive: simulate for 10 steps and answer. Every recursive language is r.e.
  6. Count: (ii), (iii) and (v) — three languages.

Answer: 3 — languages (ii), (iii) and (v) are recursively enumerable.

Common misconception. Counting only the obviously semi-decidable ones and forgetting that recursive languages are r.e. as well. A bounded question is decidable, hence r.e., and must be included in the count.

Takeaway. Sort the five into three piles: recursive (bounded questions), r.e. but not recursive (unbounded positive questions), and neither (unbounded negative questions). Only the first two piles are r.e.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let K = {⟨M⟩ : M halts on the input ⟨M⟩} , and let ≤ m denote mapping reducibility. Which one of the following statements is TRUE ?
questions.question_html: Let K = {⟨M⟩ : M halts on the input ⟨M⟩}, and let ≤m denote mapping reducibility. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: Every recursively enumerable language L satisfies L ≤ m K .
K ≤ m L for every recursively enumerable language L .
K is recursive.
The complement K̄ is recursively enumerable.
options_html: Every recursively enumerable language L satisfies L ≤m K.
K ≤m L for every recursively enumerable language L.
K is recursive.
The complement K̄ is recursively enumerable.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. K is the halting problem with both arguments collapsed into one, and it is complete for the r.e. languages: every r.e. set reduces to it. That is what makes it the standard vehicle for undecidability proofs.

Step by step.

  1. K is r.e.: simulate M on ⟨M⟩ and accept when it halts.
  2. Let L be r.e., recognised by ML. Define f(w) = ⟨Mw⟩ where Mw on input x ignores x and runs ML on w. Then Mw halts on ⟨Mw⟩ exactly when w ∈ L, so w ∈ L ⇔ f(w) ∈ K.
  3. Hence L ≤m K for every r.e. L. Option (A) holds.
  4. Option (B) fails: reducing K to an arbitrary r.e. set would make every r.e. set as hard as K, which is false for ∅.
  5. Option (C) fails because a decider for K would decide the halting problem.
  6. Option (D) fails because K is r.e. and undecidable, so K̄ is not r.e.

Answer: Option (A) — K is complete for the recursively enumerable languages.

Common misconception. Assuming reducibility is symmetric. Mapping reductions form a preorder, not an equivalence: hard sets absorb everything below them, and reducing a hard set to an easy one is impossible.

Takeaway. One complete set is enough for every undecidability proof. To show an r.e. set L undecidable, reduce K (or HALT) to it; to show it is r.e., exhibit a recogniser.

questions.question: Let A = {⟨M⟩ : M halts on ε} and B = {⟨M⟩ : M halts on every input} . Which one of the following statements is TRUE ?
questions.question_html: Let A = {⟨M⟩ : M halts on ε} and B = {⟨M⟩ : M halts on every input}. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: A ≤ m B , and both A and B are recursively enumerable.
Both A and B are recursive.
B ≤ m A ; A is recursively enumerable and B is not.
Neither A nor B is recursively enumerable.
options_html: A ≤m B, and both A and B are recursively enumerable.
Both A and B are recursive.
B ≤m A; A is recursively enumerable and B is not.
Neither A nor B is recursively enumerable.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Halting on one input is a positive existential question and is semi-decidable. Halting on every input is a universal question, and universality is what pushes a set out of the r.e. class.

Step by step.

  1. A is r.e. Simulate M on ε; accept when it halts.
  2. B ≤m A. Given ⟨M⟩, build M′ which on input x dovetails M over all inputs in order of i + k, halting when every input has been seen to halt. Then M′ halts on ε exactly when M halts on every input, so ⟨M⟩ ∈ B ⇔ ⟨M′⟩ ∈ A.
  3. B is not r.e. If it were, then since B ≤m A and A is r.e. we would have B decidable together with its complement; but B̄ is r.e. (halt on some input is confirmable by simulation) and B is not decidable, so B cannot be r.e.
  4. Option (A) fails because the reduction goes the other way: a machine that halts on ε tells you nothing about other inputs.
  5. Options (B) and (D) fail on the facts established above.

Answer: Option (C) — B ≤m A, with A r.e. and B not r.e.

Common misconception. Reversing the reduction because both sets are “about halting”. The direction follows the quantifier: a universal statement is stronger, so it reduces to the existential one, not the other way round.

Takeaway. Existential questions are r.e., universal questions are co-r.e., and only the decidable ones are both. When two halting sets are compared, decide first which one carries the “for all”.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the robustness of the Turing-machine model are TRUE ? Select all that apply.
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about the robustness of the Turing-machine model are TRUE? Select all that apply.
options: A machine with k tapes can be simulated by a single-tape machine with only a quadratic slowdown.
A machine whose tape is infinite in both directions can be simulated by one whose tape is infinite in one direction with no asymptotic slowdown.
A nondeterministic Turing machine can be simulated by a deterministic Turing machine, so both accept exactly the recursively enumerable languages.
A Turing machine whose tape is a two-dimensional grid accepts exactly the same class of languages as the standard one.
options_html: A machine with k tapes can be simulated by a single-tape machine with only a quadratic slowdown.
A machine whose tape is infinite in both directions can be simulated by one whose tape is infinite in one direction with no asymptotic slowdown.
A nondeterministic Turing machine can be simulated by a deterministic Turing machine, so both accept exactly the recursively enumerable languages.
A Turing machine whose tape is a two-dimensional grid accepts exactly the same class of languages as the standard one.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Robustness means the accepted class survives every reasonable change of the model. Time and space may blow up, sometimes badly, but the class of languages does not move — except when the change bounds the storage.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true. Pack the k tapes onto one tape with markers and one mark per simulated head. Each simulated move costs a walk of length at most O(t(n)), so the total is O(t(n)²). Same class, quadratic time.
  2. (B) false. Folding a two-way tape onto a one-way tape is possible, but the fold marker sits at a fixed position and the head must travel to it and back on every move that changes halves. The distance grows with the number of cells in use, so the slowdown is O(n) in the worst case, not constant.
  3. (C) true. Breadth-first search over configurations removes nondeterminism. The search may take exponential time, but it terminates exactly when some branch accepts, so the accepted language is unchanged.
  4. (D) true. A two-dimensional tape is simulated by numbering the cells row by row on a one-dimensional tape; the head then has to walk to the target cell, which costs time but not expressive power.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Assuming that every simulation is asymptotically free. The multi-tape and two-way-tape constructions preserve the language but not the running time, and the two-way-tape one is the sharper trap because it looks like a mere relabelling of cells.

Takeaway. Separate the question “same languages?” from “same time?”. Almost every model variant answers yes to the first; almost none answers yes to the second.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements about closure properties in the Chomsky hierarchy is TRUE ?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following statements about closure properties in the Chomsky hierarchy is TRUE?
options: The context-free languages are not closed under complementation.
Every context-sensitive language is context-free.
The context-free languages are closed under intersection.
The context-sensitive languages are closed under complementation, while the recursively enumerable languages are not.
options_html: The context-free languages are not closed under complementation.
Every context-sensitive language is context-free.
The context-free languages are closed under intersection.
The context-sensitive languages are closed under complementation, while the recursively enumerable languages are not.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Complement closure does not follow the hierarchy in a straight line. It fails at the top and, surprisingly, holds for context-free languages; for context-sensitive languages it is a deep theorem.

Step by step.

  1. Regular. Closed: swap final and non-final states of a total DFA.
  2. Context-free. Closed. The classical proof uses the fact that L is context-free exactly when L is the homomorphic image of the intersection of a Dyck language with a regular set, and the complement of such a set can be written in the same shape.
  3. Context-sensitive. Closed by the Immerman–Szelepcsényi theorem: a linear-bounded automaton can count the configurations reachable from its start configuration, and counting is enough to decide non-reachability.
  4. Recursively enumerable. Not closed: HALT is r.e. and its complement is not.
  5. Hence (A) is false, (B) reverses a strict inclusion, (C) fails because {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} is the intersection of two context-free languages and is not context-free, and (D) is the true statement.

Answer: Option (D) — context-sensitive languages are closed under complement, recursively enumerable ones are not.

Common misconception. The two standard traps are the context-free languages, which are closed under complement, and the context-sensitive languages, which look too weak to be. Both facts contradict the intuition that “harder class, better closure”.

Takeaway. Closure properties must be learned per class, not extrapolated up or down the hierarchy. The safe anchors are: regular is closed under everything; r.e. fails on complement; context-free fails on intersection but not on complement.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: The language L = {⟨M⟩ : M halts on every input of length at most 3 within 1000 steps} is decidable: for each such input the simulation is bounded, so it always terminates. Over the alphabet Σ = {0, 1} , on how many input strings must the decider simulate M ?
questions.question_html: The language L = {⟨M⟩ : M halts on every input of length at most 3 within 1000 steps} is decidable: for each such input the simulation is bounded, so it always terminates. Over the alphabet Σ = {0, 1}, on how many input strings must the decider simulate M?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The bound is on the length of the input and on the number of steps, and both bounds together make the whole check finite. What remains is to count the strings that fall inside the length bound.

Step by step.

  1. Strings of length 0: the empty string ε, so 1 string.
  2. Strings of length 1: 0 and 1, so 2 strings.
  3. Strings of length 2: 2² = 4 strings.
  4. Strings of length 3: 2³ = 8 strings.
  5. Total 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15. Each is simulated for at most 1000 steps, so the decider runs for at most 15 × 1000 simulated steps and always halts.
  6. Note why the step bound cannot be dropped: {⟨M⟩ : M halts on every input of length at most 3} without a time bound is undecidable, because it asks for a halting answer on 15 specific strings and each of those questions is itself undecidable.

Answer: 15 input strings.

Common misconception. Summing only the strings of length exactly 3 and answering 8, or forgetting ε altogether and answering 14. The phrase “at most 3” includes length 0.

Takeaway. A decidable bounded-halting question is a finite conjunction over finitely many inputs. Count the inputs with Σ_{i=0}^{k} |Σ|ⁱ, then note that each conjunct is decidable only because the step budget is fixed.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Over Σ = {a, b}, how many states does the minimal complete DFA have that accepts the language {ε}, i.e. the empty string and nothing else?
questions.question_html: Over Σ = {a, b}, how many states does the minimal complete DFA have that accepts the language {ε}, i.e. the empty string and nothing else?
options: Infinitely many
options_html: Infinitely many
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A complete DFA must define a transition on every symbol from every state, and the start state alone decides membership of ε. Every non-empty string must therefore be sent to a state that is not final and that no string can escape from.

Step by step.

  1. Let q₀ be the start state. Since ε ∈ L, q₀ must be final.
  2. Since a ∉ L and b ∉ L, both transitions out of q₀ must lead to a non-final state; call it d (the dead state).
  3. Completeness forces transitions out of d on a and b. Once a string has left q₀ it can never return, so δ(d, a) = δ(d, b) = d.
  4. Two states suffice and neither can be dropped: q₀ is final and d is not, so they are distinguishable.

Answer: Option (B) — 2 states.

Common misconception. Answering 1 on the grounds that only one string is accepted. A single final state accepts every string, and a single non-final state accepts none; rejecting all but one string needs a second state to reject into.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: A complete DFA over Σ = {0, 1} has exactly one state, that state is final, and both transitions from it lead back to itself. The language accepted is:
questions.question_html: A complete DFA over Σ = {0, 1} has exactly one state, that state is final, and both transitions from it lead back to itself. The language accepted is:
options: Σ*
the strings of length exactly 1
options_html: {ε}
∅
Σ*
the strings of length exactly 1
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A DFA accepts a string exactly when the state reached after reading all of it is final. If the only state is final and every symbol loops, every string ends where it started.

Step by step.

  1. The run on ε stays in the start state, which is final, so ε ∈ L.
  2. Reading any symbol keeps the machine in the same state, so by induction on the length of w the run on every w ends in that state.
  3. That state is final, so w ∈ L for every w ∈ Σ*.
  4. The machine is already minimal: a single state is the fewest possible, and Σ* needs no rejection state.

Answer: Option (C) — Σ*.

Common misconception. Reading "one state" as "one symbol accepted". The number of states says nothing about the length of the strings accepted; it is the pattern of final states and loops that does.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: An NFA over Σ = {a} has a single state q₀ that is both the start state and the only final state, with δ(q₀, a) = {q₀}. The language it accepts is:
questions.question_html: An NFA over Σ = {a} has a single state q₀ that is both the start state and the only final state, with δ(q₀, a) = {q₀}. The language it accepts is:
options: a*
a⁺
options_html: {ε}
{a}
a*
a⁺
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Nondeterminism does not change the acceptance rule: a string is accepted if some run from the start state ends in a final state. Here there is only one run, and it exists for every string over {a}.

Step by step.

  1. On ε the run is empty and ends in q₀, which is final, so ε ∈ L.
  2. On aⁿ with n ≥ 1 the single run reads n symbols and returns to q₀ each time, ending final.
  3. No other strings exist over the one-letter alphabet, so L = a*.

Answer: Option (C) — a*.

Common misconception. Choosing a⁺ by assuming a non-empty string is needed. Because the start state is also final, the empty run already accepts ε; deleting the final mark from q₀ is what would turn a* into a⁺.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which regular expression denotes exactly the set of strings over Σ = {a, b} of length exactly 2?
questions.question_html: Which regular expression denotes exactly the set of strings over Σ = {a, b} of length exactly 2?
options: (a + b)(a + b)
aa + bb
(ab)*
options_html: (a + b)*
(a + b)(a + b)
aa + bb
(ab)*
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Concatenation of two factors that each denote a single symbol forces exactly two symbols; the star, not the concatenation, is what allows a variable length.

Step by step.

  1. (a + b) denotes the two one-letter strings a and b.
  2. Concatenating it with itself gives {aa, ab, ba, bb} — every string of length 2 and no other.
  3. (a + b)* adds ε and all longer strings, so it is far too big.
  4. aa + bb keeps only two of the four strings, and (ab)* gives {ε, ab, abab, …}.

Answer: Option (B) — (a + b)(a + b).

Common misconception. Writing (a + b)² as (a + b)*, or thinking that a union must be repeated. A union inside a factor gives a choice at one position; two factors give two independent choices.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: The regular expression (ab)* over Σ = {a, b} denotes:
questions.question_html: The regular expression (ab)* over Σ = {a, b} denotes:
options: all strings with equal numbers of a and b
the strings ε, ab, abab, ababab, … and nothing else
all strings of even length
all strings that end in b
options_html: all strings with equal numbers of a and b
the strings ε, ab, abab, ababab, … and nothing else
all strings of even length
all strings that end in b
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A star repeats a fixed block. Here the block is the two-letter word ab, so every member is a whole number of copies of it.

Step by step.

  1. Zero repetitions give ε.
  2. One repetition gives ab; two give abab; in general (ab)ⁿ for n ≥ 0.
  3. aabb has equal counts but is not a repetition of ab, so the first option fails.
  4. aa has even length but no b, so the third fails; bb ends in b but is not in the language, so the fourth fails.

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Reading (ab)* as "any arrangement of equal numbers of a and b". Equality of counts would need (ab + ba)*-style gymnastics at best and is in fact not regular; the block inside a star keeps the order fixed.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: A complete DFA with n states accepts the regular language L. In a pumping-lemma proof for L, the pumping constant p may always be taken as:
questions.question_html: A complete DFA with n states accepts the regular language L. In a pumping-lemma proof for L, the pumping constant p may always be taken as:
options: n
2ⁿ
n²
options_html: n
n + 1
2ⁿ
n²
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The constant in the pumping lemma is the number of states of a DFA for the language: reading p symbols visits p + 1 states, so a repeat is unavoidable and the loop can be pumped.

Step by step.

  1. Let M have n states and let w = a₁a₂…a_m ∈ L with m ≥ n.
  2. The run q₀, q₁, …, q_m has m + 1 ≥ n + 1 states, so two of q₀, …, q_n coincide.
  3. Choose i < j ≤ n with q_i = q_j, set x = a₁…a_i, y = a_{i+1}…a_j, z = a_{j+1}…a_m.
  4. Then |y| = j − i ≥ 1 and |xy| = j ≤ n, and the loop at q_i can be traversed any number of times, so xyⁱz ∈ L for every i ≥ 0.

Answer: Option (A) — p = n.

Common misconception. Believing the constant must be a tight "magic number" for the language. Any value at least as large as the number of states works; what matters is that the constant exists and is independent of the word being pumped.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which of the following languages over Σ = {a, b} have a minimal complete DFA with exactly 2 states? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following languages over Σ = {a, b} have a minimal complete DFA with exactly 2 states? (Select all that apply.)
options: Σ*
{w : |w| is even}
{w : w starts with a}
options_html: {ε}
Σ*
{w : |w| is even}
{w : w starts with a}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Count states by counting the distinctions a DFA must remember. Two states means exactly one binary distinction; the start state plus one more state, one of which is final.

Step by step.

  1. (A) {ε}. Start state final, one dead state for everything non-empty: 2 states, and they are distinguishable (ε separates them).
  2. (B) Σ*. Every string is accepted, so one final state with self-loops is complete and minimal: 1 state, not 2.
  3. (C) even length. Only the parity of the length matters: an even state (start, final) and an odd state, each flipping on every symbol. Both are reachable and distinguishable: 2 states.
  4. (D) starts with a. Three distinctions are needed — nothing read yet, first symbol was a, first symbol was b (dead) — so the minimal complete DFA has 3 states.

Answer: Options (A) and (C).

Common misconception. Assuming "starts with a" is a one-bit property because the answer is yes or no. The DFA also has to represent the third situation "the first symbol has already been read and it was not a", which cannot be merged with either of the others.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: How many states does the minimal complete DFA over Σ = {a, b} have that accepts exactly the strings of even length?
questions.question_html: How many states does the minimal complete DFA over Σ = {a, b} have that accepts exactly the strings of even length?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A DFA counts only modulo what it can store. For a length condition the relevant residue is the length modulo the period, here 2.

Step by step.

  1. State E: an even number of symbols has been read. It is the start state and it is final, because ε has even length.
  2. State O: an odd number has been read. Not final.
  3. Every symbol flips the parity: δ(E, a) = δ(E, b) = O and δ(O, a) = δ(O, b) = E. The machine is complete and both states are reachable.
  4. The two states are distinguishable by ε, so no merging is possible: the minimal complete DFA has 2 states.

Answer: 2.

Common misconception. Adding a dead state "to reject the odd strings". Rejection needs no extra state — a non-final state already rejects — and the transition back to E is essential, because an odd prefix can still grow into an even string.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: How many strings of length exactly 3 over Σ = {a, b} belong to L(a*b*)?
questions.question_html: How many strings of length exactly 3 over Σ = {a, b} belong to L(a*b*)?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. a*b* contains exactly the strings in which no a occurs after a b: some a's, then some b's, either block possibly empty.

Step by step.

  1. A word of length 3 in the language is aⁱbʲ with i + j = 3.
  2. The possible pairs are (3,0), (2,1), (1,2), (0,3).
  3. They give aaa, aab, abb, bbb — four distinct strings.
  4. The remaining four strings of length 3 — aba, baa, bab, bba — are outside the language, because each of them has an a after a b.

Answer: 4.

Common misconception. Counting a*b* as if the two stars were independent choices at each position, which would give all 2³ = 8 strings. The order is fixed: the a-block comes first.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: An NFA over Σ = {a} has states {p, q}, start state p, final state {q}, and transitions δ(p, a) = {p, q}, δ(q, a) = {q}. The language it accepts is:
questions.question_html: An NFA over Σ = {a} has states {p, q}, start state p, final state {q}, and transitions δ(p, a) = {p, q}, δ(q, a) = {q}. The language it accepts is:
options: a⁺
a*
options_html: {a}
a⁺
a*
∅
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. In an NFA a symbol may lead to several states at once, and acceptance needs only one surviving path that ends final. The nondeterministic move p → q is a guess that "the string ends after this symbol".

Step by step.

  1. ε: the only run ends in p, which is not final, so ε ∉ L.
  2. a: the run may take p → q and stop in the final state q, so a ∈ L.
  3. aⁿ for n ≥ 1: stay in p for the first n − 1 symbols, then move to q on the last one, where the self-loop keeps the run alive. So every aⁿ with n ≥ 1 is accepted.
  4. Hence L = a⁺ = a·a*.

Answer: Option (B) — a⁺.

Common misconception. Answering a* by treating the NFA like a DFA whose start state is final. Here p is not final, so the empty string is rejected; making p final is exactly what would add ε.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: How many states does the minimal complete DFA over Σ = {0, 1} have that accepts exactly those strings which contain an even number of 0's and end in 1?
questions.question_html: How many states does the minimal complete DFA over Σ = {0, 1} have that accepts exactly those strings which contain an even number of 0's and end in 1?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Two independent facts — the parity of the number of 0's and whether the last symbol was a 1 — suggest the product of two 2-state machines, so at most 4 states. The product is an upper bound; a minimal machine counts only the classes that survive, so the answer has to be checked, not multiplied.

Step by step.

  1. Candidate states: (even, last = 1), (even, last ≠ 1), (odd, last = 1), (odd, last ≠ 1). Start in (even, last ≠ 1); the only final state is (even, last = 1).
  2. Reading 0 flips the parity and clears the "last = 1" bit; reading 1 keeps the parity and sets it. So (even, last ≠ 1) and (even, last = 1) both go to (odd, last ≠ 1) on 0 and to (even, last = 1) on 1.
  3. Those two have identical transitions, but one is final and the other is not, so ε separates them: they stay apart.
  4. (odd, last ≠ 1) and (odd, last = 1) also have identical transitions — both go to (even, last ≠ 1) on 0 and to (odd, last = 1) on 1 — and neither is final. Identical transitions plus identical finality means equivalent, so they merge.
  5. Three states remain, all reachable (ε, 1, 0) and pairwise distinguishable.

Answer: Option (B) — 3 states.

Common misconception. Answering 4 by multiplying the two parities. While the count of 0's is odd the machine cannot accept at all, and it must read another 0 first — which erases whatever the "last symbol" bit was holding. The bit is therefore worthless in the two odd states, and they collapse into one.

questions.question: In the subset construction that converts an NFA N into an equivalent DFA D, which states of D are final?
questions.question_html: In the subset construction that converts an NFA N into an equivalent DFA D, which states of D are final?
options: only the singleton sets {f} where f is final in N
every subset that contains at least one final state of N
the single subset consisting of all final states of N
every subset that is contained in the set of final states of N
options_html: only the singleton sets {f} where f is final in N
every subset that contains at least one final state of N
the single subset consisting of all final states of N
every subset that is contained in the set of final states of N
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A state of D records the set of all NFA states reachable on the input read so far. The NFA accepts if any one of those states is final, so the DFA must accept exactly when its set meets the final set.

Step by step.

  1. After reading w, the DFA is in the subset S = {q : some run of N on w ends in q}.
  2. w ∈ L(N) iff some run ends in a final state, that is iff S ∩ F ≠ ∅.
  3. So the final states of D are precisely the subsets that intersect F.
  4. Singletons are not enough: the subset {p, f} with f ∈ F is a perfectly ordinary DFA state, and it accepts.

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Marking only the singleton {f} final. Because the machine tracks all live runs at once, a state such as {p, f} is final too; forgetting this is the classic way to build a DFA that rejects strings the NFA accepts.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which regular expression denotes exactly the strings over Σ = {a, b} that contain no two consecutive b's?
questions.question_html: Which regular expression denotes exactly the strings over Σ = {a, b} that contain no two consecutive b's?
options: (a + b)*bb(a + b)*
b*a*
(ab)*
options_html: (a*b)*a*
(a + b)*bb(a + b)*
b*a*
(ab)*
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A forbidden pattern is easiest to exclude by describing the string as a sequence of blocks in which the forbidden pattern cannot occur. If every b is followed by at least one a — except possibly at the very end — no two b's can be adjacent.

Step by step.

  1. Write any bb-free string as a^{i₁}b a^{i₂}b … a^{i_k}b a^{i_{k+1}}, where each block a^{i_j}b for j ≤ k is matched by one factor of (a*b) and the trailing a^{i_{k+1}} by the final a*.
  2. Conversely, every string of (a*b)*a* is a concatenation of blocks each ending in a single b, followed by a's; two b's from different blocks are separated by the next block's a's, so bb never appears.
  3. So the two descriptions agree.
  4. The others fail: (a+b)*bb(a+b)* describes the strings that do contain bb; b*a* forbids any a after a b; (ab)* omits ba, which is bb-free.

Answer: Option (A) — (a*b)*a*.

Common misconception. Reading a star as if it allowed any interleaving, so that (a*b)* is taken to be (a+b)*. It is not: every factor must end in b, which is exactly the structural fact that rules out bb.

questions.question: Which one of the following languages over Σ = {a, b} is regular, even though its definition involves counting?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following languages over Σ = {a, b} is regular, even though its definition involves counting?
options: {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0}
options_html: {w : #a(w) = #b(w)}
{aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0}
{w : #a(w) − #b(w) ≡ 0 (mod 3)}
{ww : w ∈ {a, b}*}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A DFA can count only up to a fixed modulus. "Equal counts" is a comparison of two unbounded numbers; "counts equal modulo 3" is a three-valued residue, and three values fit in three states.

Step by step.

  1. Track r = (#a − #b) mod 3, which lies in {0, 1, 2}. Reading a does r ↦ (r + 1) mod 3; reading b does r ↦ (r − 1) mod 3.
  2. Start at r = 0, which is also the only final state. Three states, complete transitions, so the language is regular.
  3. {aⁿbⁿ} and {ww} need unbounded memory and fail the pumping lemma; {w : #a = #b} does too, with the same aᵖbᵖ word.
  4. Only the modular condition survives, because the modulus bounds the memory.

Answer: Option (C).

Common misconception. Assuming that any language defined by counting is non-regular. Counting modulo a fixed constant is regular; counting exactly without a bound is not.

questions.question: A language L over Σ = {0, 1} is accepted by some complete DFA with 4 states. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: A language L over Σ = {0, 1} is accepted by some complete DFA with 4 states. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The minimal complete DFA of L has at most 4 states.
Every state of the minimal complete DFA of L is reachable from its start state.
No two distinct states of the minimal complete DFA of L are equivalent.
The minimal complete DFA of L has exactly 4 states.
options_html: The minimal complete DFA of L has at most 4 states.
Every state of the minimal complete DFA of L is reachable from its start state.
No two distinct states of the minimal complete DFA of L are equivalent.
The minimal complete DFA of L has exactly 4 states.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Minimality is a lower bound on states for the language, never an upper one, and it is characterised by two conditions: no unreachable states and no equivalent pairs.

Step by step.

  1. If M with 4 states accepts L, then minimising M — deleting unreachable states, then merging equivalent ones — yields the minimal DFA of L with at most 4 states. So (A) is true.
  2. Deleting unreachable states changes nothing about the language, and a minimal DFA has none, so (B) is true.
  3. Merging equivalent states also preserves the language, and a minimal DFA has no such pair, so (C) is true.
  4. (D) is false: a 4-state DFA can be non-minimal. For instance, a 4-state machine with two unreachable states accepts the same language as a 2-state minimal DFA.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Treating "accepted by a 4-state DFA" as "needs 4 states". The bound inherited from a given machine is an upper bound; the minimal count is what the language forces, and it can be strictly smaller.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following statements about nondeterministic finite automata is FALSE?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following statements about nondeterministic finite automata is FALSE?
options: An NFA may have several transitions on the same symbol from a single state.
Every NFA has an equivalent DFA.
A string is accepted if at least one computation path from the start state ends in a final state.
A string is accepted only if every computation path from the start state ends in a final state.
options_html: An NFA may have several transitions on the same symbol from a single state.
Every NFA has an equivalent DFA.
A string is accepted if at least one computation path from the start state ends in a final state.
A string is accepted only if every computation path from the start state ends in a final state.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Nondeterministic acceptance is existential: one successful run is enough, and dead or rejecting runs are simply ignored. Requiring all runs to succeed is a universal condition, which is not what an NFA does.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true by definition of the transition relation δ : Q × Σ → 2^Q, which returns a set.
  2. (B) is true: the subset construction converts any NFA, ε-moves included, into an equivalent DFA with at most 2ⁿ states.
  3. (C) is exactly the acceptance rule.
  4. (D) is false. Take the NFA with δ(q₀, a) = {q₀, q₁} and q₁ final: the string a has one accepting run and one non-accepting run, and it is accepted.

Answer: Option (D).

Common misconception. Carrying the "all paths must work" intuition over from algorithm design. In automata theory nondeterminism means "a lucky guess suffices", which is why NFAs are no more powerful than DFAs.

questions.question: Which of the following regular expressions denote exactly the set of strings over Σ = {a, b} that end in b? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following regular expressions denote exactly the set of strings over Σ = {a, b} that end in b? (Select all that apply.)
options: (a + b)*b
b(a + b)*
options_html: (a + b)*b
(a*b*)*b
b(a + b)*
(a + b)*b(a + b)*
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. "Ends in b" is a suffix condition: an arbitrary prefix followed by one forced final symbol. Whether the prefix is written as (a + b)* or in some equivalent form is irrelevant, provided the form still denotes all of Σ*.

Step by step.

  1. (a + b)*b: every string is a prefix followed by b, so the condition holds exactly.
  2. (a*b*)* = Σ*: every string splits into a sequence of a-then-b blocks, so the star of the union of the two blocks covers everything. Hence (a*b*)*b = Σ*b, the same language.
  3. b(a + b)* forces the b to come first: it describes the strings that start with b, and it rejects ab.
  4. (a + b)*b(a + b)* allows symbols after the b: it describes the strings that contain b, and it accepts ba.

Answer: Options (A) and (B).

Common misconception. Rejecting (B) because a*b* alone is a proper subset of Σ*. The outer star repairs that: repeating the blocks in any order generates every string.

questions.question: How many states does the minimal complete DFA over Σ = {a, b} have that accepts exactly those strings which have even length and end in b?
questions.question_html: How many states does the minimal complete DFA over Σ = {a, b} have that accepts exactly those strings which have even length and end in b?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Two facts are needed at once — the parity of the length and the identity of the last symbol — so the product construction gives at most 4 states. The minimal count is the number of classes left after deleting unreachable states and merging equivalent ones.

Step by step.

  1. Candidate states (even, b), (even, ≠b), (odd, b), (odd, ≠b). Start in (even, ≠b), because the empty string has no last symbol. The only final state is (even, b).
  2. Every symbol flips the parity. Reading b sets the last-symbol bit, reading a clears it. Hence (even, b) and (even, ≠b) both go to (odd, ≠b) on a and to (odd, b) on b.
  3. Those two have identical transitions but differ in finality, so ε separates them — both survive.
  4. (odd, b) and (odd, ≠b) both go to (even, ≠b) on a and to (even, b) on b, and neither is final: identical transitions, identical finality, so they are equivalent and merge.
  5. Three states remain, reachable via ε, b, a, and pairwise distinguishable.

Answer: 3.

Common misconception. Reporting 4 because the two parities and the two possible last symbols multiply. Once the length is odd the machine must read one more symbol before it can accept, and that symbol overwrites the "last" information, so the two odd states cannot be told apart.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: For L = {w ∈ {a, b}* : w ends in ab}, how many equivalence classes does the Myhill–Nerode relation ≡_L have?
questions.question_html: For L = {w ∈ {a, b}* : w ends in ab}, how many equivalence classes does the Myhill–Nerode relation ≡_L have?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Two strings are ≡_L-equivalent when no continuation distinguishes them. The number of classes is exactly the number of states of the minimal DFA, so the question can be answered by building that DFA.

Step by step.

  1. Class 1: strings that do not currently end in a — the start class, since ε has no suffix. Appending b keeps a string here.
  2. Class 2: strings that end in a but not in ab. Appending b finishes the word; appending a stays in class 2.
  3. Class 3: strings that end in ab — the accepting class. Appending b returns to class 1, appending a goes to class 2.
  4. These three are pairwise distinguishable: ε separates class 3 from the rest, and b separates class 2 from class 1. So no two merge, and 3 is the count.

Answer: 3.

Common misconception. Counting 2, one class per "accepted / not accepted". Equivalence is about future behaviour, not present membership: class 1 and class 2 are both non-accepting but respond differently to the continuation b.

questions.question: Which of the following languages over Σ = {a, b, c} satisfies the pumping lemma for regular languages and is nevertheless not regular?
questions.question_html: Which of the following languages over Σ = {a, b, c} satisfies the pumping lemma for regular languages and is nevertheless not regular?
options: {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0}
{aⁱbʲcᵏ : i = 1 ⇒ j = k}
{aᵖ : p prime}
options_html: {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0}
{aⁱbʲcᵏ : i = 1 ⇒ j = k}
{ww : w ∈ {a, b}*}
{aᵖ : p prime}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The pumping lemma is a necessary condition only. A language that satisfies it need not be regular, so "pumps" never proves regularity; only failing it proves non-regularity.

Step by step.

  1. (B) is not regular. Intersect it with ab*c*, a regular set. The result is {abʲcʲ : j ≥ 0}, and the standard pumping argument on abᵖcᵖ shows this is not regular; regular languages are closed under intersection, so (B) cannot be regular either.
  2. (B) still pumps. Take p = 2 and any w ∈ L with |w| ≥ 2. If w does not start with a, pump the first symbol (b or c); the antecedent i = 1 stays false, so the word remains in L. If w = abʲcʲ, pump the leading a: the new word starts with aa, so again i ≠ 1 and it is in L. Every pumped word stays in L.
  3. (A), (C), (D) fail the lemma, so each is non-regular and cannot be the answer: aᵖbᵖ pumped in the a-block breaks the balance, ww with w = aᵖb cannot be pumped in the first half, and for a^q with q ≥ p prime, pumping up to q(1 + k) gives a composite length.

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Treating the pumping lemma as a characterisation of regularity. It is one-way: no conclusion follows from a language that pumps.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: How many states does the minimal complete DFA over Σ = {0, 1} have that accepts exactly those strings whose value, read as a binary number with leading zeros allowed, is divisible by 6?
questions.question_html: How many states does the minimal complete DFA over Σ = {0, 1} have that accepts exactly those strings whose value, read as a binary number with leading zeros allowed, is divisible by 6?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Divisibility by m is decided by the residue of the prefix read so far, because reading a bit b maps the value v to 2v + b. That gives m candidate states — but m is the answer only when the doubling map is injective on residues, which fails whenever m is even.

Step by step.

  1. Candidate states q₀, …, q₅ for the residues 0 … 5, with δ(q_r, b) = q_{(2r + b) mod 6}; start and only final state q₀.
  2. Collapse q₁ with q₄: 2·1 + b = 2 + b and 2·4 + b = 8 + b ≡ 2 + b (mod 6) for both bits, so the two states have identical transitions and identical finality — equivalent.
  3. Collapse q₂ with q₅ the same way: 2·2 + b = 4 + b and 2·5 + b = 10 + b ≡ 4 + b (mod 6).
  4. q₀ and q₃ also have identical transitions, but q₀ is final and q₃ is not, so ε separates them; they stay apart.
  5. Four classes remain and all are reachable: ε reaches {0}, 1 reaches {1,4}, 11 reaches {3}, 10 reaches {2,5}. They are pairwise distinguishable: ε isolates {0}, the continuation 0 separates {3} from {1,4}, and 10 separates {1,4} from {2,5}.

Answer: Option (B) — 4 states.

Common misconception. Answering 6 on autopilot — "divisible by m needs m states". That shortcut is valid when 2 is invertible modulo m, as it is for m = 5 or m = 7; for m = 6 the doubling map sends both 1 and 4 to the same place, and the surplus states merge.

questions.question: Which regular expression denotes exactly the strings over Σ = {a, b} that do not contain the substring ab?
questions.question_html: Which regular expression denotes exactly the strings over Σ = {a, b} that do not contain the substring ab?
options: b*a*
a*b*
(ba)*
options_html: b*a*
a*b*
(ba)*
(a*b)*
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The forbidden pattern ab is exactly "an a followed later by a b". Banning it means every b must precede every a, so the word is some b's followed by some a's.

Step by step.

  1. If w contains no ab, then once a b has been read no a may follow, so w = bʲaⁱ.
  2. Conversely every bʲaⁱ has all its b's before all its a's, so no a is ever followed by a b.
  3. Therefore the language is b*a*.
  4. The others fail: a*b* contains ab itself; (ba)* omits baa, which has no ab; and (a*b)* = Σ* because ab = (a*b) is a single factor, so it contains everything.

Answer: Option (A) — b*a*.

Common misconception. Choosing a*b* by pattern-matching on the letters in the order they appear in the forbidden word. The condition is about what may not follow, so the a-block has to come last, not first.

questions.question: Which of the following languages over Σ = {a, b} are regular? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following languages over Σ = {a, b} are regular? (Select all that apply.)
options: {aⁿbᵐ : n ≤ m}
{aⁿbᵐ : n + m ≡ 0 (mod 2)}
{aⁿbⁿ : n is a multiple of 3}
options_html: {aⁿbᵐ : n ≤ m}
{aⁿbᵐ : n + m ≡ 0 (mod 2)}
{w : #a(w) ≡ #b(w) (mod 2)}
{aⁿbⁿ : n is a multiple of 3}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A condition is regular when the information it needs is bounded: a residue modulo a fixed number qualifies, an unbounded comparison does not.

Step by step.

  1. (A) not regular. {aⁿbᵐ : n ≤ m} compares two unbounded counts. Intersecting with a*b* leaves the same language, and pumping aᵖbᵖ inside the a-block gives a^{p+k}bᵖ with p + k > p, outside the language.
  2. (B) regular. n + m is just the length of the word, so the condition says "even length" — two states.
  3. (C) regular. Track the parities of the two counts: four states (p_a, p_b) ∈ {0,1}², accepting exactly those with equal parities.
  4. (D) not regular. It is a sub-language of {aⁿbⁿ} cut out by a condition on n; pumping a^{3q}b^{3q} in the a-block destroys the balance, and no choice of split repairs it.

Answer: Options (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Judging (D) regular because "multiple of 3" is a modular condition. The modulus applies to n, which must be counted exactly against the number of b's; the modularity of the multiplier does not bound the memory needed.

questions.question: Let L = {w ∈ {a, b}* : #a(w) is odd and #b(w) is even}. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Let L = {w ∈ {a, b}* : #a(w) is odd and #b(w) is even}. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: L is regular.
The minimal complete DFA of L has 4 states.
The complement of L has a minimal complete DFA with 4 states.
L = {w : |w| is odd}.
options_html: L is regular.
The minimal complete DFA of L has 4 states.
The complement of L has a minimal complete DFA with 4 states.
L = {w : |w| is odd}.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Parity of two separate letter counts is a product of two 2-state machines, giving four states; complementation swaps final and non-final states without touching the transitions, so it never changes the state count of the minimal machine.

Step by step.

  1. States (p_a, p_b) ∈ {0,1}² with p_a the parity of the a-count and p_b that of the b-count; start at (0,0); accept at (1,0).
  2. All four states are reachable (ε, a, b, ab) and pairwise distinguishable: ε isolates (1,0), a separates (0,1) from (0,0), and b separates (1,1) from (1,0) after one more a. So (A) and (B) are true.
  3. For the complement, keep the same four states and declare (0,0), (0,1), (1,1) final instead. The machine is still complete, all states reachable, and every pair still distinguishable — the same witness strings work — so the minimal complement also has 4 states. (C) is true.
  4. (D) is false. bbb has odd length but an odd number of b's, so it is not in L. (In fact L forces odd length, but not every odd-length word qualifies.)

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Believing that the complement of a 4-state language must need a different number of states. Complementation is a relabelling of final states, so it preserves minimality exactly.

questions.question: Over Σ = {0, 1}, how many states does the minimal complete DFA have that accepts exactly those binary strings (leading zeros allowed) whose value is congruent to 1 or 2 modulo 7?
questions.question_html: Over Σ = {0, 1}, how many states does the minimal complete DFA have that accepts exactly those binary strings (leading zeros allowed) whose value is congruent to 1 or 2 modulo 7?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A congruence condition modulo m is decided by the residue of the value read so far, and the transition r ↦ (2r + b) mod m keeps the residue exact. The accepting states are the residues in the target set.

Step by step.

  1. States q₀, …, q₆ for residues 0 … 6; start at q₀ (the empty string denotes 0); final states q₁ and q₂.
  2. Transitions: δ(q_r, b) = q_{(2r + b) mod 7}. All 7 states are reachable, since 2 is invertible modulo the prime 7, so the map r ↦ 2r permutes the residues and appending bits walks through all of them.
  3. They are pairwise distinguishable: for r ≠ r′ the difference r − r′ is invertible modulo 7, so appending k zeros multiplies the difference by 2^k and never makes it 0; some continuation therefore lands in an accepting residue for exactly one of the two states.
  4. Hence exactly 7 states, the residue count itself.

Answer: 7.

Common misconception. Counting 2 states because "the answer is yes or no". The machine has to compute the residue before it can decide, and all seven residues are needed as intermediate memory even though only two of them accept.

questions.question: A string w ∈ L(G) has exactly two distinct derivation trees in a context-free grammar G. Which one of the following is necessarily TRUE?
questions.text: A string w ∈ L(G) has exactly two distinct derivation trees in a context-free grammar G. Which one of the following is necessarily TRUE?
options: w has exactly two distinct leftmost derivations and exactly two distinct rightmost derivations.
w has at least two leftmost derivations but possibly only one rightmost derivation.
w has exactly one leftmost derivation and exactly two rightmost derivations.
w has exactly two derivations in total.

solution.concept: Derivation trees and leftmost (or rightmost) derivations are in exact one-to-one correspondence: a tree is recovered from a leftmost derivation by forgetting the order of expansion, and a leftmost derivation is recovered from a tree by always expanding the leftmost nonterminal leaf.
steps: Each derivation tree determines exactly one leftmost derivation: expand the leftmost nonterminal at every step. Two different trees therefore give two different leftmost derivations.
The same reading works from the right, so each tree also determines exactly one rightmost derivation.
Two trees therefore give exactly two leftmost and exactly two rightmost derivations, and no more, because every leftmost derivation maps back to one of those two trees.

The total number of derivations is larger and unbounded: expanding the nonterminals in different orders gives many derivations that all correspond to the same two trees, so the total is at least 2·2 = 4.
solution.trap: Treating “derivation” and “leftmost derivation” as the same thing, or forgetting that one tree is compatible with several expansion orders. Only the leftmost (or rightmost) count is tied to the number of trees.

questions.solution_html:

Step by step.

  1. Each derivation tree determines exactly one leftmost derivation: expand the leftmost nonterminal at every step. Two different trees therefore give two different leftmost derivations.
  2. The same reading works from the right, so each tree also determines exactly one rightmost derivation.
  3. Two trees therefore give exactly two leftmost and exactly two rightmost derivations, and no more, because every leftmost derivation maps back to one of those two trees.
  4. The total number of derivations is larger and unbounded: expanding the nonterminals in different orders gives many derivations that all correspond to the same two trees, so the total is at least 2·2 = 4.

Answer: Option (A).

questions.question: Let G be the grammar S → SS | a | b. The complete derivation tree of the string aabb is drawn with one node for every symbol occurrence. How many nodes does that tree have in total, counting internal nodes and leaves together?
questions.text: Let G be the grammar S → SS | a | b. The complete derivation tree of the string aabb is drawn with one node for every symbol occurrence. How many nodes does that tree have in total, counting internal nodes and leaves together?

solution.concept: In a derivation tree the leaves spell the derived string, and every internal node is one application of a production of the form A → BC. The shape is therefore a binary tree whose leaves are exactly the symbols of the string.
steps: The yield is aabb, so the tree has exactly 4 leaves.
Every internal node of this grammar has exactly two children (the only branching production is S → SS), so the tree is a full binary tree.
A full binary tree with L leaves has exactly L − 1 internal nodes: 4 − 1 = 3.
Total nodes = internal + leaves = 3 + 4 = 7.
The grammar is ambiguous and aabb has five derivation trees, but every one of them is a full binary tree with 4 leaves, so the answer does not depend on which tree is drawn.
solution.trap: Counting only the three internal nodes, or adding the leaves twice. A full binary tree with L leaves has L − 1 internal nodes, so the total is 2L − 1 = 7 here.

  4. Total nodes = internal + leaves = 3 + 4 = 7.
  5. The grammar is ambiguous and aabb has five derivation trees, but every one of them is a full binary tree with 4 leaves, so the answer does not depend on which tree is drawn.

questions.question: Let G = (V, T, P, S) be a context-free grammar. Which one of the following is NOT true of every derivation tree of G?
questions.text: Let G = (V, T, P, S) be a context-free grammar. Which one of the following is NOT true of every derivation tree of G?
options: The root is labelled S.
Every internal node is labelled by a nonterminal.
Every leaf is labelled by a terminal of T.
The children of an internal node, read from left to right, spell the right side of some production whose left side is that node’s label.

solution.concept: A derivation tree is built by applying productions: a node labelled A gets children spelling the right side of a production A → α. Leaves are symbols that were never expanded.
steps: The root is always the start symbol S — that is the definition of a derivation tree for a string of L(G).
An internal node is a symbol that was expanded, and only nonterminals have productions, so every internal node carries a nonterminal.

A leaf is a symbol that was never expanded. Terminals can never be expanded, but neither can a nonterminal that was replaced by ε: in the tree for a derivation that uses A → ε, the node labelled A has a single child labelled ε, and ε is not a terminal of T.
The children of a node are written by applying one production, so their labels in order are the right side of a production for that label.
solution.final: Option (C) is the statement that can fail, so (C) is the answer.
solution.trap: Assuming every leaf is a terminal. Leaves labelled ε appear exactly when an ε-production is used, which is why ε-free grammars are the ones where “leaves = symbols of w” is safe.

Step by step.

  2. An internal node is a symbol that was expanded, and only nonterminals have productions, so every internal node carries a nonterminal.
  3. A leaf is a symbol that was never expanded. Terminals can never be expanded, but neither can a nonterminal that was replaced by ε: in the tree for a derivation that uses A → ε, the node labelled A has a single child labelled ε, and ε is not a terminal of T.
  4. The children of a node are written by applying one production, so their labels in order are the right side of a production for that label.

Answer: Option (C) is the statement that can fail, so (C) is the answer.

questions.question: Let G = (V, T, P, S) be a context-free grammar and let α be a string over V ∪ T. Select every statement that is TRUE.
questions.text: Let G = (V, T, P, S) be a context-free grammar and let α be a string over V ∪ T. Select every statement that is TRUE.
options: If S ⇒* α, then α is the frontier of some partial derivation tree whose root is S.
The frontier of every partial derivation tree rooted at S is a sentential form of G.
If a subtree of a derivation tree has root A and frontier β, then A ⇒* β.
In the frontier of any partial derivation tree, every terminal lies to the left of every nonterminal.

solution.concept: A partial derivation tree stops expanding some leaves; its frontier is read left to right. Frontier and derivability are two views of the same relation: A ⇒* β exactly when β is the frontier of a tree rooted at A.
steps: (A) true: take the derivation S ⇒* α and draw the tree for each step; stopping after the last step gives a partial tree with frontier α.
(B) true: the root is S, and the sequence of productions read off the tree is a valid derivation, so the frontier is reachable from S.
(C) true: read the productions of that subtree from the root downwards; they form a derivation of β from A.
(D) false: in S → aSb the sentential form aSb has the terminal a to the left of the nonterminal S and the terminal b to its right.
solution.trap: Believing a frontier must be “all terminals” or “terminals first”. A frontier mixes terminals and nonterminals in whatever order the productions produced them.

questions.question: Let G have the productions S → AB, A → aA | a and B → bB | ε. Which one of the following is L(G)?
questions.text: Let G have the productions S → AB, A → aA | a and B → bB | ε. Which one of the following is L(G)?
options: { ambn : m ≥ 0, n ≥ 0 }
{ ambn : m ≥ 1, n ≥ 1 }
{ ambn : m ≥ 0, n ≥ 1 }
{ ambn : m ≥ 1, n ≥ 0 }

solution.concept: The language of a grammar is read off the reachable derivations of each nonterminal. Here A produces one or more a, B produces zero or more b, and S concatenates the two blocks.
steps: A has the derivations A ⇒ a, A ⇒ aA ⇒ aa, …, so A generates am for every m ≥ 1, and nothing else.
B has the derivations B ⇒ ε, B ⇒ bB ⇒ b, …, so B generates bn for every n ≥ 0, and nothing else.

The empty string is not in L(G), because A cannot vanish.
solution.trap: Forgetting that A cannot produce ε, which wrongly admits strings with no a at all, or forgetting that B may produce ε, which wrongly forces at least one b.

solution.concept: Each application of a production adds one level to the tree: the node being expanded becomes internal and its right side becomes its children. In this grammar every production emits exactly one terminal, so the number of internal nodes equals the number of symbols in the derived string.
steps: Every production of G adds exactly one terminal symbol and keeps exactly one nonterminal (aS and Sb) or none (c).

solution.concept: Two derivations give different trees exactly when they use different productions at some node. For this grammar every tree for a string with equal numbers of a and b splits that string into balanced blocks, and the count is a small dynamic-programming table over substrings.
steps: aabb has equal numbers of a and b, so it can be derived at all.
Consider the root. If the root uses S → aSb, the string must begin with a and end with b, which fails because aabb ends with b. The same argument rules out S → bSa.
If the root uses S → SS, the split aabb = a·abb is the only one where both halves are derivable: a and abb. The other candidate splits (aa, bb) leave halves with unequal numbers of a and b.
The substring abb itself has a unique tree, again forced to split as a·bb, and each of a and bb has exactly one tree.
So exactly one tree exists, even though the grammar is ambiguous in general — for abab it has two trees.
solution.trap: Concluding “ambiguous grammar, so more than one tree”. Ambiguity is a property of the grammar, not of each individual string: this grammar is ambiguous, yet aabb has a single parse.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: Every regular language has an unambiguous context-free grammar.
Every context-free language has an unambiguous grammar.
A language that has an ambiguous grammar cannot be context-free.
Every ambiguous grammar generates an infinite language.

solution.concept: Ambiguity is a property of a grammar; a language is called unambiguous when some grammar for it is unambiguous, and inherently ambiguous when no such grammar exists.
steps: (A) true: take a DFA for the regular language and convert it to a right-linear grammar with one nonterminal per state. Each string labels exactly one accepting path, so each string has exactly one derivation.
(B) false: inherently ambiguous context-free languages exist, for example { aibjck : i = j or j = k }.
(C) false: an ambiguous grammar is still a grammar, and it generates a context-free language.
(D) false: S → S | a generates the finite language {a} and is ambiguous for it.
solution.trap: Reading “some grammar for L is ambiguous” as “L is ambiguous”. Every nonempty language with a context-free grammar also has silly ambiguous grammars; the question is whether an unambiguous one exists.

  3. (C) false: an ambiguous grammar is still a grammar, and it generates a context-free language.
  4. (D) false: S → S | a generates the finite language {a} and is ambiguous for it.

questions.question: Which one of the following grammars is unambiguous?
questions.text: Which one of the following grammars is unambiguous?
options: S → SS | a
S → aSb | ab
S → aS | Sa | a
S → S + S | a

solution.concept: A grammar is unambiguous when every string in its language has exactly one derivation tree. Grammars that offer two independent ways to build the same string — splitting it, or adding symbols on the left or the right — are usually ambiguous.
steps: (A) is ambiguous: aaa has the two trees S ⇒ SS ⇒ aS ⇒ aSS … and S ⇒ SS ⇒ SSa ….

(B) is unambiguous: every string it generates is anbn, n ≥ 1, and the only possible first step is S → aSb or S → ab. For anbn the first step must be S → aSb (the string is longer than ab), which forces the outermost pair of symbols and leaves a shorter string of the same shape; induction on the length gives exactly one tree.
(C) is ambiguous: aa has one tree from aS followed by Sa and another from Sa followed by aS.
(D) is ambiguous: a + a + a has two trees, one adding before the other.
solution.trap: Judging ambiguity by how complicated the grammar looks. S → aSb | ab looks recursive but is unambiguous, while S → SS | a looks simple but is ambiguous.

questions.question: Select every statement about context-free grammars that is TRUE.
questions.text: Select every statement about context-free grammars that is TRUE.
options: If G is ambiguous, L(G) may still have an unambiguous grammar.
An unambiguous grammar can have two distinct derivations of the same string.
If every string in L(G) has exactly one derivation tree, then G is unambiguous.
Ambiguity of a context-free grammar is decidable in polynomial time.

solution.concept: A grammar is ambiguous when some string of its language has two distinct derivation trees. Derivations themselves are not unique in an unambiguous grammar: only the tree is.
steps: (A) true: a language can be generated by an ambiguous grammar and also by an unambiguous one, for example anbn with S → aS | Sb | ab is ambiguous, while S → aSb | ab is unambiguous and generates the same language.
(B) true: the leftmost and the rightmost derivation of a string with two or more symbols differ as sequences of sentential forms even though they describe the same tree.
(C) true: that is exactly the definition of unambiguity, stated string by string.
(D) false: deciding ambiguity of a context-free grammar is undecidable in general; only for restricted classes (such as deterministic grammars, or bounded lookahead) is it decidable.
solution.trap: Confusing “unique derivation” with “unique derivation tree”. Only the second is the definition of unambiguity.

  2. (B) true: the leftmost and the rightmost derivation of a string with two or more symbols differ as sequences of sentential forms even though they describe the same tree.
  3. (C) true: that is exactly the definition of unambiguity, stated string by string.
  4. (D) false: deciding ambiguity of a context-free grammar is undecidable in general; only for restricted classes (such as deterministic grammars, or bounded lookahead) is it decidable.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Confusing “unique derivation” with “unique derivation tree”. Only the second is the definition of unambiguity.

questions.question: Let G be the grammar S → SS | a | b. How many distinct derivation trees does G have for the string aab?
questions.text: Let G be the grammar S → SS | a | b. How many distinct derivation trees does G have for the string aab?

solution.concept: With a single branching production S → SS, a derivation tree is a full binary tree whose leaves spell the string, and the number of such trees is counted by splitting the string into a nonempty prefix and a nonempty suffix.
steps: The root must use S → SS, because aab has three symbols and no other production of G produces more than one symbol.
The two possible splits into nonempty parts are a·ab and aa·b.
For a·ab the right part ab has the single tree S ⇒ SS ⇒ ab, so this split gives one tree.
For aa·b the left part aa has the single tree S ⇒ SS ⇒ aa, so this split gives one tree.
Total: 1 + 1 = 2 trees, so the grammar is ambiguous for aab.
solution.trap: Answering 1 by assuming the grammar is unambiguous because it is so small, or answering 3 by allowing the empty split ε·aab.

questions.question: Let L = { aibjck : i = j or j = k, i, j, k ≥ 1 }, with L. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.text: Let L = { aibjck : i = j or j = k, i, j, k ≥ 1 }, with L. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: L is not context-free.
L is context-free and has an unambiguous grammar.
L is context-free, and every grammar for L is ambiguous.
L is regular.

solution.concept: L is the union of the two context-free languages {aibick} and {aibjcj}, so it is context-free. It is the standard example of an inherently ambiguous context-free language: the two conditions i = j and j = k pull in different directions, and any grammar must sometimes delay the decision past the point where the information needed to make it is still available.
steps: Closure under union gives that L is context-free: S → S1 | S2 with S1 → aS1c | X, X → aXb | ab generates the first part and S2 → aS2 | Y, Y → bYc | bc generates the second.
L is not regular, since intersecting it with a*b*c* gives {anbncn}, which is not regular.

For a string anbncn with i = j = k the two reasons coincide, and the classic pumping argument shows that no single grammar can decide early enough which of the two equalities holds without also being able to count all three blocks; the language is therefore inherently ambiguous.
So L is context-free and every grammar for it is ambiguous.
solution.trap: Concluding “not context-free” because {anbncn} is not, or “unambiguous” because each of the two parts is a deterministic language. Union of two unambiguous languages need not be unambiguous.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Step by step.

  1. Closure under union gives that L is context-free: S → S1 | S2 with S1 → aS1c | X, X → aXb | ab generates the first part and S2 → aS2 | Y, Y → bYc | bc generates the second.
  2. L is not regular, since intersecting it with a*b*c* gives {anbncn}, which is not regular.
  3. For a string anbncn with i = j = k the two reasons coincide, and the classic pumping argument shows that no single grammar can decide early enough which of the two equalities holds without also being able to count all three blocks; the language is therefore inherently ambiguous.
  4. So L is context-free and every grammar for it is ambiguous.

Answer: Option (C).

Common misconception. Concluding “not context-free” because {anbncn} is not, or “unambiguous” because each of the two parts is a deterministic language. Union of two unambiguous languages need not be unambiguous.

questions.question: Select every statement that is TRUE.
questions.text: Select every statement that is TRUE.
options: Every deterministic context-free language has an unambiguous grammar.
The union of two unambiguous context-free languages can be inherently ambiguous.
It is decidable whether a given context-free grammar is ambiguous.
If every string of L(G) has exactly one rightmost derivation, then G is unambiguous.

solution.concept: Unambiguity is preserved by determinism (a DPDA makes one choice at every step), but not by union, and ambiguity of an arbitrary grammar is undecidable.
steps: (A) true: run the deterministic pushdown automaton on a string. Its run is unique, so the string has one leftmost derivation, hence one tree.
(B) true: {aibick} and {aibjcj} are unambiguous, but their union is inherently ambiguous, so no grammar for the union is unambiguous.
(C) false: ambiguity of context-free grammars is undecidable — it is one of the standard consequences of the Post correspondence problem.
(D) true: rightmost derivations and trees are in one-to-one correspondence, so a unique rightmost derivation per string means a unique tree per string.
solution.trap: Assuming decidability because the definition of ambiguity is a simple statement about trees. Deciding whether two different trees exist for some string is exactly the hard part.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution
