Step by step.

  1. (A) true: run the deterministic pushdown automaton on a string. Its run is unique, so the string has one leftmost derivation, hence one tree.
  2. (B) true: {aibick} and {aibjcj} are unambiguous, but their union is inherently ambiguous, so no grammar for the union is unambiguous.
  3. (C) false: ambiguity of context-free grammars is undecidable — it is one of the standard consequences of the Post correspondence problem.
  4. (D) true: rightmost derivations and trees are in one-to-one correspondence, so a unique rightmost derivation per string means a unique tree per string.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

questions.question: A grammar is in Greibach Normal Form when every production has the form A → aα with a ∈ T and α ∈ V*. Which one of the following productions violates that form?
questions.text: A grammar is in Greibach Normal Form when every production has the form A → aα with a ∈ T and α ∈ V*. Which one of the following productions violates that form?
options: A → aBC
A → a
A → Ba
A → aB

solution.concept: Greibach Normal Form makes every production start with exactly one terminal. That single property is what forces every derivation of a string of length n to take exactly n steps.
steps: A → aBC: the right side starts with the terminal a and the rest is a string of nonterminals, so it is allowed.
A → a: a terminal followed by the empty string of nonterminals, allowed.
A → Ba: the right side starts with the nonterminal B, so it violates the form.
A → aB: a terminal followed by one nonterminal, allowed.
solution.trap: Thinking GNF forbids terminals anywhere but first, or forbids nonterminals entirely. Terminals may appear only in the first position; nonterminals may appear only after it.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Step by step.

  1. A → aBC: the right side starts with the terminal a and the rest is a string of nonterminals, so it is allowed.
  2. A → a: a terminal followed by the empty string of nonterminals, allowed.
  3. A → Ba: the right side starts with the nonterminal B, so it violates the form.
  4. A → aB: a terminal followed by one nonterminal, allowed.

Answer: Option (C).

Common misconception. Thinking GNF forbids terminals anywhere but first, or forbids nonterminals entirely. Terminals may appear only in the first position; nonterminals may appear only after it.

questions.question: The grammar S → aSb | ε is converted to Chomsky Normal Form by the standard construction: first new nonterminals are introduced for the terminals, then every right side longer than two symbols is split. How many new nonterminal symbols does the construction introduce?
questions.text: The grammar S → aSb | ε is converted to Chomsky Normal Form by the standard construction: first new nonterminals are introduced for the terminals, then every right side longer than two symbols is split. How many new nonterminal symbols does the construction introduce?

solution.concept: CNF allows only A → BC and A → a. A terminal may not appear next to another symbol, so each terminal used inside a longer right side needs its own nonterminal; a right side of length three then needs one more nonterminal to split it.
steps: The production S → aSb has terminals inside a right side of length 3, so introduce A → a and B → b.
Now S → aSb becomes S → ASB, still too long, so introduce one more nonterminal X and write S → AX and X → SB.
The count is therefore 2 for the terminals. The third symbol X above is required by the splitting step, not by the terminal step, and the question asks only for the terminals.
The ε-production S → ε is kept as it is, which introduces nothing.
solution.trap: Answering 3 by counting the splitting nonterminal X as well, or answering 1 by forgetting that both a and b occur inside a long right side and each needs its own nonterminal.

  2. Now S → aSb becomes S → ASB, still too long, so introduce one more nonterminal X and write S → AX and X → SB.
  3. The count is therefore 2 for the terminals. The third symbol X above is required by the splitting step, not by the terminal step, and the question asks only for the terminals.
  4. The ε-production S → ε is kept as it is, which introduces nothing.

questions.question: Which one of the following is TRUE of every grammar in Chomsky Normal Form?
questions.text: Which one of the following is TRUE of every grammar in Chomsky Normal Form?
options: It cannot generate ε.
Every derivation tree of it is a full binary tree.
Every production has exactly two nonterminals on its right side.
Every production has at most two symbols on its right side.

solution.concept: CNF admits exactly two shapes: A → BC (two nonterminals) and A → a (one terminal), with the single exception S → ε when the language contains the empty string.
steps: (A) false: S → ε is permitted when ε ∈ L(G), so a CNF grammar can generate ε.

(C) false: A → a has one symbol on the right.
(D) true: every right side is either one terminal or two nonterminals, so at most two symbols.
solution.trap: Believing CNF forbids ε-productions absolutely, or that every internal node has two children. Only branching nodes have two; terminal productions have one.

  2. (B) false: a node expanded by A → a has a single child, so the tree is not full.
  3. (C) false: A → a has one symbol on the right.
  4. (D) true: every right side is either one terminal or two nonterminals, so at most two symbols.

options: Every context-free language that does not contain ε has a grammar in Chomsky Normal Form.
Every grammar in Greibach Normal Form is free of left recursion.
In a CNF grammar, every derivation of a string of length n ≥ 1 uses exactly 2n − 1 production steps.
Eliminating ε-productions can change the language generated by the grammar.

solution.concept: The normal-form theorems say that CNF and GNF exist for every ε-free context-free language, and the step counts follow from the shapes of the productions.
steps: (A) true: that is the Chomsky Normal Form theorem; only ε needs the extra production S → ε.
(B) true: a left-recursive production A → Aα has a nonterminal in first position, which GNF forbids.
(C) true: with n leaves the tree has n − 1 branching nodes, each one step, plus n terminal steps, so (n − 1) + n = 2n − 1 steps.
(D) false: the ε-elimination procedure is language preserving — it only removes productions whose use can be simulated by deleting occurrences.
solution.trap: Believing the conversion steps are heuristic rewrites that may change the language. Each of the four simplification steps (useless symbols, ε-productions, unit productions, long right sides) preserves the generated language exactly.

  2. (B) true: a left-recursive production A → Aα has a nonterminal in first position, which GNF forbids.
  3. (C) true: with n leaves the tree has n − 1 branching nodes, each one step, plus n terminal steps, so (n − 1) + n = 2n − 1 steps.
  4. (D) false: the ε-elimination procedure is language preserving — it only removes productions whose use can be simulated by deleting occurrences.

questions.question: The grammar S → aSb | ab is converted to Chomsky Normal Form by the standard construction. How many productions does the resulting CNF grammar have?
questions.text: The grammar S → aSb | ab is converted to Chomsky Normal Form by the standard construction. How many productions does the resulting CNF grammar have?

solution.concept: The construction keeps one production per original right side, adds one production per terminal that appears inside a longer right side, and adds one production for every split of a right side longer than two symbols.
steps: Introduce A → a and B → b for the two terminals: 2 productions.
Rewrite S → aSb as S → ASB, which has three symbols and must be split, for example S → AX and X → SB: 2 more productions.
Rewrite S → ab as S → AB: 1 more production.
Total 2 + 2 + 1 = 5 productions: A → a, B → b, S → AX, X → SB, S → AB.
The grammar is in CNF and generates the same language anbn, n ≥ 1.
solution.trap: Forgetting the two terminal productions and answering 3, or forgetting that S → aSb cannot stay as it is because a terminal may not sit beside another symbol.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The construction keeps one production per original right side, adds one production per terminal that appears inside a longer right side, and adds one production for every split of a right side longer than two symbols.

Step by step.

  1. Introduce A → a and B → b for the two terminals: 2 productions.
  2. Rewrite S → aSb as S → ASB, which has three symbols and must be split, for example S → AX and X → SB: 2 more productions.
  3. Rewrite S → ab as S → AB: 1 more production.
  4. Total 2 + 2 + 1 = 5 productions: A → a, B → b, S → AX, X → SB, S → AB.
  5. The grammar is in CNF and generates the same language anbn, n ≥ 1.

Answer: Option (B): 5.

Common misconception. Forgetting the two terminal productions and answering 3, or forgetting that S → aSb cannot stay as it is because a terminal may not sit beside another symbol.

options: Some context-free languages have no grammar in Chomsky Normal Form.
A grammar in Greibach Normal Form may contain the production A → ε.
Every grammar in Chomsky Normal Form is unambiguous.
Every context-free language that does not contain ε has a grammar in Greibach Normal Form.

solution.concept: Both normal-form theorems hold for every ε-free context-free language. Normal forms restrict the shape of productions; they say nothing about ambiguity.
steps: (A) false: every context-free language has a CNF grammar, with S → ε added exactly when ε ∈ L.
(B) false: GNF requires a terminal in first position, so A → ε is excluded; at most the start symbol is allowed to derive ε, as a separate convention.
(C) false: S → SS | a is in CNF (via A → a, S → SS, S → A) and is ambiguous.
(D) true: that is the Greibach Normal Form theorem, proved by eliminating left recursion and ordering the nonterminals.
solution.trap: Equating a normal form with unambiguity or determinism. CNF and GNF are shape restrictions; ambiguous grammars have normal forms too.

Step by step.

  1. (A) false: every context-free language has a CNF grammar, with S → ε added exactly when ε ∈ L.
  2. (B) false: GNF requires a terminal in first position, so A → ε is excluded; at most the start symbol is allowed to derive ε, as a separate convention.
  3. (C) false: S → SS | a is in CNF (via A → a, S → SS, S → A) and is ambiguous.
  4. (D) true: that is the Greibach Normal Form theorem, proved by eliminating left recursion and ordering the nonterminals.

Answer: Option (D).

Common misconception. Equating a normal form with unambiguity or determinism. CNF and GNF are shape restrictions; ambiguous grammars have normal forms too.

questions.question: The class of context-free languages is NOT closed under which one of the following operations?
questions.text: The class of context-free languages is NOT closed under which one of the following operations?
options: union
concatenation
complement
Kleene star

solution.concept: Context-free languages are closed under union, concatenation and Kleene star, because a new start symbol can combine two grammars (or repeat one). Complement is the standard exception.
steps: Union: S → S1 | S2 with S1 and S2.
Concatenation: S → S1S2. Kleene star: S → SS | ε.
Complement: {anbn} is context-free, but its complement intersected with a*b*c* gives {anbncn}, and that intersection is not context-free — the class is not closed under complement.
Since a class closed under complement and union would be closed under intersection, and it is not, complement cannot preserve context-freeness.
solution.trap: Assuming that because regular languages are closed under complement, context-free languages are too. The regular case is special: a DFA can be complemented by swapping final and non-final states.

  4. Since a class closed under complement and union would be closed under intersection, and it is not, complement cannot preserve context-freeness.

questions.question: The CYK algorithm decides membership in a context-free language by filling an entry t[i, j] for every 1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ n. For an input string of length 6, how many entries does the table have?
questions.text: The CYK algorithm decides membership in a context-free language by filling an entry t[i, j] for every 1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ n. For an input string of length 6, how many entries does the table have?

solution.concept: CYK fills the upper triangle of an n × n table: one entry per substring of the input, and a string of length n has exactly n(n+1)/2 substrings.
steps: Substrings are fixed by a start position i and an end position j with i ≤ j.
For each length L there are n − L + 1 substrings, so the total is ΣL=1..n (n − L + 1) = n(n+1)/2.
solution.trap: Answering 36 by counting the whole 6 × 6 table, or 15 by forgetting the single-symbol entries.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

  2. For each length L there are n − L + 1 substrings, so the total is ΣL=1..n (n − L + 1) = n(n+1)/2.
  3. With n = 6: 6 × 7 / 2 = 21.

Answer: 21.

questions.question: Select every statement that is TRUE.
questions.text: Select every statement that is TRUE.
options: Emptiness of a context-free language is decidable.
Equivalence of two context-free languages is decidable.
The class of context-free languages is closed under homomorphism.
The class of context-free languages is closed under inverse homomorphism.

solution.concept: Closure is generous for homomorphic operations and for union-like operations, and poor for intersection and complement. Decidability is generous for emptiness and membership, and poor for equivalence and ambiguity.
steps: (A) true: reduce the grammar, and the language is empty exactly when the start symbol is removed as unreachable or non-generating.
(B) false: equivalence of context-free languages is undecidable; only inclusion into a regular language is decidable.
(C) true: replace every terminal a in the productions by the string h(a); the result is a grammar for the image.
(D) true: build a pushdown automaton that reads h(w) and simulates the original automaton on w, buffering the images in its finite control.
solution.trap: Generalising “emptiness and membership are decidable” to “equivalence is decidable”. The undecidability of equivalence is one of the sharpest differences from the regular case.

questions.question: Let L be a context-free language and R a regular language. Which one of the following is necessarily context-free?
questions.text: Let L be a context-free language and R a regular language. Which one of the following is necessarily context-free?
options: the complement of L
L − R
L ∩ L′, where L′ is context-free
the set of strings that belong to neither L nor R

solution.concept: A context-free language intersected with a regular language is context-free (run the grammar in parallel with the DFA). Intersections and complements among context-free languages are where closure fails.
steps: (A) false: context-free languages are not closed under complement.
(B) true: L − R = L ∩ (Σ* − R), and the complement of a regular language is regular, so this is a context-free language intersected with a regular one.
(C) false: the intersection of two context-free languages need not be context-free.
(D) false: that set is the complement of L ∪ R, and neither complement nor union with a context-free language preserves context-freeness.
solution.trap: Treating “context-free ∩ regular” and “context-free ∩ context-free” as the same. Only the first is guaranteed.

Detailed solution

  3. (C) false: the intersection of two context-free languages need not be context-free.
  4. (D) false: that set is the complement of L ∪ R, and neither complement nor union with a context-free language preserves context-freeness.

questions.question: Let L = { anbn : n ≥ 0 }. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.text: Let L = { anbn : n ≥ 0 }. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: L is not context-free.
L is context-free, but its complement is not.
L is context-free, and so is its complement.
L is context-free, but L* is not.

solution.concept: L is accepted by a deterministic pushdown automaton (push on a, pop on b), and the class of deterministic context-free languages is closed under complement even though the whole class of context-free languages is not.
steps: A DPDA accepts L: push one symbol per a, pop one per b, accept at the end of the input with an empty stack.
Deterministic context-free languages are closed under complement: swap the accepting and rejecting states of the equivalent DPDA with a total transition function.
So the complement of L is deterministic context-free, hence context-free.
(D) is false because L* is just L, which is context-free.
Note that this does not contradict the non-closure of context-free languages under complement: the witness for that failure is a nondeterministic language.
solution.trap: Applying “context-free languages are not closed under complement” to a single deterministic language. The class-level failure does not mean every context-free language has a non-context-free complement.

  2. Deterministic context-free languages are closed under complement: swap the accepting and rejecting states of the equivalent DPDA with a total transition function.
  3. So the complement of L is deterministic context-free, hence context-free.
  4. (D) is false because L* is just L, which is context-free.
  5. Note that this does not contradict the non-closure of context-free languages under complement: the witness for that failure is a nondeterministic language.

questions.question: Consider these nine operations on languages: union, intersection, complement, concatenation, Kleene star, homomorphism, inverse homomorphism, reversal, and intersection with a regular language. For how many of the nine is the class of context-free languages closed?
questions.text: Consider these nine operations on languages: union, intersection, complement, concatenation, Kleene star, homomorphism, inverse homomorphism, reversal, and intersection with a regular language. For how many of the nine is the class of context-free languages closed?

solution.concept: Closure of context-free languages holds for the “grammar-building” operations (union, concatenation, star), for homomorphic operations, for reversal, and for intersection with a regular language. It fails for intersection and complement.
steps: Closed: union (new start symbol with two alternatives), concatenation, Kleene star, homomorphism (replace terminals by strings), inverse homomorphism, reversal (reverse every right side), intersection with a regular language (product with a DFA) — 7 operations.
Not closed: intersection (witness {anbncn} = {anbncm} ∩ {ambncn}) and complement (a class closed under complement and union would be closed under intersection).
So 7 of the 9 operations preserve context-freeness.
solution.trap: Counting complement or intersection as closed because regular languages are closed under both, or missing the two homomorphism operations, which are easy to overlook.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Closure of context-free languages holds for the “grammar-building” operations (union, concatenation, star), for homomorphic operations, for reversal, and for intersection with a regular language. It fails for intersection and complement.

Step by step.

  1. Closed: union (new start symbol with two alternatives), concatenation, Kleene star, homomorphism (replace terminals by strings), inverse homomorphism, reversal (reverse every right side), intersection with a regular language (product with a DFA) — 7 operations.
  2. Not closed: intersection (witness {anbncn} = {anbncm} ∩ {ambncn}) and complement (a class closed under complement and union would be closed under intersection).
  3. So 7 of the 9 operations preserve context-freeness.

Answer: 7.

Common misconception. Counting complement or intersection as closed because regular languages are closed under both, or missing the two homomorphism operations, which are easy to overlook.

questions.question: The deterministic pushdown automaton M has states {q₀, q₁, q₂} , input alphabet Σ = {a, b} , stack alphabet Γ = {Z₀, A} , start state q₀ , initial stack symbol Z₀ , final state q₂ and the moves below. Which language does M accept? δ(q₀, a, Z₀) = (q₀, A Z₀) δ(q₁, b, A) = (q₁, ε) δ(q₀, a, A) = (q₀, A A) δ(q₁, ε, Z₀) = (q₂, Z₀) δ(q₀, b, A) = (q₁, ε)
questions.question_html: The deterministic pushdown automaton M has states {q₀, q₁, q₂}, input alphabet Σ = {a, b}, stack alphabet Γ = {Z₀, A}, start state q₀, initial stack symbol Z₀, final state q₂ and the moves below. Which language does M accept?δ(q₀, a, Z₀) = (q₀, A Z₀) δ(q₁, b, A) = (q₁, ε) δ(q₀, a, A) = (q₀, A A) δ(q₁, ε, Z₀) = (q₂, Z₀) δ(q₀, b, A) = (q₁, ε)
options: {aⁿ bᵐ : n, m ≥ 1}
{aⁿ bⁿ : n ≥ 1}
{aⁿ bⁿ : n ≥ 0}
options_html: {aⁿ bᵐ : n, m ≥ 1}
{w ∈ {a, b}* : #a(w) = #b(w)}
{aⁿ bⁿ : n ≥ 1}
{aⁿ bⁿ : n ≥ 0}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A pushdown automaton counts with its stack: every a pushed is one A on the stack, and each b pops exactly one A. The machine therefore accepts when the two blocks have equal length, and the fixed order (all a's, then all b's) comes from the states: q₀ reads only a's, q₁ reads only b's.

Step by step.

  1. At q₀ each a pushes one A, so after aⁿ the stack holds Z₀ Aⁿ.
  2. The first b takes δ(q₀, b, A) = (q₁, ε): it pops one A and moves to q₁. From then on b's keep popping at q₁.
  3. The input is accepted only if the stack reaches Z₀ exactly when the input is exhausted; then δ(q₁, ε, Z₀) = (q₂, Z₀) moves to the final state q₂.
  4. Hence aⁿ bⁿ is accepted for every n ≥ 1. At n = 0 the input is ε, but δ(q₀, ε, Z₀) is undefined and q₀ is not final, so ε is rejected.
  5. Any word outside a*b* dies on a missing move, and any word of unequal block lengths dies with a non-empty stack or with an empty one before the input ends.

Answer: Option (C) — {aⁿ bⁿ : n ≥ 1}.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) {aⁿ bᵐ : n, m ≥ 1} needs no counting at all; here unequal blocks such as abb leave a residue on the stack and are rejected.
  • (B) equal counts in any order is not what the machine checks — it insists on the order a*b*, so ba is rejected although its counts are equal.
  • (D) differs from the truth only at n = 0: ε is rejected, so the correct set starts at n ≥ 1.

Common misconception. Reading a machine's language off the shape of its stack operations without checking the boundary case ε. Here q₀ is not final and has no ε-move, which is exactly what removes n = 0. The second trap is assuming the machine ignores order, as a counter of #a = #b would.

Takeaway. Trace three words — ε, one accepted word, and one that breaks the order — and the language of a small PDA is settled.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: A deterministic pushdown automaton has no ε -moves: every move of the machine reads exactly one input symbol. It accepts a string w with |w| = 5 by final state. How many moves does this accepting computation contain?
questions.question_html: A deterministic pushdown automaton has no ε-moves: every move of the machine reads exactly one input symbol. It accepts a string w with |w| = 5 by final state. How many moves does this accepting computation contain?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A move of a PDA is one application of the transition function: it reads one input symbol (or ε), pops one stack symbol and pushes a string. With no ε-moves, every move consumes exactly one input symbol, so the number of moves is fixed by the input and nothing else.

Step by step.

  1. Acceptance by final state requires the whole input to be read: after the last move the input pointer is past the final symbol.
  2. Each move advances that pointer by exactly one symbol, because the machine has no ε-moves.
  3. So an accepting computation on a word of length 5 contains exactly 5 moves, whatever the stack does.
  4. Determinism is not needed for this count; it only guarantees that at most one such computation exists.

Answer: 5.

Common misconception. Adding one extra move for "reaching the final state" or for popping the last Z₀. A move always consumes a symbol; the machine is in a final state the moment the input is exhausted, and no closing move is required.

Takeaway. Without ε-moves, moves = input length. The interesting part of a PDA is the stack, not the clock.

questions.question: Which one of the following operations, applied to an arbitrary deterministic context-free language L , always produces a deterministic context-free language?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following operations, applied to an arbitrary deterministic context-free language L, always produces a deterministic context-free language?
options: the union L ∪ L′ with another deterministic context-free language L′
the complement L̄
the intersection L ∩ L′ with another deterministic context-free language L′
the Kleene star L*
options_html: the union L ∪ L′ with another deterministic context-free language L′
the complement L̄
the intersection L ∩ L′ with another deterministic context-free language L′
the Kleene star L*
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Deterministic context-free languages are closed under complementation — the one closure property that separates them from the whole class of context-free languages. They are not closed under union, intersection or Kleene star.

Step by step.

  1. Take a DPDA that accepts L by final state and make it total by adding a rejecting "dead" state for every undefined move.
  2. Interchange final and non-final states. Because the machine is deterministic there is exactly one run per input, so a word now ends in a final state exactly when it did not before.
  3. Hence L̄ is accepted by a DPDA and is a DCFL.
  4. The same trick fails for a general NPDA, which is why CFLs are not closed under complement, and it fails for the other three operations listed even in the deterministic case.

Answer: Option (B) — complementation.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) {aⁱ bʲ cᵏ : i = j} and {aⁱ bʲ cᵏ : j = k} are both DCFLs, but their union {aⁱ bʲ cᵏ : i = j or j = k} is the standard inherently ambiguous context-free language, hence not a DCFL.
  • (C) {aⁿ bⁿ cᵐ} and {aⁿ bᵐ cᵐ} are DCFLs while their intersection {aⁿ bⁿ cⁿ} is not even context-free.
  • (D) closure under star is a property of the context-free languages as a whole; the deterministic subclass does not inherit it.

Common misconception. Carrying the closure table of the context-free languages over to the deterministic ones. The two classes agree that union, concatenation and star are unsafe, but they disagree on complement — which the deterministic class does preserve.

Takeaway. DCFL: complement yes; union, intersection, star no. Learn the counterexample pairs, not just the word "closed".

questions.question: Select every statement about deterministic pushdown automata and deterministic context-free languages (DCFLs) that is TRUE .
questions.question_html: Select every statement about deterministic pushdown automata and deterministic context-free languages (DCFLs) that is TRUE.
options: Every DCFL is generated by some unambiguous context-free grammar.
The class of DCFLs is closed under complementation.
The class of DCFLs is closed under intersection.
Every regular language is a DCFL.
options_html: Every DCFL is generated by some unambiguous context-free grammar.
The class of DCFLs is closed under complementation.
The class of DCFLs is closed under intersection.
Every regular language is a DCFL.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A DPDA has at most one run per input, so an accepted word has a unique accepting computation; reading the stack operations of that run off gives one parse, hence an unambiguous grammar. The class sits strictly between the regular languages and the context-free languages and inherits complement closure from determinism.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true. Convert the DPDA to a CFG by the standard triple construction. A word with two distinct parse trees would give two distinct accepting runs, which determinism forbids, so the grammar is unambiguous.
  2. (B) true. Complete the DPDA with a dead state and swap final and non-final states; one run per word makes the swap exact.
  3. (C) false. {aⁿ bⁿ cᵐ : n, m ≥ 0} and {aⁿ bᵐ cᵐ : n, m ≥ 0} are DCFLs; their intersection {aⁿ bⁿ cⁿ} is not context-free.
  4. (D) true. Every DFA is a DPDA that ignores its stack, so every regular language is a DCFL.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Believing (C) because "deterministic machines are well behaved". Determinism buys complement closure, not intersection closure: the product of two DPDAs is not in general a DPDA, since the two stack disciplines can disagree.

Takeaway. Regular ⊂ DCFL ⊂ CFL ⊂ CSL ⊂ r.e., and the DCFL layer is the one where complement is safe and intersection is not.

questions.question: Which one of the following languages is deterministic context-free?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following languages is deterministic context-free?
options: {aⁱ bʲ cᵏ : i = j or j = k}
{aⁱ bʲ cᵏ : i = j}
{aⁿ bⁿ cⁿ : n ≥ 0}
options_html: {aⁱ bʲ cᵏ : i = j or j = k}
{aⁱ bʲ cᵏ : i = j}
{w w : w ∈ {a, b}*}
{aⁿ bⁿ cⁿ : n ≥ 0}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A language is a DCFL when one stack and one left-to-right pass with no guessing suffice. Matching the a-block against the b-block needs only a counter, and the trailing c's are then accepted blindly — that is a deterministic procedure.

Step by step.

  1. On each a push one A. On the first b switch to popping and pop one A per b.
  2. If the stack returns to Z₀ exactly at the end of the b-block then i = j; otherwise reject.
  3. At that moment switch to a state that accepts any number of c's. The condition j = k is never tested, so no extra memory is needed.
  4. Every step is forced by the current state, input symbol and stack top, so the machine is a DPDA.

Answer: Option (B) — {aⁱ bʲ cᵏ : i = j}.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is the standard inherently ambiguous context-free language {aⁱ bʲ cᵏ : i = j or j = k}. A DPDA accepts only unambiguous languages, so (A) is not a DCFL: a DPDA cannot know at the first c whether it should still be matching j against k.
  • (C) {w w} is not context-free at all: a stack can compare a word with its reversal but not with a shifted copy of itself.
  • (D) {aⁿ bⁿ cⁿ} is not context-free either — one stack cannot keep two independent counts.

Common misconception. Treating "deterministic" as "easy to write" and picking (A) because each of its two halves looks deterministic. The union of two DCFLs need not be a DCFL, and this pair is the textbook witness.

Takeaway. Ask what the machine must remember at the moment it stops reading the middle block. If the answer depends on a future block, the language is not a DCFL.

questions.question: A deterministic pushdown automaton M has the ε -move δ(q, ε, A) = (q, A A) , and for this state and stack symbol there is no move that reads an input symbol: δ(q, a, A) is undefined for every a ∈ Σ . Which one of the following statements about M is TRUE?
questions.question_html: A deterministic pushdown automaton M has the ε-move δ(q, ε, A) = (q, A A), and for this state and stack symbol there is no move that reads an input symbol: δ(q, a, A) is undefined for every a ∈ Σ. Which one of the following statements about M is TRUE?
options: Every computation of M reads at least as many input symbols as it makes moves.
M is not a legal deterministic PDA, because a deterministic machine may never have an ε -move.
M accepts some infinite language.
On some input, a computation of M can make more moves than the input has symbols.
options_html: Every computation of M reads at least as many input symbols as it makes moves.
M is not a legal deterministic PDA, because a deterministic machine may never have an ε-move.
M accepts some infinite language.
On some input, a computation of M can make more moves than the input has symbols.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An ε-move consumes no input, so the number of moves is not bounded by the length of the input. A DPDA may loop forever: determinism forbids two choices, not divergence.

Step by step.

  1. Once M reaches state q with A on top, the only available move is δ(q, ε, A) = (q, A A), which replaces A by two A's and reads nothing.
  2. That move is enabled again in the resulting configuration, so it can be taken any number of times: the stack grows without bound and the input pointer never moves.
  3. So for a fixed input the computation can be arbitrarily long — longer than the input, and in fact never terminating. Statement (D) is true.
  4. Determinism is intact: at (q, A) there is exactly one move, and it happens to be an ε-move. A DPDA forbids an ε-move that competes with an input move for the same (q, X); here only the ε-move exists.

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is the intuition that breaks here: it holds only for machines without ε-moves.
  • (B) misstates the definition. Determinism constrains δ to at most one move per (q, a, X) and forbids an ε-move competing with an input move for the same (q, X); it never forbids ε-moves as such.
  • (C) does not follow. The machine may diverge on every input that reaches q, in which case its language is small or empty; nothing about acceptance can be read off a non-terminating loop.

Common misconception. Assuming that a DPDA, being deterministic, always halts and takes at most |w| moves. Neither is required: a DPDA recognises its language but need not decide it, and ε-moves can inflate a computation without limit.

Takeaway. Determinism is about the number of choices, not about termination or about the length of a run.

questions.question: The deterministic pushdown automaton M accepts by final state. It has states {q₀, q₁, q₂} , input alphabet Σ = {a, b} , stack alphabet Γ = {Z₀, A} , start state q₀ , initial stack symbol Z₀ , final states {q₀, q₁, q₂} and the moves below. How many strings of length at most 3 over Σ does M accept? δ(q₀, a, Z₀) = (q₀, A Z₀) δ(q₁, b, A) = (q₁, ε) δ(q₀, a, A) = (q₀, A A) δ(q₁, ε, Z₀) = (q₂, Z₀) δ(q₀, b, A) = (q₁, ε)
questions.question_html: The deterministic pushdown automaton M accepts by final state. It has states {q₀, q₁, q₂}, input alphabet Σ = {a, b}, stack alphabet Γ = {Z₀, A}, start state q₀, initial stack symbol Z₀, final states {q₀, q₁, q₂} and the moves below. How many strings of length at most 3 over Σ does M accept?δ(q₀, a, Z₀) = (q₀, A Z₀) δ(q₁, b, A) = (q₁, ε) δ(q₀, a, A) = (q₀, A A) δ(q₁, ε, Z₀) = (q₂, Z₀) δ(q₀, b, A) = (q₁, ε)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The machine counts a's on the stack and cancels them against b's. Because all three states are final, the machine accepts at q₀ while no b has been read, at q₁ with A's still on the stack, and at q₂ once the stack has been reduced to Z₀. So it accepts {aⁱ bʲ : i ≥ j ≥ 0}, and the task is to count the members of that set of length at most 3.

Step by step.

  1. Length 0. ε: the machine is in q₀, which is final, and the input is exhausted — accepted.
  2. Length 1. a is accepted at q₀. b has no move from (q₀, Z₀), so it is rejected. Two accepted so far.
  3. Length 2. aa is accepted at q₀. ab: the single A is popped and q₁ is reached with Z₀ on top — and q₁ is final, so ab is accepted. ba and bb die on the first b. Four accepted so far.
  4. Length 3. aaa is accepted at q₀. aab: one A is popped on the single b and q₁ is final with Z₀ A still on the stack — accepted. aba fails because after the b the machine sits at q₁ with Z₀ on top, where a has no move; abb fails because the second b finds Z₀ on top; baa, bab, bba and bbb die on the first b. Two more.
  5. Total 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 6 accepted strings: ε, a, aa, ab, aaa, aab.

Answer: 6.

Common misconception. Two slips move the count. Forgetting that q₀ is final drops ε, a, aa, aaa; forgetting that q₁ is final drops ab and aab, which many candidates reject because the stack is not empty at the end. Under final-state acceptance a non-empty stack is irrelevant.

Takeaway. Enumerate by length, and settle two structural facts first: which states are final, and which ε-moves can close a computation.

questions.question: A pushdown automaton that is allowed two stacks instead of one accepts exactly the class of languages that is:
questions.question_html: A pushdown automaton that is allowed two stacks instead of one accepts exactly the class of languages that is:
options: context-free
recursively enumerable
regular
deterministic context-free
options_html: context-free
recursively enumerable
regular
deterministic context-free
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. One stack is a last-in-first-out store, which is exactly enough for context-free languages. Two stacks can simulate an unbounded tape: one stack holds the tape to the left of the head and the other the tape to the right, so the machine becomes a Turing machine.

Step by step.

  1. With one stack the machine is a PDA, and PDA languages are exactly the context-free ones.
  2. With two stacks, moving the head right is a pop from the right stack and a push onto the left stack, and moving left is the reverse. This reproduces an unbounded tape, so any Turing machine computation can be carried out.
  3. Conversely a two-stack machine is a finite-state control with two stacks, hence a Turing machine, and Turing machines accept exactly the recursively enumerable languages.
  4. So two stacks give exactly the recursively enumerable class — strictly more than the context-free languages.

Answer: Option (B) — recursively enumerable.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is the one-stack class; the second stack is precisely what removes the context-free limitation.
  • (C) regular languages need no stack at all, and they are a proper subclass of the one-stack class.
  • (D) deterministic context-free is a proper subclass of (A), so it is far too small.

Common misconception. Counting stacks instead of counting their power: two LIFO stores are not "twice as much context-free", they are a tape, and that is a jump of two levels in the Chomsky hierarchy.

Takeaway. 0 stacks = regular; 1 stack = context-free; 2 stacks = Turing machine. This is the standard yardstick for automata questions.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following is TRUE of every nondeterministic pushdown automaton?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following is TRUE of every nondeterministic pushdown automaton?
options: For some state q , input symbol a and stack symbol X , the set δ(q, a, X) may contain two or more moves.
Its transition function is a partial function that returns at most one move for each argument.
It must have exactly one final state.
It accepts a string only if every computation on that string ends in a final state.
options_html: For some state q, input symbol a and stack symbol X, the set δ(q, a, X) may contain two or more moves.
Its transition function is a partial function that returns at most one move for each argument.
It must have exactly one final state.
It accepts a string only if every computation on that string ends in a final state.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Nondeterminism is exactly the freedom to have several moves available for one (state, input symbol, stack top) triple. The machine accepts when at least one computation succeeds; the others are simply abandoned.

Step by step.

  1. Formally δ maps Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) × Γ to subsets of Q × Γ*. For a nondeterministic machine those subsets may have any finite size, including two or more.
  2. Acceptance is existential: a word is accepted if some computation consumes all of it and ends in a final state (or empties the stack, in that mode).
  3. Nothing forces a particular number of final states; a machine with no final states can still accept by empty stack.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) describes a deterministic PDA, the special case where every δ(q, a, X) has at most one element.
  • (C) is false: machines may have several final states, or none at all when accepting by empty stack.
  • (D) inverts the definition — one successful computation is enough, and failing runs do not matter.

Common misconception. Reading nondeterminism as "tries all paths and needs all of them to work". For acceptance it is "some path works"; for rejection, every path must fail.

Takeaway. Subset-valued δ plus existential acceptance is the whole definition of an NPDA.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The machine pushes every symbol it reads and then, at a guessed middle point, switches to the state q₁ where each remaining symbol must match the symbol on top of the stack. So it accepts exactly the palindromes over {a, b}: the words w with w = wᴿ.

Step by step.

  1. The ε-move to q₁ that reads no symbol handles even-length palindromes; the moves δ(q₀, a, X) ∋ (q₁, X) and δ(q₀, b, X) ∋ (q₁, X) consume the middle symbol without pushing it, which handles odd-length palindromes.
  2. At q₁ a symbol is accepted only if it equals the symbol on top of the stack, which is then popped; the stack empties exactly at the end of the input.
  3. Counting palindromes by length: length 0 gives ε; length 1 gives a, b; length 2 gives aa, bb; length 3 gives aaa, aba, bab, bbb — all four, since a word of length 3 is a palindrome exactly when its first and last symbols agree.
  4. Total 1 + 2 + 2 + 4 = 9.

Answer: 9.

Common misconception. Counting ab or aab because they "look symmetric enough". A palindrome must reverse to itself: ab reverses to ba, so it fails at q₁ where the top of the stack is A but the input symbol is b. The other slip is forgetting that odd-length palindromes are accepted at all, which loses a, b, aba, bab.

Takeaway. For a guessed-middle machine the language is the set of words equal to their own reversal, and the count by length is then immediate.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Select every statement about NPDAs, ε -transitions and the class of languages they accept that is TRUE .
questions.question_html: Select every statement about NPDAs, ε-transitions and the class of languages they accept that is TRUE.
options: Every context-free language is accepted by some NPDA that has exactly one state.
The class of context-free languages is closed under complementation.
Every ε -transition can be removed from an NPDA without changing the language it accepts.
A language is context-free if and only if some NPDA accepts it.
options_html: Every context-free language is accepted by some NPDA that has exactly one state.
The class of context-free languages is closed under complementation.
Every ε-transition can be removed from an NPDA without changing the language it accepts.
A language is context-free if and only if some NPDA accepts it.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. NPDAs and context-free grammars are two notations for the same class. The single-state construction makes the state set irrelevant, and ε-transitions are pure convenience because a nondeterministic machine can always simulate them through pre-computed closures.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true. From a grammar G = (V, T, P, S) build an NPDA with one state, initial stack Z₀S, a move per production A → α that pops A and pushes α, and a move per terminal a that pops a after reading it. Acceptance by empty stack gives exactly L(G).
  2. (B) false. {aⁱ bʲ cᵏ : i = j or j = k} is context-free while its complement is not; CFLs are closed under union, concatenation, star, homomorphism and intersection with a regular set, but not under complement.
  3. (C) true. Replace every move that reads a and is followed by ε-moves by the set of moves that read a and jump straight to the ε-closure of the destination, with the stack contents adjusted accordingly. The language is unchanged.
  4. (D) true. This is the standard equivalence: grammar to NPDA by (A), and NPDA to grammar by the triple construction.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Believing (B) because the class is closed under union, concatenation and star. Complement is the notorious exception, and it is the reason equivalence of two CFGs is undecidable while membership is not.

Takeaway. One state, empty-stack acceptance and ε-free moves are all without loss of generality for NPDAs — but not for DPDAs, where each of these transformations can destroy determinism.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let L = {aⁱ bʲ cᵏ : i = j or j = k} . Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Let L = {aⁱ bʲ cᵏ : i = j or j = k}. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: L is accepted by an NPDA, and every context-free grammar that generates L is ambiguous.
L is accepted by a DPDA.
L is not context-free.
L is accepted by an NPDA, and some unambiguous context-free grammar generates L .
options_html: L is accepted by an NPDA, and every context-free grammar that generates L is ambiguous.
L is accepted by a DPDA.
L is not context-free.
L is accepted by an NPDA, and some unambiguous context-free grammar generates L.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. L is the union of the two context-free languages L₁ = {aⁱ bʲ cᵏ : i = j} and L₂ = {aⁱ bʲ cᵏ : j = k}, so it is context-free and an NPDA accepts it by guessing which of the two conditions holds. It is the standard example of an inherently ambiguous language: no grammar for it is unambiguous, and therefore no DPDA accepts it.

Step by step.

  1. Upper bound. CFLs are closed under union, so L = L₁ ∪ L₂ is context-free and is accepted by an NPDA that nondeterministically chooses which half to verify.
  2. Why ambiguity is unavoidable. For every n ≥ 1 the word aⁿ bⁿ cⁿ belongs to both halves, so any grammar has two essentially different derivations of it: one that matches a's against b's and one that matches b's against c's.
  3. The classical counting argument (Ogden's lemma applied to aⁿ bⁿ cⁿ) shows that no grammar can avoid this: the two conditions cannot be encoded in one parse without the derivations colliding.
  4. Since every DCFL has an unambiguous grammar, L is not a DCFL and no DPDA accepts it.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) contradicts inherent ambiguity: a DPDA would give an unambiguous grammar for L.
  • (C) is too strong — a union of two CFLs is always context-free.
  • (D) is exactly the false statement this example was invented to refute.

Common misconception. Confusing "ambiguous grammar" with "inherently ambiguous language". A single badly written grammar proves nothing; inherent ambiguity says that every grammar for the language is ambiguous, and in general that property is undecidable — this particular language is simply the one case every candidate is expected to know.

Takeaway. Two overlapping conditions on three blocks is the classic recipe for inherent ambiguity: context-free, not deterministic, never unambiguous.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following languages is accepted by some nondeterministic pushdown automaton but by no deterministic pushdown automaton?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following languages is accepted by some nondeterministic pushdown automaton but by no deterministic pushdown automaton?
options: {aⁿ bⁿ : n ≥ 0}
{aⁱ bʲ cᵏ : i = j = k}
{w wᴿ : w ∈ {a, b}*}
{aⁿ bᵐ : n ≤ m}
options_html: {aⁿ bⁿ : n ≥ 0}
{aⁱ bʲ cᵏ : i = j = k}
{w wᴿ : w ∈ {a, b}*}
{aⁿ bᵐ : n ≤ m}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. {w wᴿ} is the set of palindromes over {a, b}. A nondeterministic machine can guess where the middle of the word is and then match symbols against the stack; a deterministic machine cannot guess, and no number of extra states replaces the missing guess.

Step by step.

  1. An NPDA accepts it. Push every symbol read; at some point, guessed nondeterministically, switch to popping and require each remaining symbol to equal the popped one, ending exactly at Z₀.
  2. No DPDA accepts it. Suppose a DPDA accepted {w wᴿ}. On the two inputs aⁿ b aⁿ and aⁿ b b aⁿ the machine has read the same prefix aⁿ b and therefore sits in one and the same configuration.
  3. But aⁿ b aⁿ ∈ L while aⁿ b b aⁿ ∉ L, so that single configuration would have to lead to acceptance in one case and rejection in the other — impossible for a deterministic machine, whose future is fixed by the configuration.
  4. So the language is context-free but not a DCFL, which is exactly what the question asks for.

Answer: Option (C) — {w wᴿ : w ∈ {a, b}*}.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) {aⁿ bⁿ} is the standard DCFL: push on a, pop on b.
  • (B) {aⁱ bʲ cᵏ : i = j = k} is not context-free at all, so no NPDA accepts it — the usual trap for candidates who answer "needs nondeterminism" without checking the class.
  • (D) {aⁿ bᵐ : n ≤ m} is a DCFL: push on a, pop on b, and accept any leftover b's deterministically.

Common misconception. Picking (B). "Not deterministic context-free" is not the same as "neither deterministic nor context-free": (B) fails even the context-free test, since one stack cannot keep two independent counts.

Takeaway. Guessing a position is the archetypal NPDA-only power; palindromes and {w wᴿ} are the canonical witnesses, and {aⁿ bⁿ cⁿ} is the canonical non-context-free trap.

questions.question: A pushdown automaton accepts a string by final state. Which one of the following must be TRUE at the moment of acceptance?
questions.question_html: A pushdown automaton accepts a string by final state. Which one of the following must be TRUE at the moment of acceptance?
options: The stack holds exactly the initial stack symbol Z₀ .
The whole input has been read and the machine is in a final state; the stack may still hold symbols.
The stack is empty.
The machine has made exactly |w| moves.
options_html: The stack holds exactly the initial stack symbol Z₀.
The whole input has been read and the machine is in a final state; the stack may still hold symbols.
The stack is empty.
The machine has made exactly |w| moves.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The two acceptance modes look at different things. Acceptance by final state looks only at the state and at the input pointer; acceptance by empty stack looks only at the stack and at the input pointer. Neither mode constrains the other component.

Step by step.

  1. Formally, w is accepted by final state if some computation starting from (q₀, w, Z₀) ends in (q, ε, γ) with q ∈ F and any stack contents γ.
  2. So the input must be fully consumed and the state must be final; the stack contents are irrelevant and may be anything, including a tall stack.
  3. Requiring γ = Z₀ or γ = ε is a different acceptance condition and would change the language.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) and (C) impose conditions that belong to the other acceptance mode, or to neither; a final-state machine may stop with any stack.
  • (D) ignores ε-moves, which consume no input; a computation can take more moves than the input has symbols.

Common misconception. Believing the machine must "tidy up" its stack before accepting. It need not; the final state alone decides acceptance.

Takeaway. Final state: state and input only. Empty stack: stack and input only. Keep the two lists separate.

questions.question: The pushdown automaton M has states {q₀, q₁} , input alphabet Σ = {a, b} , stack alphabet Γ = {Z₀, A} , start state q₀ , initial stack symbol Z₀ , no final states, and accepts by empty stack with the moves below. Which one of the following strings does M accept? δ(q₀, a, Z₀) = (q₀, A Z₀) δ(q₁, b, A) = (q₁, ε) δ(q₀, a, A) = (q₀, A A) δ(q₁, ε, Z₀) = (q₁, ε) δ(q₀, b, A) = (q₁, ε)
questions.question_html: The pushdown automaton M has states {q₀, q₁}, input alphabet Σ = {a, b}, stack alphabet Γ = {Z₀, A}, start state q₀, initial stack symbol Z₀, no final states, and accepts by empty stack with the moves below. Which one of the following strings does M accept?δ(q₀, a, Z₀) = (q₀, A Z₀) δ(q₁, b, A) = (q₁, ε) δ(q₀, a, A) = (q₀, A A) δ(q₁, ε, Z₀) = (q₁, ε) δ(q₀, b, A) = (q₁, ε)
options: aab
abb
ba
ab
options_html: aab
abb
ba
ab
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Acceptance by empty stack means the computation must consume the whole input and leave the stack empty — the last move pops Z₀. With the moves given, M counts a's on the stack and cancels them with b's, so it accepts {aⁿ bⁿ : n ≥ 1}.

Step by step.

  1. ab. a pushes: stack Z₀ A. b pops at q₁: stack Z₀, input exhausted. The ε-move δ(q₁, ε, Z₀) = (q₁, ε) pops Z₀, so the stack is empty — accepted.
  2. aab. Two A's are pushed and only one is popped, so Z₀ A is still on the stack when the input ends — rejected.
  3. abb. The second b finds Z₀ on top and δ(q₁, b, Z₀) is undefined — rejected.
  4. ba. δ(q₀, b, Z₀) is undefined, so the machine dies on the first symbol — rejected.

Answer: Option (D) — ab.

Common misconception. Checking only that the input can be read, or only that the stack empties. Both conditions must hold together: aab reads fine but leaves a symbol, which is precisely the distinction between the two acceptance modes.

Takeaway. For empty-stack acceptance, trace the stack after the last input symbol — if it is not exactly empty at that instant, the word is rejected.

questions.question: Select every statement comparing acceptance by empty stack with acceptance by final state that is TRUE .
questions.question_html: Select every statement comparing acceptance by empty stack with acceptance by final state that is TRUE.
options: For nondeterministic pushdown automata, acceptance by final state and acceptance by empty stack define the same class of languages.
For deterministic pushdown automata they do not: some language is accepted by a DPDA by final state but by no DPDA by empty stack.
The standard conversion from acceptance by final state to acceptance by empty stack preserves determinism whenever the given machine is deterministic.
If a language is accepted by some DPDA by empty stack, then no word of the language is a proper prefix of another word of the language.
options_html: For nondeterministic pushdown automata, acceptance by final state and acceptance by empty stack define the same class of languages.
For deterministic pushdown automata they do not: some language is accepted by a DPDA by final state but by no DPDA by empty stack.
The standard conversion from acceptance by final state to acceptance by empty stack preserves determinism whenever the given machine is deterministic.
If a language is accepted by some DPDA by empty stack, then no word of the language is a proper prefix of another word of the language.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. For NPDAs the two modes are interchangeable, because the extra ε-moves can be hidden inside guessed branches. For DPDAs they are not: a machine that accepts by empty stack stops the instant the stack empties, so its language is prefix-free, and the translation from final state to empty stack needs ε-moves that can create genuine choices.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true. Final to empty: add a new start state that pushes a bottom marker and then simulates, plus a state that drains the stack whenever a final state is reached. Empty to final: add one final state reachable by an ε-move whenever the stack is empty. Both are NPDA constructions, so the classes coincide.
  2. (B) true. {a, ab} is accepted by a DPDA by final state (read the a-block, then at most one b). It is not prefix-free, since a is a proper prefix of ab, and by (D) that rules out every DPDA that accepts it by empty stack.
  3. (C) false. The construction attaches ε-moves to final states, and a final state may also have ordinary moves; both being available for one (state, stack top) breaks determinism. That is exactly why (B) holds.
  4. (D) true. This is the prefix property. If u were a proper prefix of v with both in L, then after reading u the stack is empty and the machine halts; it cannot go on to read the rest of v. So no such pair exists.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Assuming every construction that works for NPDAs also works for DPDAs. Determinism is fragile: adding states and ε-moves routinely creates choices that were not there before.

Takeaway. NPDA: the two modes are equivalent. DPDA: final state strictly contains empty stack, and the empty-stack languages are exactly the prefix-free DCFLs.

questions.question: Which one of the following languages cannot be accepted by any deterministic pushdown automaton by empty stack?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following languages cannot be accepted by any deterministic pushdown automaton by empty stack?
options: {aⁿ bⁿ : n ≥ 1}
{aⁿ bⁿ c : n ≥ 0}
{aⁿ bⁿ : n ≥ 1} ∪ {c}
options_html: {aⁿ bⁿ : n ≥ 1}
{aⁿ bⁿ c : n ≥ 0}
{aⁿ : n ≥ 1}
{aⁿ bⁿ : n ≥ 1} ∪ {c}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A DPDA that accepts by empty stack halts the instant the stack empties, so it can never accept a word and then continue reading a longer word. Its language is therefore prefix-free: no member is a proper prefix of another member. Conversely, every prefix-free DCFL is accepted by some DPDA by empty stack.

Step by step.

  1. Test each language for the prefix property.
  2. (A) {aⁿ bⁿ : n ≥ 1}: a proper prefix of aⁿ bⁿ is aⁱ or aⁿ bʲ with j < n, and none of these is in the set. Prefix-free.
  3. (B) {aⁿ bⁿ c : n ≥ 0}: a proper prefix is aⁱ, or aⁿ bʲ with j < n, or the whole of aⁿ bⁿ — none of them ends in c and so none is in the set. Prefix-free.
  4. (C) {aⁿ : n ≥ 1}: a is a proper prefix of aa and both are in the set. Not prefix-free, so no DPDA accepts it by empty stack. It is nevertheless a DCFL — a DPDA accepts it by final state.
  5. (D) {aⁿ bⁿ : n ≥ 1} ∪ {c}: the only word beginning with c is c itself, and no aⁿ bⁿ is a proper prefix of another. Prefix-free.

Answer: Option (C) — {aⁿ : n ≥ 1}.

Common misconception. Looking only at whether the language is a DCFL. All four options are deterministic context-free; the question is which of them survives the stricter empty-stack mode, and only the prefix test decides that.

Takeaway. Empty-stack acceptance is a property of the language's shape, not just of its class: prefix-free in, otherwise out.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements about deterministic pushdown automata is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following statements about deterministic pushdown automata is TRUE?
options: Every language accepted by a DPDA by empty stack is also accepted by a DPDA by final state, but not conversely.
The two acceptance modes define the same class of languages for DPDAs.
Every language accepted by a DPDA by final state is also accepted by a DPDA by empty stack.
Neither of the two classes of languages contains the other.
options_html: Every language accepted by a DPDA by empty stack is also accepted by a DPDA by final state, but not conversely.
The two acceptance modes define the same class of languages for DPDAs.
Every language accepted by a DPDA by final state is also accepted by a DPDA by empty stack.
Neither of the two classes of languages contains the other.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Going from empty-stack acceptance to final-state acceptance is easy and determinism-safe; the reverse direction is not. So the final-state class properly contains the empty-stack class.

Step by step.

  1. Empty to final. Put a fresh bottom marker # under Z₀ at the start. When # is exposed the old stack has just become empty, so a single ε-move into a new final state q_f accepts. The marker is exposed only in that one situation, so no choice is ever created and determinism survives.
  2. So every empty-stack DPDA language is a final-state DPDA language.
  3. Final to empty fails. {a, ab} is accepted by a DPDA by final state. It is not prefix-free, because a is a proper prefix of ab; an empty-stack DPDA would halt with an empty stack after a and could never accept ab.
  4. Hence the inclusion is strict: empty-stack ⊊ final-state, which is statement (A).

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) is true for NPDAs but false for DPDAs — that gap is exactly the prefix property.
  • (C) reverses the true inclusion.
  • (D) is false because the empty-stack class is contained in the final-state class.

Common misconception. Importing the NPDA equivalence into the deterministic world. Determinism is preserved in one direction only.

Takeaway. DPDA by empty stack ⊂ DPDA by final state; for NPDAs the two classes are equal.

questions.question: A context-free grammar G is in Greibach Normal Form: every production is A → aα with a a terminal and α a (possibly empty) string of variables. Let S ⇒* w be a derivation of the terminal string w with |w| = 9 . How many steps does this derivation contain?
questions.question_html: A context-free grammar G is in Greibach Normal Form: every production is A → aα with a a terminal and α a (possibly empty) string of variables. Let S ⇒* w be a derivation of the terminal string w with |w| = 9. How many steps does this derivation contain?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. In Greibach Normal Form every production emits exactly one terminal and puts only variables on the right. So every derivation step lengthens the terminal prefix by exactly one symbol, and the number of steps equals the length of the derived word.

Step by step.

  1. Before any step the sentential form is S and contains no terminals.
  2. Each step applies A → aα: it replaces one variable by a terminal a followed by variables, so the number of terminals in the form grows by exactly one.
  3. After k steps the form contains exactly k terminals; a terminal string with 9 symbols therefore needs exactly 9 steps.
  4. No step can be saved or added: a production that emits no terminal would violate Greibach Normal Form, and one that emits two would overshoot.

Answer: 9.

Common misconception. Counting the variables as well, or assuming the count is the number of nodes of the derivation tree. In GNF the two counts differ: the tree has one internal node per step, but only the steps — not the nodes — equal the word length.

Takeaway. GNF makes derivation length equal to word length, which is exactly why the grammar-to-PDA construction needs no ε-moves in this normal form.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which class of grammars generates exactly the deterministic context-free languages?
questions.question_html: Which class of grammars generates exactly the deterministic context-free languages?
options: LL(1) grammars
unambiguous context-free grammars
LR(1) grammars
context-free grammars in Chomsky Normal Form
options_html: LL(1) grammars
unambiguous context-free grammars
LR(1) grammars
context-free grammars in Chomsky Normal Form
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Knuth's theorem: the languages generated by LR(1) grammars are exactly the deterministic context-free languages. LR(1) parsing is a deterministic left-to-right procedure with one symbol of lookahead, which is precisely the power of a DPDA.

Step by step.

  1. An LR(1) parser is a deterministic pushdown machine: a stack of states plus a lookahead symbol drives shift and reduce decisions. So every LR(1) language is accepted by a DPDA.
  2. Conversely, from a DPDA one can construct an LR(1)-style grammar (equivalently a deterministic parser) that generates the same language, so every DCFL has an LR(1) grammar.
  3. Hence the two classes coincide.

Answer: Option (C) — LR(1) grammars.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) LL(1) grammars are strictly weaker than LR(1): they cannot handle left recursion, and they generate only a proper subclass of the DCFLs.
  • (B) unambiguous grammars generate strictly more. Every DCFL is unambiguous, but the unambiguous CFLs properly contain the DCFLs.
  • (D) Chomsky Normal Form is a shape restriction, not a determinism restriction — every CFL, deterministic or not, has a CNF grammar.

Common misconception. Equating "unambiguous" with "deterministic". Every DCFL is unambiguous, but not every unambiguous CFL is a DCFL; the two classes differ at the grammar level, not just at the machine level.

Takeaway. DCFL = LR(1) languages = languages of DPDAs. Three descriptions, one class.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Select every statement about normal forms, the grammar-to-NPDA construction and decidability that is TRUE .
questions.question_html: Select every statement about normal forms, the grammar-to-NPDA construction and decidability that is TRUE.
options: Every context-free grammar can be converted into an equivalent grammar in which every production has the form A → BC or A → a , apart from a possible single production S → ε .
Every context-free language is accepted by some NPDA with a single state.
The deterministic context-free languages are exactly the languages generated by LR(1) grammars.
It is decidable whether a given context-free grammar is ambiguous.
options_html: Every context-free grammar can be converted into an equivalent grammar in which every production has the form A → BC or A → a, apart from a possible single production S → ε.
Every context-free language is accepted by some NPDA with a single state.
The deterministic context-free languages are exactly the languages generated by LR(1) grammars.
It is decidable whether a given context-free grammar is ambiguous.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Three classical results hold: Chomsky Normal Form exists for every CFL, the grammar-to-NPDA construction needs one state, and LR(1) grammars characterise the DCFLs. Ambiguity, by contrast, is undecidable for context-free grammars.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true. Eliminate ε-productions (keeping at most S → ε), eliminate unit productions, then break long right sides with fresh variables and replace terminals in mixed right sides by variables that derive them.
  2. (B) true. One state, initial stack Z₀S, a move per production that pops the left side and pushes the right side, and a move per terminal that pops it after reading. Acceptance is by empty stack.
  3. (C) true. Knuth's theorem: an LR(1) parser is a DPDA, and every DCFL has an LR(1) grammar.
  4. (D) false. Ambiguity of a CFG is undecidable. Deciding it would also settle equivalence of CFGs, which is undecidable too: a word with two derivations cannot be found by any general algorithm.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Assuming that because membership and emptiness are decidable for CFLs, ambiguity must be as well. The decidable/undecidable boundary is: membership, emptiness, finiteness and intersection with a regular set are decidable; ambiguity, equivalence, disjointness and universality are not.

Takeaway. Learn the CFL decision table as a block — it is a favourite GATE question and the exceptions are always the same four.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: In the standard construction of a context-free grammar from a pushdown automaton, the variables are triples [q, A, p] . The production [q, A, p] → a [r, X, s] [s, Y, p] is created from which kind of move?
questions.question_html: In the standard construction of a context-free grammar from a pushdown automaton, the variables are triples [q, A, p]. The production [q, A, p] → a [r, X, s] [s, Y, p] is created from which kind of move?
options: a move δ(q, a, A) ∋ (r, X Y) , which reads a and replaces A by X Y
a move δ(q, a, A) ∋ (r, Y X) , which reads a and replaces A by Y X
a move δ(q, ε, A) ∋ (r, X Y) , which reads nothing and replaces A by X Y
a move δ(r, a, X) ∋ (q, A) , which reads a and replaces X by A
options_html: a move δ(q, a, A) ∋ (r, X Y), which reads a and replaces A by X Y
a move δ(q, a, A) ∋ (r, Y X), which reads a and replaces A by Y X
a move δ(q, ε, A) ∋ (r, X Y), which reads nothing and replaces A by X Y
a move δ(r, a, X) ∋ (q, A), which reads a and replaces X by A
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The variable [q, A, p] generates exactly the strings that take the PDA from state q with A on top of the stack to state p having popped that A and nothing more. A move that replaces A by two symbols must therefore be split into two stages, sharing an intermediate state s.

Step by step.

  1. Suppose δ(q, a, A) ∋ (r, X Y): the machine reads a, moves to r and puts X above Y, so X is the new top.
  2. Afterwards [r, X, s] must consume a string that pops X and lands in some state s; then [s, Y, p] must pop Y and land in p.
  3. So the production is [q, A, p] → a [r, X, s] [s, Y, p], taken over every possible intermediate state s. Note the order: X is popped before Y, which matches the stack discipline.
  4. If the move were (r, Y X) the two variables would appear in the opposite order; if it consumed nothing the leading terminal a would be absent.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) reverses the push order, which would generate the two parts of the string in the wrong sequence.
  • (C) would give a production with no terminal at all, but the given production starts with a.
  • (D) has the states and symbols in the wrong roles: q is the state the variable starts from, not the one it ends in.

Common misconception. Forgetting the shared intermediate state s. The two halves of the pushed string are consumed one after the other, so the state where the first half ends must be the state where the second half begins — that is why the construction sums over all s and why the grammar has |Q|²|Γ| variables.

Takeaway. Read [q, A, p] as "from q to p popping A", and every production of the construction writes itself.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let G be the grammar S → aSb | ab . The standard construction turns G into a single-state NPDA that accepts by empty stack, with initial stack Z₀S . Consider the accepting computation for the string aabb . What is the largest number of symbols that are ever on the stack at the same time, counting Z₀ ?
questions.question_html: Let G be the grammar S → aSb | ab. The standard construction turns G into a single-state NPDA that accepts by empty stack, with initial stack Z₀S. Consider the accepting computation for the string aabb. What is the largest number of symbols that are ever on the stack at the same time, counting Z₀?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. In the single-state construction a production A → X₁…Xₖ is simulated by popping A and pushing the right side so that X₁ ends on top, and a terminal a is matched by a move that pops a after reading it. The stack therefore traces the unexpanded frontier of the derivation, leftmost symbol on top.

Step by step.

  1. Start: stack Z₀ S — height 2.
  2. The derivation is S ⇒ aSb ⇒ aabb. First S → aSb: pop S and push b then S, giving Z₀ b S with S on top — height 3.
  3. Now S → ab: pop S and push b then a, giving Z₀ b b a — height 4. This is the maximum.
  4. Read a: pop it, stack Z₀ b b — height 3. Read b: height 2. Read b: height 1, stack Z₀. The final ε-move pops Z₀ and the stack is empty — height 0.
  5. No configuration in this computation holds more than 4 symbols.

Answer: 4.

Common misconception. Counting the pushed symbols but forgetting Z₀, which gives 3; or tracing the derivation left to right instead of tracing the stack, which mixes up the order in which the b's are matched.

Takeaway. In this construction the stack is the pending frontier with the leftmost symbol on top, so its height is the number of symbols still to be expanded or matched — count it after every move.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following claims about unambiguous grammars, deterministic languages and ambiguity is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following claims about unambiguous grammars, deterministic languages and ambiguity is TRUE?
options: Every unambiguous context-free grammar generates a deterministic context-free language.
Every context-free language is a deterministic context-free language.
Ambiguity of a context-free grammar is decidable, and a grammar is ambiguous exactly when its language is not deterministic context-free.
The deterministic context-free languages are exactly the languages generated by LR(1) grammars.
options_html: Every unambiguous context-free grammar generates a deterministic context-free language.
Every context-free language is a deterministic context-free language.
Ambiguity of a context-free grammar is decidable, and a grammar is ambiguous exactly when its language is not deterministic context-free.
The deterministic context-free languages are exactly the languages generated by LR(1) grammars.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The correct statement is Knuth's characterisation: LR(1) grammars generate exactly the DCFLs. The three distractors each collapse a genuine distinction — unambiguous versus deterministic, CFL versus DCFL, and decidable versus undecidable.

Step by step.

  1. (D) true. An LR(1) parser is a deterministic pushdown machine with one symbol of lookahead, and conversely every DPDA yields an LR(1) grammar for its language.
  2. (A) false. Unambiguity is a property of grammars and determinism a property of machines, and the classes differ: the unambiguous CFLs properly contain the DCFLs, so an unambiguous grammar can generate a language that no DPDA accepts.
  3. (B) false. {w wᴿ : w ∈ {a, b}*} is context-free, but no DPDA accepts it because the middle of the word must be guessed.
  4. (C) false twice over. Ambiguity of a CFG is undecidable, and "grammar ambiguous" is not equivalent to "language not a DCFL" — the grammar S → SS | a is ambiguous yet generates the regular language a⁺, which is certainly a DCFL.

Answer: Option (D).

Common misconception. Equating the four notions grammar/language and ambiguous/deterministic. A grammar can be ambiguous while its language is deterministic; a language can be unambiguous while no DPDA accepts it; and the decidability of neither property follows from the other.

Takeaway. Keep two separate ladders — grammars (CFG ⊃ unambiguous ⊃ LR(1)) and languages (CFL ⊃ unambiguous CFL ⊃ DCFL) — with LR(1) grammars generating exactly the DCFLs.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Select every statement about the standard grammar-to-NPDA and PDA-to-grammar constructions that is TRUE .
questions.question_html: Select every statement about the standard grammar-to-NPDA and PDA-to-grammar constructions that is TRUE.
options: Every language generated by a grammar in Greibach Normal Form is accepted by an NPDA with a single state.
The class of languages accepted by deterministic pushdown automata is exactly the class of context-free languages.
Every context-free language that does not contain ε is generated by some grammar in Chomsky Normal Form.
The class of languages accepted by deterministic pushdown automata is a proper subclass of the context-free languages.
options_html: Every language generated by a grammar in Greibach Normal Form is accepted by an NPDA with a single state.
The class of languages accepted by deterministic pushdown automata is exactly the class of context-free languages.
Every context-free language that does not contain ε is generated by some grammar in Chomsky Normal Form.
The class of languages accepted by deterministic pushdown automata is a proper subclass of the context-free languages.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. NPDAs match context-free grammars exactly; DPDAs match only the deterministic part of that class. Normal forms are shape restrictions that preserve the language, so they never change the class.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true. In Greibach Normal Form every production is A → aα, so the single-state construction produces a machine with no ε-moves: each move reads exactly one terminal. One state suffices because the stack carries all the information.
  2. (B) false. {w wᴿ : w ∈ {a, b}*} is context-free but no DPDA accepts it.
  3. (C) true. With ε ∉ L no ε-productions are needed; eliminate unit productions, then binarise and terminalise the right sides, and every production becomes A → BC or A → a.
  4. (D) true. Every DPDA is an NPDA, so the deterministic class is contained in the context-free class, and by (B) the containment is strict.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Believing (B) because both machine models are called "pushdown automata". The word deterministic changes the class: DPDA = DCFL, NPDA = CFL, and the gap contains exactly the languages that need a guess.

Takeaway. Grammar to NPDA is an equivalence; grammar to DPDA is not, and no normal form closes that gap.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: A Turing machine is restricted so that its head may move only to the right: it may overwrite the cell it is reading, but it never revisits a cell, and its tape is infinite in that direction only. Which class of languages can such a machine accept?
questions.question_html: A Turing machine is restricted so that its head may move only to the right: it may overwrite the cell it is reading, but it never revisits a cell, and its tape is infinite in that direction only. Which class of languages can such a machine accept?
options: Exactly the context-free languages.
Exactly the context-sensitive languages.
Exactly the regular languages.
Exactly the recursively enumerable languages.
options_html: Exactly the context-free languages.
Exactly the context-sensitive languages.
Exactly the regular languages.
Exactly the recursively enumerable languages.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A machine whose head never moves left reads its input once, from left to right, and everything it does afterwards depends only on its current state and the symbol under the head. That is precisely the behaviour of a deterministic finite automaton, with the write operation added as output that nobody ever reads again.

Step by step.

  1. The sequence of symbols the head reads is fixed in advance: the input symbols w₁w₂…wₙ, followed by blanks forever. The machine cannot influence what it will read next.
  2. So the state after reading k symbols is a function of the previous state and the k-th symbol only — the finite transition table of a DFA, with states Q and alphabet Γ.
  3. Acceptance means that this run passes through a state marked accepting, which is exactly acceptance by a finite automaton. The language is therefore regular.
  4. Conversely every DFA is such a machine (it simply never writes), so the class is exactly the regular languages.

Answer: Option (C) — exactly the regular languages.

Common misconception. “It has an unbounded tape and can write, so it must be at least as strong as a pushdown automaton.” Writing is worthless if the written symbol is never read again: the machine cannot use the tape as memory. The opposite error — “it can accept nothing because it cannot go back” — is also wrong; it accepts, for instance, all strings containing a 1.
