questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let L be an infinite recursively enumerable language. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Let L be an infinite recursively enumerable language. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: Every infinite subset of L is recursively enumerable.
L is recursive, because an infinite language has infinitely many strings and therefore all of them can be listed.
L contains no infinite subset that is recursive, since L need not be recursive itself.
L contains an infinite subset that is recursive.
options_html: Every infinite subset of L is recursively enumerable.
L is recursive, because an infinite language has infinitely many strings and therefore all of them can be listed.
L contains no infinite subset that is recursive, since L need not be recursive itself.
L contains an infinite subset that is recursive.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An infinite language over a finite alphabet has strings of unbounded length. That unboundedness can be exploited: keep, from an enumeration of L, only those strings that are longer than every string kept so far. The kept strings come out in strictly increasing order of length, and such an enumeration can be used as a decision procedure.

Step by step.

  1. Let M enumerate L without repetition, which is possible because L is r.e.
  2. Define S to be the set of strings that the enumerator prints and that are strictly longer than every string printed before them. Since L is infinite its strings have unbounded length, so S is infinite.
  3. To decide whether a given w lies in S: run the enumerator, keeping track of the longest string kept so far, and stop as soon as a string longer than w is kept. That happens after finitely many steps, because lengths in S are unbounded.
  4. w ∈ S exactly when w was one of the strings kept before the process stopped. So S is recursive, infinite, and a subset of L.

Answer: Option (D).

Common misconception. “A subset of a non-recursive set must be non-recursive.” Subsets inherit nothing: Σ* is recursive, yet it has non-recursive subsets, and every infinite set has both recursive and non-recursive infinite subsets. Option (A) fails for the same reason in the other direction — K is r.e. and has subsets that are not r.e.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following problems is decidable?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following problems is decidable?
options: Given a Turing machine M, does M halt when started on the empty tape?
Given a linear-bounded automaton A and a string w, does A halt on w?
Given a Turing machine M, does M ever write the blank symbol on its tape?
Given a Turing machine M, does M halt on every input?
options_html: Given a Turing machine M, does M halt when started on the empty tape?
Given a linear-bounded automaton A and a string w, does A halt on w?
Given a Turing machine M, does M ever write the blank symbol on its tape?
Given a Turing machine M, does M halt on every input?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Undecidability of halting comes from the unbounded tape: a run can be arbitrarily long, so “not yet halted” never becomes “never halts”. Bound the tape to the input and the configuration space becomes finite, so a repetition is detectable and the run can be cut short.

Step by step.

  1. A linear-bounded automaton on input w of length n uses exactly the n input cells, so it has at most |Q| · n · |Γ|ⁿ configurations.
  2. Simulate A on w step by step, recording each configuration. After more than |Q| · n · |Γ|ⁿ steps some configuration must repeat, and from a repeated configuration the run cycles forever.
  3. So the decider halts within that bound with the correct answer: the machine halts if a halting state is reached, and loops otherwise.
  4. Options (A), (C) and (D) are all properties of unbounded runs and are undecidable by reduction from the halting problem.

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. “Halting is undecidable, so it is undecidable for every machine model.” The halting problem is undecidable for machines with unbounded storage; for finite-state devices and for bounded-tape machines it is decidable. This is the same reason the emptiness problem is decidable for DFAs and undecidable for Turing machines.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Rice's theorem speaks about properties of the language L(M). Which one of the following properties is a property of L(M) rather than of the machine M?
questions.question_html: Rice's theorem speaks about properties of the language L(M). Which one of the following properties is a property of L(M) rather than of the machine M?
options: M has exactly three states.
M never moves its head to the left.
The string 0110 belongs to L(M).
The transition table of M contains the symbol 1.
options_html: M has exactly three states.
M never moves its head to the left.
The string 0110 belongs to L(M).
The transition table of M contains the symbol 1.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A property is semantic — a property of L(M) — when it is determined entirely by which strings the machine accepts, so that two machines accepting the same language must agree on it. A syntactic property is a property of the code and can differ between two machines with identical languages.

Step by step.

  1. (A) counts states — a feature of the description, not of the accepted set. Two machines with the same language may have 3 and 30 states.
  2. (B) describes the motion of the head, again a feature of the description. A machine can be rewritten to sweep left and right without changing its language.
  3. (C) asks whether a particular string is accepted. That is decided by the set L(M) alone: any two machines with the same language give the same answer.
  4. (D) refers to symbols in the transition table, a property of the encoding.

Answer: Option (C).

Common misconception. Assuming that every property of a Turing machine falls under Rice's theorem. It applies only to semantic properties; syntactic ones such as (A), (B) and (D) may well be decidable — (A) certainly is, since the description can be read off directly.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following statements about the four classes of the Chomsky hierarchy is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following statements about the four classes of the Chomsky hierarchy is TRUE?
options: The context-sensitive languages equal the recursively enumerable languages.
Each of the inclusions regular ⊂ context-free ⊂ context-sensitive ⊂ recursively enumerable is strict.
The context-free languages equal the context-sensitive languages.
The recursively enumerable languages are a proper subset of the context-sensitive languages.
options_html: The context-sensitive languages equal the recursively enumerable languages.
Each of the inclusions regular ⊂ context-free ⊂ context-sensitive ⊂ recursively enumerable is strict.
The context-free languages equal the context-sensitive languages.
The recursively enumerable languages are a proper subset of the context-sensitive languages.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Each level of the hierarchy adds exactly one kind of power: finite memory (regular), one stack (context-free), a tape bounded by the input (context-sensitive), an unbounded tape (r.e.). Each addition is genuine, so each inclusion is strict.

Step by step.

  1. {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1} is context-free but not regular, so regular ⊊ context-free.
  2. {aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 1} is context-sensitive but not context-free, so context-free ⊊ context-sensitive.
  3. The halting problem is r.e. and undecidable, while every context-sensitive language is decidable, so context-sensitive ⊊ r.e.
  4. Options (A) and (C) contradict (2) and (3); option (D) reverses the chain.

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Reading the chain as a list of conventions rather than of strict inclusions, and so accepting (A) — “both are decidable-ish”. Context-sensitive languages are decided by bounded-tape machines; r.e. languages are only recognised, and the halting problem separates the two levels.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the standard Turing machine are TRUE? Select all that apply.
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about the standard Turing machine are TRUE? Select all that apply.
options: The tape is unbounded, yet every configuration of the machine is a finite object.
Every Turing machine can be simulated by one whose tape alphabet is {␣, 0, 1}.
A Turing machine with a fixed number of states has only finitely many configurations in total.
Every Turing machine must have at least one accepting state.
options_html: The tape is unbounded, yet every configuration of the machine is a finite object.
Every Turing machine can be simulated by one whose tape alphabet is {␣, 0, 1}.
A Turing machine with a fixed number of states has only finitely many configurations in total.
Every Turing machine must have at least one accepting state.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A configuration is the triple (state, head position, tape contents). The tape is infinite, but at any moment all but finitely many cells hold the blank, so the contents can be written as a finite string, and the triple is a finite description.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true. After finitely many steps only finitely many cells can differ from the blank, so each configuration is a finite object even though the tape is not.
  2. (B) true. Replace each symbol of the original alphabet by a fixed block of binary digits; one step of the original machine becomes a fixed number of steps over the new alphabet, so the accepted language is unchanged.
  3. (C) false. The head position is unbounded and the tape contents can be arbitrarily long, so there are infinitely many configurations. Finiteness holds only when the tape length is bounded, as for a linear-bounded automaton.
  4. (D) false. A machine may have no accepting state at all; then it accepts nothing. Nothing in the definition forces an accepting state to exist.

Answer: Options (A and B).

Common misconception. Reading “unbounded tape” as “infinitely many configurations at each instant”. The unboundedness is over time and over possible runs; a single configuration is always finite. The finiteness of the configuration set is what makes bounded-tape machines decidable, so mixing the two up costs marks in both this unit and the decidability questions that follow.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the size of these classes are TRUE? Select all that apply.
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about the size of these classes are TRUE? Select all that apply.
options: The set of all Turing machines over a fixed finite tape alphabet is countably infinite.
Every language over the alphabet {0, 1} is recursively enumerable.
The set of all recursively enumerable languages over {0, 1} is countably infinite.
The set of all languages over the alphabet {0, 1} is countably infinite.
options_html: The set of all Turing machines over a fixed finite tape alphabet is countably infinite.
Every language over the alphabet {0, 1} is recursively enumerable.
The set of all recursively enumerable languages over {0, 1} is countably infinite.
The set of all languages over the alphabet {0, 1} is countably infinite.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Every Turing machine over a fixed finite alphabet is a finite object, and a finite object can be encoded as a finite string over a fixed alphabet, so the machines can be listed: countably many. A language is an arbitrary set of strings, and the set of all such sets has the cardinality of the power set of a countable set, which is uncountable.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true. Order all strings over the encoding alphabet by length and then lexicographically, and keep those that are valid encodings of machines. This lists every machine exactly once, so the set is countably infinite.
  2. (C) true. Each r.e. language is L(M) for some machine M, and there are only countably many machines, so there are at most countably many r.e. languages; there are infinitely many of them, for instance all finite languages.
  3. (D) false. The languages over {0, 1} correspond to subsets of the countable set {0, 1}*, and the power set of a countable set is uncountable — by the same diagonal argument that shows ℝ is uncountable.
  4. (B) false. Uncountably many languages exist but only countably many are r.e., so almost every language is not r.e.

Answer: Options (A and C).

Common misconception. Believing that “there are only countably many languages because there are only countably many strings”. The strings are countable, but a language is a set of strings, and the collection of all sets of a countable set is uncountable. This counting argument is the reason non-r.e. languages must exist even before any specific one is exhibited.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which of the following statements about Rice's theorem are TRUE? Select all that apply.
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about Rice's theorem are TRUE? Select all that apply.
options: It applies only to properties of the language L(M), and not to properties of the machine's code.
It shows that {⟨M⟩ : M has an even number of states} is undecidable.
It shows that every undecidable language has the form {⟨M⟩ : L(M) has the property P} for some property P.
It applies only to non-trivial properties, that is, properties that some r.e. language has and some other r.e. language does not.
options_html: It applies only to properties of the language L(M), and not to properties of the machine's code.
It shows that {⟨M⟩ : M has an even number of states} is undecidable.
It shows that every undecidable language has the form {⟨M⟩ : L(M) has the property P} for some property P.
It applies only to non-trivial properties, that is, properties that some r.e. language has and some other r.e. language does not.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Rice's theorem: for any non-trivial semantic property P — non-trivial meaning that P holds for at least one r.e. language and fails for at least one — the language {⟨M⟩ : P(L(M))} is undecidable.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true. The theorem is about the set L(M). If a property can distinguish two machines with the same language, the theorem says nothing about it.
  2. (D) true. Trivial properties are excluded for a reason: if every r.e. language has P, the language is all of Σ*, which is decidable; if no r.e. language has P, it is ∅, also decidable.
  3. (B) false. “M has an even number of states” is a property of the description. It is in fact decidable: read the number of states off the encoding.
  4. (C) false. The theorem says that every non-trivial semantic property yields an undecidable language; it does not say that every undecidable language arises that way. {⟨M⟩ : M halts on ε} is undecidable and is not of that form.

Answer: Options (A and D).

Common misconception. Treating Rice's theorem as a complete characterisation of undecidability. It is a one-way tool: semantic and non-trivial implies undecidable. It says nothing about syntactic properties and nothing about the many undecidable languages that are not of the form “L(M) has P”.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: For the Chomsky hierarchy, which of the following membership and closure facts are TRUE? Select all that apply.
questions.question_html: For the Chomsky hierarchy, which of the following membership and closure facts are TRUE? Select all that apply.
options: Every regular language is context-sensitive.
Membership of a string in a context-free language can be decided.
The context-sensitive languages are closed under complementation.
The context-free languages are closed under intersection.
options_html: Every regular language is context-sensitive.
Membership of a string in a context-free language can be decided.
The context-sensitive languages are closed under complementation.
The context-free languages are closed under intersection.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The hierarchy is a chain of inclusions, and each level has its own closure table. Two entries of that table are counter-intuitive: the context-free languages are closed under complementation, but not under intersection.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true. Regular ⊂ context-free ⊂ context-sensitive, so every regular language is context-sensitive.
  2. (B) true. CYK on the Chomsky normal form decides membership in time O(n³).
  3. (C) true. The context-sensitive languages are closed under complementation — the Immerman–Szelepcsényi theorem, proved in 1988, which also earned the authors the Gödel Prize.
  4. (D) false. {aⁿbⁿcᵐ : n, m ≥ 1} and {aᵐbⁿcⁿ : n, m ≥ 1} are both context-free, but their intersection is {aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 1}, which is not. Closure under union, concatenation and star does hold.

Answer: Options (A, B and C).

Common misconception. Believing that closure under complementation and closure under intersection always travel together. For the context-free languages they do not: complementation holds, intersection fails. The pair is a favourite GATE trap precisely because the intuition runs the other way.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Five languages are listed below, where M ranges over all Turing machines and ε is the empty string. (i) {⟨M⟩ : M halts on ε within 100 steps} (ii) {⟨M⟩ : M halts on ε} (iii) {⟨M⟩ : M never moves its head to the left of its starting cell when run on ε} (iv) {⟨M⟩ : M has at most 3 states and L(M) ≠ ∅} (v) {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = ∅} How many of these five are decidable?
questions.question_html:
Five languages are listed below, where M ranges over all Turing machines and ε is the empty string.
(i) {⟨M⟩ : M halts on ε within 100 steps}
(ii) {⟨M⟩ : M halts on ε}
(iii) {⟨M⟩ : M never moves its head to the left of its starting cell when run on ε}
(iv) {⟨M⟩ : M has at most 3 states and L(M) ≠ ∅}
(v) {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = ∅}
How many of these five are decidable?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A language is decidable if a machine always answers it in finite time. Bounded simulation gives decidability; a finite candidate set gives decidability for a different reason — every finite language is decidable, whatever its members are.

Step by step.

  1. (i) decidable. Simulate 100 steps; the bound is a constant.
  2. (ii) undecidable. This is the halting problem on ε, undecidable by reduction from HALT.
  3. (iii) undecidable. Whether the head ever leaves the starting cell is a question about the whole run, and it is undecidable for the same reason as halting: a negative answer requires ruling out arbitrarily long runs.
  4. (iv) decidable. There are only finitely many machines with at most 3 states over a fixed alphabet, so this language is finite, and every finite language is decidable — a lookup table decides it, even though nobody may know which entries are which.
  5. (v) undecidable. By Rice's theorem, emptiness is a non-trivial property of L(M).

Decidable: (i) and (iv), so the count is 2.

Answer: 2.

Common misconception. Marking (iv) undecidable because “we do not know which 3-state machines have non-empty languages”. Not knowing the answer is different from the problem being undecidable: a finite set is decidable in principle, since one of the finitely many lookup tables answers it. The other common slip is marking (iii) decidable because the machine starts on a single cell — the question is about the whole, possibly unbounded, run.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: A nondeterministic Turing machine N decides a language L, and on every input of length n every branch of its computation has length at most t(n). Which one of the following statements about simulating N by a deterministic Turing machine is TRUE?
questions.question_html: A nondeterministic Turing machine N decides a language L, and on every input of length n every branch of its computation has length at most t(n). Which one of the following statements about simulating N by a deterministic Turing machine is TRUE?
options: A deterministic machine simulates N in time O(t(n)²), by exploring the computation tree breadth-first.
A deterministic machine simulates N in time 2^{O(t(n))} by exploring the computation tree; whether some deterministic machine can do it in polynomial time is not known.
A deterministic machine simulates N in time O(t(n)), by keeping every branch on the tape at once.
No deterministic machine can simulate N at all, because nondeterministic machines accept strictly more languages.
options_html: A deterministic machine simulates N in time O(t(n)²), by exploring the computation tree breadth-first.
A deterministic machine simulates N in time 2^{O(t(n))} by exploring the computation tree; whether some deterministic machine can do it in polynomial time is not known.
A deterministic machine simulates N in time O(t(n)), by keeping every branch on the tape at once.
No deterministic machine can simulate N at all, because nondeterministic machines accept strictly more languages.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A nondeterministic machine is a tree of computations, not a line. Simulating it deterministically means visiting that tree, and the tree is exponentially wide: at every step a branch splits into at most b = |Q| · |Γ| · 2 children, a constant. A tree of depth t(n) with branching b has at most b^{t(n)} nodes.

Step by step.

  1. Search the tree of configurations in breadth-first order, so that a branch that halts after few steps is not hidden behind a branch that loops.
  2. The search visits at most b^{t(n)} = 2^{O(t(n))} nodes, and each node costs a constant number of steps to record and expand.
  3. Polynomial simulation would put every language decided by a polynomial-time nondeterministic machine into P, that is, it would prove P = NP. No such simulation is known.
  4. Option (D) is false: a nondeterministic machine accepts exactly the same class as a deterministic one — the recursively enumerable languages — because a deterministic machine can always simulate all branches.

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Treating the simulation as “quadratic”, by analogy with the multi-tape simulation. That analogy is wrong: the cost here is exponential in the running time, not polynomial in it, because it is the number of branches rather than the amount of tape that multiplies.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let Ld = {⟨M⟩ : M is a Turing machine and M does not accept ⟨M⟩} be the diagonal language. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Let Ld = {⟨M⟩ : M is a Turing machine and M does not accept ⟨M⟩} be the diagonal language. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: Ld is recursively enumerable but not recursive.
Ld is not recursively enumerable, while its complement is recursively enumerable but not recursive.
Ld is recursive, because M can simply be run on ⟨M⟩ and the answer inverted.
Both Ld and its complement are recursively enumerable.
options_html: Ld is recursively enumerable but not recursive.
Ld is not recursively enumerable, while its complement is recursively enumerable but not recursive.
Ld is recursive, because M can simply be run on ⟨M⟩ and the answer inverted.
Both Ld and its complement are recursively enumerable.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The diagonal language is the set of machines that do not accept their own description. Its complement, K = {⟨M⟩ : M accepts ⟨M⟩}, is recognisable by a universal machine; the diagonal language itself is the classic example of a set that is not even r.e.

Step by step.

  1. K is r.e.: on input ⟨M⟩, simulate M on ⟨M⟩ and accept when that simulation accepts. If M does not accept, the simulation may run forever, so this recogniser need not halt.
  2. Ld is not r.e.: if some machine D accepted exactly Ld, then D accepts ⟨D⟩ exactly when ⟨D⟩ ∉ Ld, that is, exactly when D does not accept ⟨D⟩ — a contradiction.
  3. Since K is r.e. and Ld is not, K is not recursive either: if it were, its complement would be recursive and hence r.e.
  4. Option (C) fails exactly at the point that makes the halting problem hard: running M on ⟨M⟩ may never terminate, so the answer cannot be inverted in finite time.

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Supposing that complementing a recogniser is easy. Complementing a decider is easy; complementing a recogniser is not, because “has not accepted yet” is not the same as “will never accept”. This is exactly why the r.e. languages are not closed under complementation.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following languages is NOT recursively enumerable?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following languages is NOT recursively enumerable?
options: {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w}
{⟨M⟩ : M halts on ε within 10 steps}
{⟨M⟩ : M does not halt on ε}
options_html: {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w}
{⟨M⟩ : L(M) ≠ ∅}
{⟨M⟩ : M halts on ε within 10 steps}
{⟨M⟩ : M does not halt on ε}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Positive questions — “there exists a run that halts” — are r.e., because a halting run can be exhibited by simulation. Negative questions — “no run ever halts” — are the co-r.e. side and generally are not r.e.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is the halting problem, r.e.: simulate and accept when the simulation stops.
  2. (B) is r.e.: dovetail M over all inputs and accept as soon as one input is accepted.
  3. (C) is decidable, hence r.e.: simulate exactly 10 steps and look at the result.
  4. (D) is the complement of the r.e. non-recursive language {⟨M⟩ : M halts on ε}, so it is not r.e. — otherwise the halting problem on ε would be decidable.

Answer: Option (D).

Common misconception. Believing that the complement of an r.e. language is r.e. The r.e. languages are closed under union and intersection but not under complementation, and (D) is exactly that failure. Note also that (D) is co-r.e.: a machine can confirm non-halting by waiting, never by concluding.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let EMPTY = {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = ∅} and let NE be its complement. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Let EMPTY = {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = ∅} and let NE be its complement. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: EMPTY is recursively enumerable but not recursive.
EMPTY is decidable, because a machine can be run on every input in parallel and will never accept anything if the language is empty.
Neither EMPTY nor NE is recursively enumerable.
EMPTY is co-recursively enumerable but not recursively enumerable, while NE is recursively enumerable.
options_html: EMPTY is recursively enumerable but not recursive.
EMPTY is decidable, because a machine can be run on every input in parallel and will never accept anything if the language is empty.
Neither EMPTY nor NE is recursively enumerable.
EMPTY is co-recursively enumerable but not recursively enumerable, while NE is recursively enumerable.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. “Non-empty” is an existential statement about the language — some string is accepted — so it can be confirmed by finding one witness. “Empty” is a universal statement — no string is ever accepted — so it can never be confirmed by a finite amount of simulation.

Step by step.

  1. NE is r.e.: on input ⟨M⟩, dovetail M over all strings x₁, x₂, …, and accept as soon as any simulation accepts. If L(M) ≠ ∅ this happens after finitely many steps.
  2. EMPTY is the complement of an r.e. language and is therefore co-r.e. by definition.
  3. EMPTY is not r.e.: if both EMPTY and NE were r.e., EMPTY would be decidable, contradicting Rice's theorem, since emptiness is a non-trivial property of L(M).
  4. Option (B) mistakes a recogniser for a decider: running in parallel never tells you that nothing will ever be accepted, so it can confirm non-emptiness but never emptiness.

Answer: Option (D).

Common misconception. Placing the existential and universal sides the same way round. A good rule: a “there exists” question about L(M) tends to be r.e., a “for all” question tends to be co-r.e., and undecidability by Rice's theorem holds in both cases.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following problems is undecidable?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following problems is undecidable?
options: Given a context-free grammar G and a string w, is w ∈ L(G)?
Given a context-free grammar G, is L(G) = ∅?
Given two context-free grammars G₁ and G₂, is L(G₁) = L(G₂)?
Given a regular expression r and a string w, is w ∈ L(r)?
options_html: Given a context-free grammar G and a string w, is w ∈ L(G)?
Given a context-free grammar G, is L(G) = ∅?
Given two context-free grammars G₁ and G₂, is L(G₁) = L(G₂)?
Given a regular expression r and a string w, is w ∈ L(r)?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The context-free class has a sharp and slightly surprising boundary: membership, emptiness and finiteness are decidable, while equivalence, universality, ambiguity, disjointness and inclusion are not. Equivalence of CFGs is undecidable because it would decide the Post correspondence problem, and because deciding whether a grammar is ambiguous is already undecidable.

Step by step.

  1. (A) decidable. Convert G to Chomsky normal form and run the CYK algorithm: O(n³ · |G|) time.
  2. (B) decidable. Mark the productive non-terminals — those that can derive a terminal string — by iterating over the productions until nothing changes; L(G) = ∅ exactly when the start symbol is not productive.
  3. (D) decidable. Convert r to an NFA and simulate it on w.
  4. (C) undecidable. Equivalence of two context-free grammars is undecidable; it subsumes deciding whether a grammar generates Σ*, which in turn decides ambiguity.

Answer: Option (C).

Common misconception. Extending the decidability of membership to every natural question about CFGs. A useful memory hook: questions about one grammar are usually decidable, questions comparing two grammars, or asking about all strings, usually are not. The same split holds for regular languages only in part — equivalence of DFAs is decidable, because a DFA has no stack.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let L₁ and L₂ be recursively enumerable, accepted by Turing machines M₁ and M₂. A machine D, on input w, simulates M₁ on w and M₂ on w in parallel — one step of each, alternately — and halts and accepts when both simulations have accepted. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Let L₁ and L₂ be recursively enumerable, accepted by Turing machines M₁ and M₂. A machine D, on input w, simulates M₁ on w and M₂ on w in parallel — one step of each, alternately — and halts and accepts when both simulations have accepted. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: D decides L₁ ∩ L₂, because running the two simulations in parallel guarantees that D halts on every input.
D accepts exactly L₁ ∪ L₂, because it stops as soon as one of the two simulations accepts.
D accepts exactly L₁ ∩ L₂, so the intersection of two r.e. languages is r.e.; D does not decide it, because it may run forever when w ∉ L₁ ∩ L₂.
D is not a legal Turing machine, because no machine can simulate two machines at the same time.
options_html: D decides L₁ ∩ L₂, because running the two simulations in parallel guarantees that D halts on every input.
D accepts exactly L₁ ∪ L₂, because it stops as soon as one of the two simulations accepts.
D accepts exactly L₁ ∩ L₂, so the intersection of two r.e. languages is r.e.; D does not decide it, because it may run forever when w ∉ L₁ ∩ L₂.
D is not a legal Turing machine, because no machine can simulate two machines at the same time.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Dovetailing: interleave two unbounded computations so that neither can starve the other. The point of interleaving is that M₁ might need a million steps while M₂ needs three; running M₁ to completion first would never reach M₂'s answer.

Step by step.

  1. If w ∈ L₁ ∩ L₂ then both simulations accept after finitely many steps, and D observes both acceptances and halts accepting.
  2. If w ∉ L₁ ∩ L₂ then at least one simulation never accepts. The other may accept, but D waits for both, so D never halts. Hence D accepts exactly L₁ ∩ L₂ and is a recogniser, not a decider.
  3. That is enough to prove closure: a language is r.e. exactly when some machine accepts precisely its members, and D is such a machine for L₁ ∩ L₂.
  4. Interleaving is realised on one tape by a universal machine that keeps a record of both simulations and alternates between them, so option (D) is false.

Answer: Option (C).

Common misconception. “Running in parallel makes the machine total.” Parallel simulation removes the risk of one branch starving another; it does not remove the possibility that a branch never terminates. Only a bound on the number of steps — as in bounded halting — turns a recogniser into a decider.

questions.question: Which one of the following languages is undecidable, yet lies outside the scope of Rice's theorem?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following languages is undecidable, yet lies outside the scope of Rice's theorem?
options: {⟨M⟩ : M halts on ε}
{⟨M⟩ : L(M) is a finite set}
{⟨M⟩ : L(M) contains the string 0101}
options_html: {⟨M⟩ : M halts on ε}
{⟨M⟩ : L(M) is a finite set}
{⟨M⟩ : L(M) = Σ*}
{⟨M⟩ : L(M) contains the string 0101}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Rice's theorem covers exactly the properties of the set L(M). A property of the machine's behaviour on one input is not a property of the set, because two machines with the same language can differ on whether they halt on ε.

Step by step.

  1. (B), (C) and (D) are all statements about which strings the machine accepts, that is, about the set L(M). Each is non-trivial: some r.e. language is finite and some is not; some equals Σ* and some does not; some contains 0101 and some does not. Rice's theorem therefore applies to all three.
  2. (A) is a statement about the run of M on one fixed input, not about the set of accepted strings. Exhibit two machines with the same language: one that halts rejecting ε, and one that loops forever on ε but rejects everything else. Both have empty language; only the first is in (A). So the property is not determined by L(M).
  3. (A) is nevertheless undecidable — it is the halting problem on ε — but that has to be proved by a direct reduction, not by Rice's theorem.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Using Rice's theorem for every undecidability proof. It is a shortcut available only for semantic properties; invoking it for a halting-type question is an argument that does not apply, even though the conclusion happens to be true. In an exam answer the distinction is the mark.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which of the following decision problems can always be settled by an algorithm in finite time? Select all that apply.
questions.question_html: Which of the following decision problems can always be settled by an algorithm in finite time? Select all that apply.
options: Given a context-free grammar G over Σ = {0, 1}, is L(G) = Σ*?
Given a DFA A and a string w, does A accept w?
Given a Turing machine M, does M halt on ε?
Given a Turing machine M, does M halt on ε within 2^{|⟨M⟩|} steps?
options_html: Given a context-free grammar G over Σ = {0, 1}, is L(G) = Σ*?
Given a DFA A and a string w, does A accept w?
Given a Turing machine M, does M halt on ε?
Given a Turing machine M, does M halt on ε within 2^{|⟨M⟩|} steps?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A bounded question is decidable as soon as the bound is a computable function of the input: simulate that many steps and look. An unbounded question about halting is not. Universality of a context-free grammar is the interesting third case — it looks like a finite-state question but is not.

Step by step.

  1. (D) decidable. Read ⟨M⟩, compute the number 2^{|⟨M⟩|}, and simulate M on ε for exactly that many steps. The answer is yes if the simulation has halted, no otherwise. The bound depends only on the input, not on whether M halts.
  2. (B) decidable. Run the DFA on w: at most |w| transitions, then look at the final state.
  3. (C) undecidable. This is the halting problem with a fixed input, and HALT ≤m it.
  4. (A) undecidable. Universality of a context-free grammar is undecidable — it would decide the equivalence of two grammars, and CFG equivalence is undecidable. Contrast emptiness, which is decidable for CFGs.

Answer: Options (B and D).

Common misconception. Marking (A) because “context-free languages are simple”. Membership and emptiness are decidable for CFGs; universality, equivalence, ambiguity and disjointness are not. The dividing line inside the context-free class is worth memorising separately from the hierarchy itself.

questions.question: A Turing machine has states q₀ (scan), q₁ (carry) and qa (accept, a halting state), tape alphabet {␣, 0, 1}, and the transitions below; every pair not listed sends the machine into a halting reject state. The tape is infinite in both directions and the head starts on the leftmost symbol of the input. δ(q₀,0) = (q₀,0,R)   δ(q₀,1) = (q₀,1,R)   δ(q₀,␣) = (q₁,␣,L) δ(q₁,1) = (q₁,0,L)   δ(q₁,0) = (qa,1,L)   δ(q₁,␣) = (qa,1,L) On the input 1011, how many transitions does the machine execute before it halts? Count every transition, including the last one, which enters qa.
questions.question_html:
A Turing machine has states q₀ (scan), q₁ (carry) and qa (accept, a halting state), tape alphabet {␣, 0, 1}, and the transitions below; every pair not listed sends the machine into a halting reject state. The tape is infinite in both directions and the head starts on the leftmost symbol of the input.
δ(q₀,0) = (q₀,0,R)   δ(q₀,1) = (q₀,1,R)   δ(q₀,␣) = (q₁,␣,L)
δ(q₁,1) = (q₁,0,L)   δ(q₁,0) = (qa,1,L)   δ(q₁,␣) = (qa,1,L)
On the input 1011, how many transitions does the machine execute before it halts? Count every transition, including the last one, which enters qa.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A configuration is (state, head position, tape contents); a transition rewrites one cell, moves the head and changes the state. The machine above is the standard “add one to a binary number” machine: q₀ walks right to the blank after the input, and q₁ then walks left turning each 1 into a 0 until it meets a 0, which it turns into a 1 and halts.

Step by step. The cells are numbered from 1, with 1011 in cells 1–4 and blanks elsewhere.

  1. δ(q₀,1) = (q₀,1,R) — cell 1 to cell 2. (step 1)
  2. δ(q₀,0) = (q₀,0,R) — cell 2 to cell 3. (step 2)
  3. δ(q₀,1) = (q₀,1,R) — cell 3 to cell 4. (step 3)
  4. δ(q₀,1) = (q₀,1,R) — cell 4 to cell 5. (step 4)
  5. δ(q₀,␣) = (q₁,␣,L) — the scan ends, the head returns to cell 4. (step 5)
  6. δ(q₁,1) = (q₁,0,L) — cell 4 becomes 0, head at cell 3. (step 6)
  7. δ(q₁,1) = (q₁,0,L) — cell 3 becomes 0, head at cell 2. (step 7)
  8. δ(q₁,0) = (qa,1,L) — cell 2 becomes 1 and the machine halts in qa. (step 8)

The tape now reads 1100, which is 12 = 11 + 1, as it should. The total is 8 transitions: four scanning steps, one turnaround, two carries and one final write.

Answer: 8 steps.

Common misconception. Counting the four scanning steps but forgetting the turnaround transition δ(q₀,␣), which gives 7, or forgetting the last transition into qa, which gives 7 as well. The transition that enters the halting state is a real step — it is the step that writes the final 1.

The machine above is the standard “add one to a binary number” machine: q₀ walks right to the blank after the input, and q₁ then walks left turning each 1 into a 0 until it meets a 0, which it turns into a 1 and halts.Step by step. The cells are numbered from 1, with 1011 in cells 1–4 and blanks elsewhere.δ(q₀,1) = (q₀,1,R) — cell 1 to cell 2. (step 1)δ(q₀,0) = (q₀,0,R) — cell 2 to cell 3. (step 2)δ(q₀,1) = (q₀,1,R) — cell 3 to cell 4. (step 3)δ(q₀,1) = (q₀,1,R) — cell 4 to cell 5. (step 4)δ(q₀,␣) = (q₁,␣,L) — the scan ends, the head returns to cell 4. (step 5)δ(q₁,1) = (q₁,0,L) — cell 4 becomes 0, head at cell 3. (step 6)δ(q₁,1) = (q₁,0,L) — cell 3 becomes 0, head at cell 2. (step 7)δ(q₁,0) = (qa,1,L) — cell 2 becomes 1 and the machine halts in qa. (step 8)The tape now reads 1100, which is 12 = 11 + 1, as it should. The total is 8 transitions: four scanning steps, one turnaround, two carries and one final write.Answer: 8 steps.Common misconception. Counting the four scanning steps but forgetting the turnaround transition δ(q₀,␣), which gives 7, or forgetting the last transition into qa, which gives 7 as well. The transition that enters the halting state is a real step — it is the step that writes the final 1.

questions.question: Consider the four classes: regular, context-free, context-sensitive and recursively enumerable. For how many of these four classes is the class closed under complementation?
questions.question_html: Consider the four classes: regular, context-free, context-sensitive and recursively enumerable. For how many of these four classes is the class closed under complementation?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Complementing a language means swapping accepted and rejected. That is free when the machine always halts, and expensive when it does not — so the answer depends on whether the model at that level can always be made total.

Step by step.

  1. Regular: closed. Swap final and non-final states of the DFA; every run already terminates.
  2. Context-free: closed. Yes — the context-free languages are closed under complementation, although the proof is not a simple automaton flip and the result was only established in 1987. (Intersection, by contrast, fails.)
  3. Context-sensitive: closed. Immerman–Szelepcsényi: nondeterministic linear-bounded automata are closed under complement, which settles the deterministic case a fortiori.
  4. Recursively enumerable: not closed. K is r.e. and its complement is not; if the class were closed, every r.e. language would be recursive.

Three of the four classes are closed, so the answer is 3.

Answer: 3.

Common misconception. Answering 2 by assuming the context-free languages are not closed under complementation, on the strength of their failure for intersection. The two closure properties are independent; only the r.e. level fails complementation, and that failure is exactly the halting problem.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements about the running time of Turing machines is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following statements about the running time of Turing machines is TRUE?
options: For every fixed integer c ≥ 1 and every machine that runs in time t(n) on all sufficiently long inputs, there is an equivalent machine that runs in time ⌈t(n)/c⌉, at the cost of a larger tape alphabet and more states.
A machine that runs in time t(n) can always be replaced by an equivalent machine that runs in time O(log t(n)), by compressing the tape.
The running time cannot be reduced by more than a factor of 2, because every cell of the tape must be visited at least once.
A machine that runs in time t(n) runs in constant time once its tape alphabet is made large enough.
options_html: For every fixed integer c ≥ 1 and every machine that runs in time t(n) on all sufficiently long inputs, there is an equivalent machine that runs in time ⌈t(n)/c⌉, at the cost of a larger tape alphabet and more states.
A machine that runs in time t(n) can always be replaced by an equivalent machine that runs in time O(log t(n)), by compressing the tape.
The running time cannot be reduced by more than a factor of 2, because every cell of the tape must be visited at least once.
A machine that runs in time t(n) runs in constant time once its tape alphabet is made large enough.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Tape compression plus state enlargement. Encode c consecutive tape cells in a single cell of a larger alphabet, and let each state of the new machine remember the position of the head inside its block together with the relevant part of the old state. One step of the new machine then reproduces c steps of the old one.

Step by step.

  1. The new tape alphabet is Γ^c, which is still finite, so the new machine is still a legal Turing machine.
  2. The first pass copies the input into the compressed format, which costs O(n) steps — this is why the speed-up is claimed only for sufficiently long inputs, where n is dominated by t(n).
  3. Each subsequent step of the new machine covers c steps of the old machine, so t(n) steps become t(n)/c steps.
  4. Repeating the construction for larger c gives any constant factor; no unbounded improvement is possible, and the time hierarchy theorem says the improvement cannot be asymptotic.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. “Compressing the tape makes the machine exponentially faster.” Compression divides both the number of cells and the number of steps by the same constant c; a constant factor never changes the asymptotic class, which is why complexity theory measures time up to O(·) and why the time hierarchy theorem needs a genuine separation such as t(n) log t(n).

questions.question: For each n ≥ 1, let B(n) be the largest number of steps taken before halting by any Turing machine with exactly n states and tape alphabet {␣, 0, 1} that halts when started on the empty tape. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.question_html: For each n ≥ 1, let B(n) be the largest number of steps taken before halting by any Turing machine with exactly n states and tape alphabet {␣, 0, 1} that halts when started on the empty tape. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: B(n) is well defined but not computable, because a program that computed it would also decide whether an n-state machine halts on the empty tape.
B(n) is computable, because there are only finitely many machines with n states, and a maximum over a finite set can always be computed.
B(n) is not well defined, because some machines with n states never halt, so no maximum exists.
B(n) is computable for every n, but it grows more slowly than any computable function.
options_html: B(n) is well defined but not computable, because a program that computed it would also decide whether an n-state machine halts on the empty tape.
B(n) is computable, because there are only finitely many machines with n states, and a maximum over a finite set can always be computed.
B(n) is not well defined, because some machines with n states never halt, so no maximum exists.
B(n) is computable for every n, but it grows more slowly than any computable function.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Two different questions are being confused: whether a maximum exists (a mathematical question) and whether it can be computed (an algorithmic one). For fixed n there are finitely many machines, each halting one runs for finitely many steps, so the maximum exists. Computing it is a different matter.

Step by step.

  1. Well definedness: the set of n-state machines over a fixed alphabet is finite. Discard those that never halt on the empty tape; the remaining set is finite, and a finite set of natural numbers has a maximum. So B(n) exists.
  2. Suppose a machine C computed B. To decide whether an n-state machine M halts on ε: compute B(n) and simulate M on ε for B(n) steps. If M has not halted by then it never will, because B(n) dominates the running time of every halting n-state machine.
  3. That would decide a problem already known to be undecidable, so no such C exists.
  4. Option (C) is wrong because the maximum is taken only over the machines that halt; machines that loop contribute nothing and do not destroy the maximum.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. “Finitely many candidates, therefore computable.” Finiteness guarantees that the answer exists, not that it can be found: deciding which of the finitely many machines halt is itself the undecidable part. This function is the busy-beaver function, and its uncomputability is the sharpest illustration that a well-defined function need not be computable.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following questions is still open?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following questions is still open?
options: Are the deterministic and the nondeterministic linear-bounded automata equally powerful?
Is every context-free language recursive?
Is every context-sensitive language context-free?
Is every regular language context-sensitive?
options_html: Are the deterministic and the nondeterministic linear-bounded automata equally powerful?
Is every context-free language recursive?
Is every context-sensitive language context-free?
Is every regular language context-sensitive?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Most questions about the hierarchy were settled long ago: the inclusions are strict and the decidability of each level is known. The one famous exception is whether nondeterminism adds power to machines whose tape is bounded by the input.

Step by step.

  1. (B) settled. Every context-free language is recursive: CYK decides membership in polynomial time, so a decider exists.
  2. (C) settled, negatively. {aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 1} is context-sensitive and not context-free.
  3. (D) settled, positively. Every regular language is context-free, and every context-free language is context-sensitive.
  4. (A) open. Whether deterministic and nondeterministic linear-bounded automata accept the same class — that is, whether DLBA = NLBA — has resisted proof in either direction since the 1960s. Note that at the level above, nondeterministic Turing machines are known to be equivalent to deterministic ones.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Assuming that determinism never matters for recognition, since every nondeterministic Turing machine can be simulated deterministically. That simulation is correct but costs exponential time; for bounded tape the question is not about time but about which languages are accepted at all, and there the answer is unknown. Do not confuse this with P = NP, which asks about time on ordinary machines.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let K = {⟨M⟩ : M halts on the input ⟨M⟩} and let K̄ be its complement in the set of all strings over the encoding alphabet. Consider the four languages K, K̄, ∅ and Σ*. How many of these four are recursively enumerable?
questions.question_html: Let K = {⟨M⟩ : M halts on the input ⟨M⟩} and let K̄ be its complement in the set of all strings over the encoding alphabet. Consider the four languages K, K̄, ∅ and Σ*. How many of these four are recursively enumerable?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. K is the canonical r.e. set that is not recursive; its complement is therefore not r.e. The two trivial languages ∅ and Σ* are decided by machines that reject everything and accept everything respectively, so they are recursive and hence r.e.

Step by step.

  1. K is r.e.: a universal machine simulates M on ⟨M⟩ and accepts when that simulation halts. — counted.
  2. K̄ is not r.e.: if both K and K̄ were r.e., then K would be recursive, which the diagonal argument refutes. — not counted.
  3. ∅ is decided by the machine that rejects every input. — counted.
  4. Σ* is decided by the machine that accepts every input. — counted.

So 3 of the four are r.e.: K, ∅ and Σ*.

Answer: 3.

Common misconception. Answering 2 by discarding ∅ — some candidates feel an empty language is “not really a language”, or that a recogniser must accept something. A recogniser for ∅ simply never accepts; that is a perfectly good Turing machine. The other common slip is to assume K̄ must be r.e. because K is; the halting problem is precisely the counterexample.

questions.question: Let M be a Turing machine and w a string, and suppose M halts on w after exactly 3 steps. Define M′ as follows: on input x over Σ = {0, 1}, the machine M′ simulates M on w for exactly |x| steps and accepts x if and only if that simulation has not halted within those |x| steps. How many strings does M′ accept?
questions.question_html: Let M be a Turing machine and w a string, and suppose M halts on w after exactly 3 steps. Define M′ as follows: on input x over Σ = {0, 1}, the machine M′ simulates M on w for exactly |x| steps and accepts x if and only if that simulation has not halted within those |x| steps. How many strings does M′ accept?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The gadget that turns a halting question into a question about a language is a simulation whose budget is the length of the input. Because the budget grows with |x|, a machine that halts after a fixed number of steps stops being able to “outrun” the budget, and the accepted set becomes a finite set of short strings instead of everything.

Step by step. There is exactly one string of length 0, two of length 1 and four of length 2.

  1. |x| = 0: the budget is 0 steps, so the simulation has certainly not halted. M′ accepts. — 1 string.
  2. |x| = 1: one step is simulated; M needs 3, so it has not halted. M′ accepts. — 2 strings.
  3. |x| = 2: two steps are simulated; still not halted. M′ accepts. — 4 strings.
  4. |x| = 3: three steps are simulated and M halts on the third, so M′ rejects. — 0 strings.
  5. |x| ≥ 4: the halt happens inside the budget, so M′ rejects every longer string.

Total accepted: 1 + 2 + 4 = 7.

Answer: 7.

Common misconception. Reading “not halted within |x| steps” as “never halts”, which would make the accepted set empty or infinite and the count meaningless. The budget is per input string, so the answer differs from one length to the next — that dependence on |x| is the whole point of the gadget, and it is why the same construction with a fixed constant budget fails to characterise the property.

questions.question: Let L ⊆ Σ* be a language whose minimal complete DFA has exactly n states, where n ≥ 1. The minimal complete DFA that accepts the complement Σ* \ L has:
questions.question_html: Let L ⊆ Σ* be a language whose minimal complete DFA has exactly n states, where n ≥ 1. The minimal complete DFA that accepts the complement Σ* \ L has:
options: exactly n states
exactly n + 1 states
at most 2ⁿ states, and possibly fewer than n states
exactly n − 1 states
options_html: exactly n states
exactly n + 1 states
at most 2ⁿ states, and possibly fewer than n states
exactly n − 1 states
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A complete DFA decides membership by the state the run ends in, so complementing a language means declaring the non-final states final and leaving every transition alone. The transition graph, and therefore reachability, is untouched.

Step by step.

  1. Let M = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F) be the minimal complete DFA of L, with |Q| = n.
  2. Build M′ = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, Q \ F): same states, same transitions, finals swapped.
  3. M′ is still complete, and every state is still reachable, because the transitions did not change.
  4. Two states are equivalent when δ̂(p, w) ∈ F ⇔ δ̂(q, w) ∈ F for every w. Replacing F by Q \ F negates both sides of that test, so the same pairs stay equivalent and no new pair becomes equivalent.
  5. Hence M′ has the same n equivalence classes, so it is minimal.

Answer: Option (A) — exactly n states.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) A new trap state is only needed if the automaton was incomplete; a complete DFA already has one when the language requires it.
  • (C) 2ⁿ is the subset-construction bound for an NFA. Complementation never changes the number of states of a complete DFA.
  • (D) A one-state DFA would give a zero-state complement, which cannot decide anything.

Common misconception. Transferring the NFA fact — that complementation needs determinisation — to complete DFAs. Once the automaton is deterministic and complete, complementation costs nothing.

Takeaway. For complete DFAs, |min DFA(L)| = |min DFA(Σ* \ L)|. The cheapest way to build a complement is to minimise first, then swap the finals.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: How many states does the minimal complete DFA over Σ = {a, b} have that accepts exactly those strings which contain at most two a's?
questions.question_html: How many states does the minimal complete DFA over Σ = {a, b} have that accepts exactly those strings which contain at most two a's?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A DFA can count only up to a fixed bound. "At most two" needs to know whether the count so far is 0, 1, 2 or already 3 — four facts, so four states.

Step by step.

  1. States c₀, c₁, c₂, c₃, where c_i means "i a's have been read", with c₃ standing for "three or more".
  2. δ(c_i, a) = c_{i+1} for i < 3, and δ(c₃, a) = c₃ — once three a's are seen the answer can never change.
  3. δ(c_i, b) = c_i: a b changes nothing.
  4. Start c₀; finals {c₀, c₁, c₂}, non-final {c₃}.
  5. All four are reachable, and no two are equivalent: c₀, c₁, c₂ are separated by appending enough a's to push one of them into c₃, and c₃ is separated from the rest by ε.

Answer: Option (B) — 4 states.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) 3 states can only count to two with no overflow state, so a third a would have nowhere to go.
  • (C) and (D) A fifth state would be unreachable or equivalent to c₃, so neither survives minimisation.

Common misconception. Forgetting the sink. Any bounded-count language needs one state for "the bound has been passed", even though it is never final.

Takeaway. "At most k" over a single letter costs k + 2 states: 0, 1, …, k and the overflow. Here k = 2, so 4.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: How many states does the minimal complete DFA over Σ = {0, 1} have that accepts exactly those strings which contain both 01 and 10 as substrings?
questions.question_html: How many states does the minimal complete DFA over Σ = {0, 1} have that accepts exactly those strings which contain both 01 and 10 as substrings?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Two facts must be remembered: which of the two patterns has already been seen, and what the last symbol was (because a new pattern can only be completed by the next symbol). That is a product of 4 flag pairs with 2 last-symbol values, plus the start state.

Step by step.

  1. Start state I. Every later state is a triple (last, h₀₁, h₁₀) where last ∈ {0, 1} and each flag says whether that pattern has been seen.
  2. Raw count: 1 + 2 · 4 = 9 candidate states.
  3. Two of them are unreachable. (1, seen 10, not seen 01) would need a string ending in 1 that contains 10 but not 01; appending 1 to a string ending in 0 always creates 01. Symmetrically (0, seen 01, not seen 10) is unreachable.
  4. That leaves 7 reachable states: I, (0,−,−), (1,−,−), (1, seen 01), (0, seen 10), (0, both), (1, both).
  5. The two accepting states (0, both) and (1, both) are equivalent: each maps to the other on the other symbol and to itself on its own, and both are final, so no suffix separates them. Merge them.
  6. 7 − 1 = 6 states.

Answer: Option (C) — 6 states.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) 4 would only track the two flags, and could not tell when a new pattern has just been completed.
  • (B) 5 is what a naive count gives if only one of the two unreachable states is noticed.
  • (D) 7 is the count before the two accepting states are merged — minimisation is required, not optional.

Common misconception. Treating "contains both" as a simple union of two conditions and forgetting that the last symbol matters. Also stopping at the reachable count and skipping the merge.

Takeaway. For substring conditions, build the product of (last symbol) with (flags for each pattern), delete unreachable states, then merge equivalent accepting states.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: How many states does the minimal complete DFA over Σ = {a, b} have that accepts exactly those strings in which every b is immediately followed by an a? (The string must not end in b.)
questions.question_html: How many states does the minimal complete DFA over Σ = {a, b} have that accepts exactly those strings in which every b is immediately followed by an a? (The string must not end in b.)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The condition is a local one, so the automaton only has to remember whether the previous symbol was a b that is still waiting for its a. The language is L((a | ba)*).

Step by step.

  1. q₀: no pending b. This is the start state and is final, since the empty string satisfies the condition.
  2. q₁: the last symbol read was a b, so the next symbol must be an a.
  3. q_d: some b was not followed by an a. Once here, every string is rejected.
  4. Transitions: δ(q₀, a) = q₀, δ(q₀, b) = q₁, δ(q₁, a) = q₀, δ(q₁, b) = q_d, and q_d loops on both letters.
  5. All three states are reachable, and they are pairwise distinguishable: q₀ and q₁ differ on ε (final against non-final), and q_d differs from both on every suffix.

Answer: 3.

Common misconception. Building four or five states by tracking how many b's have been seen. Only the most recent symbol matters, and a violation is permanent — that is one state, not one per position.

Takeaway. "Every X is followed by Y" needs three states: clean, waiting for Y, and broken.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: For L = a*b over Σ = {a, b}, how many equivalence classes does the Myhill–Nerode relation ≡_L have?
questions.question_html: For L = a*b over Σ = {a, b}, how many equivalence classes does the Myhill–Nerode relation ≡_L have?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. u ≡_L v when for every suffix z, uz ∈ L ⇔ vz ∈ L. The number of classes equals the number of states of the minimal complete DFA, so counting classes and counting states are the same exercise.

Step by step.

  1. Class 1: [ε] = {ε, a, aa, aaa, …} = a*. Every member is non-final, and every member reaches acceptance by appending b. Any two members behave identically on every suffix, so they are one class.
  2. Class 2: [b]. The word b is in L, but b + a = ba ∉ L and b + b = bb ∉ L, so nothing except ε keeps it in L.
  3. Class 3: [ab], the dead class. ab itself is not in L and no suffix can rescue it: after a b has already been read, no further string is in a*b.
  4. Is b ≡ ab? No: b + ε ∈ L but ab + ε ∉ L. Is a ≡ b? No: a + b ∈ L but b + b ∉ L. So the three classes are distinct.

Answer: 3.

Common misconception. Counting a class per length of the a-prefix. All of a* collapses into one class, because the DFA does not need to know how many a's were read — only that no b has been seen yet.

Takeaway. For a*b: "no b yet", "just read the b", "too late". Three classes, and the minimal complete DFA has three states.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Two complete DFAs A₁ = (Q₁, Σ, δ₁, q₁, F₁) and A₂ = (Q₂, Σ, δ₂, q₂, F₂) are combined by the product construction into an automaton that accepts L(A₁) ∩ L(A₂). Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Two complete DFAs A₁ = (Q₁, Σ, δ₁, q₁, F₁) and A₂ = (Q₂, Σ, δ₂, q₂, F₂) are combined by the product construction into an automaton that accepts L(A₁) ∩ L(A₂). Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The product automaton has |Q₁| × |Q₂| states, with start state (q₁, q₂).
A product state (p, q) is final exactly when p ∈ F₁ or q ∈ F₂.
Some product states may be unreachable, so the minimal DFA of the intersection can have fewer than |Q₁| × |Q₂| states.
The product of two complete DFAs is complete.
options_html: The product automaton has |Q₁| × |Q₂| states, with start state (q₁, q₂).
A product state (p, q) is final exactly when p ∈ F₁ or q ∈ F₂.
Some product states may be unreachable, so the minimal DFA of the intersection can have fewer than |Q₁| × |Q₂| states.
The product of two complete DFAs is complete.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The product runs the two automata in lockstep: the state is the pair of states reached by the same input word. It decides the intersection, because a word is accepted by both exactly when the pair it reaches has both coordinates final.

Step by step.

  1. (A) The state set is Q₁ × Q₂, size |Q₁| · |Q₂|, with transitions (p, q) → (δ₁(p, a), δ₂(q, a)) and start (q₁, q₂). TRUE ✓
  2. (B) For the intersection the pair must satisfy both conditions: p ∈ F₁ and q ∈ F₂. The "or" version gives the union, not the intersection. FALSE ✗
  3. (C) Pairs that no input word can drive the automaton into are not reachable — for example when the two automata constrain each other — so the reachable part, and hence the minimal DFA, can be smaller. TRUE ✓
  4. (D) If both automata define a transition on every symbol at every state, so does the pair: every product state has exactly one successor per symbol. TRUE ✓

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Swapping "and" for "or" in the final-state rule, which silently turns an intersection into a union. The two differ by one word in the definition and by an entire language in effect.

Takeaway. Product construction: states are pairs, the transition is coordinatewise, and the final-state rule is what encodes union, intersection or difference.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: How many states does the minimal complete DFA over Σ = {a, b} have for the language L = {w : #a(w) ≡ #b(w) (mod 3)}?
questions.question_html: How many states does the minimal complete DFA over Σ = {a, b} have for the language L = {w : #a(w) ≡ #b(w) (mod 3)}?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The condition compares two counts, and only their difference modulo 3 matters. Reading an a adds 1 to that difference, reading a b subtracts 1, so the state is a single residue rather than a pair of residues.

Step by step.

  1. Let d = (#a − #b) mod 3. States q₀, q₁, q₂, where q_r means d = r.
  2. Transitions: δ(q_r, a) = q_{(r+1) mod 3} and δ(q_r, b) = q_{(r−1) mod 3}.
  3. Start q₀; final q₀ only.
  4. All three are reachable: ε gives q₀, a gives q₁, aa gives q₂.
  5. They are pairwise distinguishable: q₀ is final while q₁, q₂ are not, and q₁ against q₂ is separated by the suffix a, since q₁ → q₂ (non-final) while q₂ → q₀ (final).

Answer: Option (D) — 3 states.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) 6 is the count for tracking two independent residues, as in #a ≡ 0 and #b ≡ 0 separately. Here only the difference is constrained.
  • (B) 9 is the full product of two mod-3 counters, which is what the language would need if the two counts were constrained independently.
  • (C) 12 has no natural reading at all — it is the product count multiplied by the alphabet size, a common arithmetic slip.

Common misconception. Building the 3 × 3 = 9 product before asking whether both residues are actually needed. A congruence on a difference collapses to one counter.

Takeaway. Whenever a condition fixes f(#a, #b) rather than each count, ask which single quantity the automaton must remember. Here it is #a − #b, and three states suffice.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: N is an NFA with final states F, and N′ is obtained from N by keeping every transition but taking F′ = Q \ F as the set of final states. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html: N is an NFA with final states F, and N′ is obtained from N by keeping every transition but taking F′ = Q \ F as the set of final states. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: L(N′) = Σ* \ L(N) for every NFA N.
L(N′) = L(N) for every NFA N.
L(N′) = Σ* \ L(N) only when N is deterministic and complete.
L(N′) ⊆ L(N) for every NFA N.
options_html: L(N′) = Σ* \ L(N) for every NFA N.
L(N′) = L(N) for every NFA N.
L(N′) = Σ* \ L(N) only when N is deterministic and complete.
L(N′) ⊆ L(N) for every NFA N.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An NFA accepts a string when at least one run accepts it. Flipping which states are final flips the verdict of each individual run, but "some run accepts" does not become "no run accepts".

Step by step.

  1. Take an NFA that has both an accepting and a rejecting run on the same word w — for instance w = a with one path to a final state and one to a non-final state.
  2. In N, w is accepted. In N′ the same word still has a run that ends in F′ (the old rejecting run), so w is still accepted.
  3. So L(N′) need not be the complement, and (A) fails.
  4. If N is deterministic and complete there is exactly one run per word, so its single endpoint is final in N′ exactly when it was non-final in N — the complement is then correct.

Answer: Option (C) — the complement works only for a deterministic, complete automaton.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Contradicted by step 2; the complement of an NFA's language is not obtained by swapping finals.
  • (B) Swapping finals does change the language whenever some state is final and some is not.
  • (D) Nothing forces L(N′) ⊆ L(N); in the two-run example the languages are equal, and with a single accepting run the new language can gain words.

Common misconception. Assuming complementation is a local edit of the automaton. For NFAs it is not: determinise first (subset construction), then swap finals.

Takeaway. NFA complementation = subset construction + swap finals. The detour through determinisation is what makes the complement correct.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: An ε-NFA over Σ = {0, 1} has states {A, B, C}, start state A, and the transitions below (— means no move). What is ε-closure({B})? | ε | 0 | 1 -------+-------+-------+------ A | B | A | — B | C | — | C C | — | B | —
questions.question_html:
An ε-NFA over Σ = {0, 1} has states {A, B, C}, start state A, and the transitions below (— means no move). What is ε-closure({B})?

| ε | 0 | 1 -------+-------+-------+------ A | B | A | — B | C | — | C C | — | B | —
options: {B, C}
{A, B, C}
options_html: {B}
{B, C}
{A, B, C}
{C}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. ε-closure(S) is the set of states reachable from S using ε-moves only, and it always contains S itself, since a path of zero ε-moves is allowed.

Step by step.

  1. Start with {B}.
  2. B has the ε-move B → C, so add C: the set is now {B, C}.
  3. C has no ε-move, so nothing further is added.
  4. A is not reachable from B: the only ε-edge out of A points into B, and ε-moves are directed.

Answer: Option (B) — {B, C}.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Omits C, forgetting that the closure follows ε-edges transitively.
  • (C) Adds A, which would require an ε-edge from B or C back to A; the edges run the other way.
  • (D) Drops B itself — the closure of a set always contains that set.

Common misconception. Treating ε-closure as "all states connected to S by ε-paths in either direction". It is directed reachability.

Takeaway. Compute a closure by a small BFS over ε-edges only, seeded with the given set.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: In the subset construction that turns an ε-NFA N = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F) into a DFA D, the transition δ_D(S, a) from a state S ⊆ Q on a symbol a ∈ Σ is:
questions.question_html: In the subset construction that turns an ε-NFA N = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F) into a DFA D, the transition δ_D(S, a) from a state S ⊆ Q on a symbol a ∈ Σ is:
options: δ(q₀, a)
the plain union ∪_{q ∈ S} δ(q, a), with no ε-moves applied
ε-closure(∪_{q ∈ S} δ(q, a))
ε-closure(S) ∩ δ(q₀, a)
options_html: δ(q₀, a)
the plain union ∪_{q ∈ S} δ(q, a), with no ε-moves applied
ε-closure(∪_{q ∈ S} δ(q, a))
ε-closure(S) ∩ δ(q₀, a)
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. From the set S the NFA may consume a from any of its states, so the immediate successors are the union of the individual δ(q, a). Having consumed a, it may then move any number of ε-steps for free, so the result must be closed under ε-moves.

Step by step.

  1. Take one a-transition from each q ∈ S — the union T = ∪_{q ∈ S} δ(q, a).
  2. Follow every ε-path from T, giving ε-closure(T).
  3. That closed set is the new DFA state: δ_D(S, a) = ε-closure(∪_{q ∈ S} δ(q, a)).
  4. The start state is ε-closure({q₀}) and a state is final when it meets F — consistent with the same "read one symbol, then close" discipline.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Uses only the start state's transitions and ignores the rest of S entirely.
  • (B) Drops the closure, so ε-moves after the consumed symbol are lost and the constructed DFA accepts too few strings.
  • (D) Intersects with a single state's transitions, which has no meaning in the construction.

Common misconception. Applying the closure to S before reading the symbol instead of after. The order is: take the a-moves, then close.

Takeaway. One line covers the whole construction: read the symbol from every state of the subset, then take the ε-closure.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Two NFAs N₁ and N₂ accept the same language. The subset construction applied to N₁ gives a DFA with 5 states, and applied to N₂ gives a DFA with 7 states. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Two NFAs N₁ and N₂ accept the same language. The subset construction applied to N₁ gives a DFA with 5 states, and applied to N₂ gives a DFA with 7 states. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: Both DFAs minimise to the same minimal DFA, up to renaming of states.
The premise is impossible: two NFAs for the same language always produce DFAs of the same size.
The minimal DFA of the language has 5 states, because the smaller construction is always the minimal one.
Neither DFA can be minimised, because the subset construction always produces a minimal automaton.
options_html: Both DFAs minimise to the same minimal DFA, up to renaming of states.
The premise is impossible: two NFAs for the same language always produce DFAs of the same size.
The minimal DFA of the language has 5 states, because the smaller construction is always the minimal one.
Neither DFA can be minimised, because the subset construction always produces a minimal automaton.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The minimal complete DFA of a regular language is unique up to isomorphism — its states are exactly the Myhill–Nerode classes of the language. Any DFA for that language therefore minimises to that same automaton.

Step by step.

  1. The subset construction preserves the language, so both 5-state and 7-state DFAs accept L.
  2. The Myhill–Nerode relation ≡_L depends only on L, not on which NFA produced the automaton.
  3. Minimising a DFA merges exactly the states that lie in the same ≡_L class and deletes unreachable ones, so both automata collapse to the same quotient.
  4. The two results are therefore isomorphic; the state count of each before minimisation says nothing about the minimal size.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) Different NFAs for one language routinely give subset automata of different sizes — extra guesses create extra subsets.
  • (C) The smaller of two constructions need not be minimal; a third NFA could give a 6-state DFA that minimises further.
  • (D) The subset construction makes no attempt at minimisation, and its output usually contains equivalent states.

Common misconception. Reading the size of a subset-construction output as a property of the language. It is a property of the particular NFA, including its redundant guesses.

Takeaway. Language → unique minimal DFA. NFA → many subset automata, all minimising to that one.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: An NFA over Σ = {0, 1} has states {p, q, r, s}, start state p, final state {s}, and the transitions below. Counting only reachable subsets, how many states does the DFA produced by the subset construction have? | 0 | 1 ------+-------+------ p | p, q | p q | q | r r | s | r s | s | s
questions.question_html:
An NFA over Σ = {0, 1} has states {p, q, r, s}, start state p, final state {s}, and the transitions below. Counting only reachable subsets, how many states does the DFA produced by the subset construction have?

| 0 | 1 ------+-------+------ p | p, q | p q | q | r r | s | r s | s | s
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Each DFA state is a set of NFA states: everything the NFA could be in after reading the same prefix. Only subsets actually reachable from the start subset are states.

Step by step.

  1. Start subset {p}.
  2. {p} on 0 gives {p, q}; on 1 gives {p}.
  3. {p, q} on 0 gives {p, q} ∪ {q} = {p, q}; on 1 gives {p} ∪ {r} = {p, r}.
  4. {p, r} on 0 gives {p, q} ∪ {s} = {p, q, s}; on 1 gives {p} ∪ {r} = {p, r}.
  5. {p, q, s} on 0 gives {p, q} ∪ {q} ∪ {s} = {p, q, s}; on 1 gives {p} ∪ {r} ∪ {s} = {p, r, s}.
  6. {p, r, s} on 0 gives {p, q} ∪ {s} ∪ {s} = {p, q, s}; on 1 gives {p} ∪ {r} ∪ {s} = {p, r, s}.
  7. Reachable subsets: {p}, {p, q}, {p, r}, {p, q, s}, {p, r, s} — five, and the closure of the list is complete.

Answer: 5.

Common misconception. Counting all 2⁴ = 16 subsets, or forgetting that s keeps s alive once it has been reached — that is what produces {p, r, s} from {p, q, s}.

Takeaway. Work the subsets breadth-first from the start and stop when no new subset appears. Nothing outside the reachable set is a state.
