questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the subset construction and the automata it produces are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about the subset construction and the automata it produces are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Every state of the constructed DFA is a subset of Q, and the start state is ε-closure({q₀}).
If N has no ε-transitions, the construction still applies and the formula reduces to the plain union of the δ(q, a).
Subsets that are unreachable from the start subset are nevertheless states of the constructed DFA.
The constructed DFA may still have to be minimised before it is the minimal DFA of the language.
options_html: Every state of the constructed DFA is a subset of Q, and the start state is ε-closure({q₀}).
If N has no ε-transitions, the construction still applies and the formula reduces to the plain union of the δ(q, a).
Subsets that are unreachable from the start subset are nevertheless states of the constructed DFA.
The constructed DFA may still have to be minimised before it is the minimal DFA of the language.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The subset construction is a language-preserving translation, not an optimiser. It builds exactly the subsets that some input word can reach, and it says nothing about equivalence of states.

Step by step.

  1. (A) By definition the DFA state set is a collection of subsets of Q, and before any symbol is read the NFA can be in q₀ or anything ε-reachable from it. TRUE ✓
  2. (B) With no ε-moves, ε-closure(S) = S, so δ_D(S, a) = ∪_{q ∈ S} δ(q, a); the general formula degenerates gracefully. TRUE ✓
  3. (C) The construction is defined by reachability from the start subset; an unreachable subset is never created. Building all 2ⁿ subsets would add states the automaton can never enter. FALSE ✗
  4. (D) Distinct subsets can be equivalent — they accept the same set of suffixes — and the construction never checks this, so minimisation may still remove states. TRUE ✓

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Believing the subset construction yields the minimal DFA. It yields a DFA, often with redundant states, and minimisation is a separate step.

Takeaway. Subset construction answers "is there an equivalent deterministic automaton?" — yes, and at most 2ⁿ states. Optimality is a different question with a different algorithm.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following regular expressions denotes exactly Σ* for Σ = {a, b}?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following regular expressions denotes exactly Σ* for Σ = {a, b}?
options: (ab)*
a*b*
(a|b)*ab(a|b)*
options_html: (ab)*
a*b*
(a|b)*ab(a|b)*
(a*b*)*
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. (a*b*)* concatenates any number of blocks, each of which is some a's followed by some b's. Every string can be cut into single letters, and each single letter is itself such a block, so everything is generated; and nothing outside {a, b}* can be.

Step by step.

  1. a*b* already contains every string of the form a^i b^j.
  2. Starring it allows a sequence of such blocks: (a^i b^j)(a^k b^l)…, which reaches every alternation pattern, including ba (as εb · aε).
  3. Formally, (a + b)* = (a*b*)* is a standard identity: each side is contained in the other because a single symbol is a block and a block is a string.
  4. So the language is Σ*.

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) (ab)* gives only the even-length alternating strings ε, ab, abab, …; it misses a and ba.
  • (B) a*b* forces all a's before all b's, so it misses ba.
  • (C) Requires at least one occurrence of ab, so ε, a and ba are all missing.

Common misconception. Reading (a*b*)* as "a's then b's, once", which would be a*b* without the star. The outer star is what restores the full alternation.

Takeaway. Remember the pair (a + b)* = (a*b*)*; it is the standard way to show that a starred block expression reaches everything.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Arden’s lemma states that for languages A and B with ε ∉ A, the equation X = AX + B has the unique solution X = A*B. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Arden’s lemma states that for languages A and B with ε ∉ A, the equation X = AX + B has the unique solution X = A*B. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: With ε ∉ A, the equation X = XA + B has the unique solution X = BA*.
The condition ε ∉ A is what makes the solution unique.
Arden’s lemma is used to convert the right-linear equations of an automaton into a regular expression by eliminating one variable at a time.
Arden’s lemma applies only when B is a single string.
options_html: With ε ∉ A, the equation X = XA + B has the unique solution X = BA*.
The condition ε ∉ A is what makes the solution unique.
Arden’s lemma is used to convert the right-linear equations of an automaton into a regular expression by eliminating one variable at a time.
Arden’s lemma applies only when B is a single string.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. X = AX + B says "either one more A then recurse, or stop with B". Unrolling gives B + AB + AAB + … = A*B, and the condition ε ∉ A guarantees that each unrolling step consumes at least one symbol, so the recursion is well founded and the solution is unique.

Step by step.

  1. (A) X = XA + B unrolls on the right: B + BA + BAA + … = BA*. The mirror form is equally valid. TRUE ✓
  2. (B) If ε ∈ A, then X = AX + B can have several solutions, so the hypothesis is not decoration — it is what makes A*B the only answer. TRUE ✓
  3. (C) Writing one equation per state, X_i = Σ_{a} a · X_{δ(i,a)} + (ε if i final), and substituting with Arden’s lemma from the last state backwards yields the regular expression of the automaton. TRUE ✓
  4. (D) B is an arbitrary language — typically a union of several terms — not a single string. FALSE ✗

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Using Arden’s lemma when ε ∈ A, which is exactly the case where the answer may not be unique.

Takeaway. State elimination and Arden’s lemma are the same idea: solve for the unknown language, absorb loops with a star, and require the loop body to be non-empty.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: For a language L and a symbol a, the (Brzozowski) derivative is D_a(L) = {w : aw ∈ L}. What is D_a(L) for L = L((ab)*)?
questions.question_html: For a language L and a symbol a, the (Brzozowski) derivative is D_a(L) = {w : aw ∈ L}. What is D_a(L) for L = L((ab)*)?
options: L(b(ab)*)
options_html: L((ab)*)
L(b(ab)*)
L((ba)*)
∅
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The derivative strips one leading symbol and asks what must follow. If the stripped word is to be in (ab)*, then after the leading a the remainder must be a b followed by any number of complete ab pairs.

Step by step.

  1. Let aw ∈ (ab)*. Words of (ab)* that begin with a are exactly ab, abab, ababab, …
  2. Remove the leading a: the remainders are b, bab, babab, …
  3. Those are precisely b(ab)*.
  4. So D_a((ab)*) = L(b(ab)*).
  5. Check the endpoints: b ∈ D_a because ab ∈ L; ε ∉ D_a because a ∉ L; and D_b((ab)*) = ∅, since no word of (ab)* begins with b.

Answer: Option (B) — L(b(ab)*).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Would require a·(ab)* ⊆ (ab)*, but a·ε = a ∉ L.
  • (C) (ba)* starts with b, so it contains ε, which is not in the derivative.
  • (D) Is the derivative with respect to b, not a.

Common misconception. Assuming the derivative is always another starred expression of the same shape. Stripping one symbol from (ab)* leaves an unmatched b in front.

Takeaway. Differentiate by asking "which words of L start with a, and what is left when that a is removed?"

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the class of regular languages are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about the class of regular languages are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: It is closed under union, intersection and complementation.
It is closed under reversal and under concatenation.
It is closed under countable union, so the union of infinitely many regular languages is regular.
It is closed under homomorphism and under inverse homomorphism.
options_html: It is closed under union, intersection and complementation.
It is closed under reversal and under concatenation.
It is closed under countable union, so the union of infinitely many regular languages is regular.
It is closed under homomorphism and under inverse homomorphism.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Closure under an operation means that applying it to regular languages yields a regular language again. Each positive case has a construction — a product automaton, a reversed NFA, a substitution of expressions — and the negative case fails for a counting reason.

Step by step.

  1. (A) Union: a new start state with ε-moves into both. Intersection: the product construction. Complement: determinise, complete, then swap finals. TRUE ✓
  2. (B) Reversal: reverse every edge and swap start with final (with a new start and ε-moves). Concatenation: ε-edges from the finals of one into the start of the other. TRUE ✓
  3. (C) Every finite union of regular languages is regular, but an infinite one need not be: {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0} is the union of the infinitely many regular languages {aⁿbⁿ} taken one n at a time, and it is not regular. FALSE ✗
  4. (D) Homomorphism: substitute a regular expression for each letter, then combine. Inverse homomorphism: run the automaton on the images of the letters. Both keep regularity. TRUE ✓

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Extending "closed under finite union" to "closed under infinite union". Finite closure is a theorem; the infinite version is false, and it is the usual way to accidentally "prove" that a non-regular language is regular.

Takeaway. The regular languages are a Boolean algebra closed under concatenation, star, reversal and homomorphic images — but not under infinite union.

questions.question: How many strings of length exactly 4 over Σ = {a, b} belong to L(a*b*)?
questions.question_html: How many strings of length exactly 4 over Σ = {a, b} belong to L(a*b*)?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. a*b* contains exactly the strings in which no a appears after a b. For a fixed length the only freedom is where the switch from a's to b's happens.

Step by step.

  1. A word of a*b* of length 4 has the form aib4−i.
  2. The number of a's, i, can be 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
  3. Each choice gives a different word: bbbb, abbb, aabb, aaab, aaaa.
  4. So there are 5.

Answer: 5.

Common misconception. Counting 2⁴ = 16 by treating the two letters as independent. Eleven of those sixteen words contain ba and are excluded, leaving exactly the five above.

Takeaway. For a*b* the length-n count is n + 1, one word per position of the switch.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following regular expressions denotes exactly the strings over Σ = {a, b} that contain an even number of a's and an even number of b's?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following regular expressions denotes exactly the strings over Σ = {a, b} that contain an even number of a's and an even number of b's?
options: (aa | bb | (ab | ba)(aa | bb)*(ab | ba))*
(aa | bb)*
(ab | ba)*
(aabb | bbaa)*
options_html: (aa | bb | (ab | ba)(aa | bb)*(ab | ba))*
(aa | bb)*
(ab | ba)*
(aabb | bbaa)*
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An even number of a's means the a's pair up; the same for b's. Inside the star the expression must therefore generate every block in which the a's and b's are balanced locally, so that concatenating blocks keeps both counts even.

Step by step.

  1. aa and bb add two of one letter — both counts stay even.
  2. (ab | ba)(aa | bb)*(ab | ba) starts with one a and one b and ends with one a and one b; the middle part is even in each letter. So the whole block has two a's and two b's, again preserving evenness.
  3. Every block generated therefore keeps both counts even, and a star of such blocks does too — so the expression is contained in the language.
  4. Conversely, scan any word with even counts and cut it as soon as both counts are even again. The first such cut either is aa, or bb, or begins with ab/ba and ends with ab/ba with an even middle — exactly the three cases above.
  5. So the two languages are equal. A brute-force check over all strings up to length 9 finds no mismatch.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) (aa|bb)* cannot produce abab, which has two a's and two b's.
  • (C) (ab|ba)* forces strict alternation, so it misses aabb and abba.
  • (D) (aabb|bbaa)* misses abab and abba.

Common misconception. Writing (aa + bb)* and assuming the pairs can interleave freely. They cannot: an a and a b may have to travel together, which is what the middle term of (A) handles.

Takeaway. For "even count of each letter", the star must contain a block that pairs an a with a b; aa and bb alone are not enough.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let L be a finite language over Σ. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Let L be a finite language over Σ. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: L is regular only if it is empty.
L may be non-regular, because a finite automaton cannot store a finite set of strings.
L is regular, and it satisfies the pumping lemma for every p greater than the length of its longest word.
L satisfies the pumping lemma only if it contains the empty string.
options_html: L is regular only if it is empty.
L may be non-regular, because a finite automaton cannot store a finite set of strings.
L is regular, and it satisfies the pumping lemma for every p greater than the length of its longest word.
L satisfies the pumping lemma only if it contains the empty string.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A finite language is a finite union of singletons, and each singleton is regular, so the language is regular. The pumping lemma is a necessary condition for regularity, so it must hold — and for a finite language it holds trivially.

Step by step.

  1. Let m be the length of the longest word of L (take m = −1 if L = ∅).
  2. Choose any p > m. The pumping lemma asks: for every w ∈ L with |w| ≥ p, there is a decomposition w = xyz that pumps.
  3. No word of L has length ≥ p, so the condition is vacuously true.
  4. Hence L satisfies the pumping lemma, and it is regular by the finite-union argument.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Every finite language is regular, empty or not.
  • (B) A finite automaton can perfectly well recognise a finite set — a trie is such a DFA.
  • (D) The empty string plays no role; a finite language such as {ab} satisfies the lemma for p ≥ 3 without containing ε.

Common misconception. Thinking the pumping lemma "proves" regularity. For finite languages it holds for a reason that has nothing to do with structure — there is simply nothing to pump.

Takeaway. Vacuous truth is legitimate: a condition quantified over an empty set is true. This is also why the pumping lemma cannot be used to show that a finite language is regular.

questions.question: Consider L = {an² : n ≥ 0} over Σ = {a}, and a pumping-lemma proof that takes the constant p and the word w = ap², with w = xyz, |xy| ≤ p and |y| = k ≥ 1. Why does the pumped word xy²z = ap² + k give the contradiction?
questions.question_html: Consider L = {an² : n ≥ 0} over Σ = {a}, and a pumping-lemma proof that takes the constant p and the word w = ap², with w = xyz, |xy| ≤ p and |y| = k ≥ 1. Why does the pumped word xy²z = ap² + k give the contradiction?
options: Because p² + k lies strictly between p² and (p+1)², so it is not a perfect square.
Because k may be zero, so the pumped word can equal w.
Because ap² is not in L to begin with.
Because pumping down always keeps the word inside L.
options_html: Because p² + k lies strictly between p² and (p+1)², so it is not a perfect square.
Because k may be zero, so the pumped word can equal w.
Because ap² is not in L to begin with.
Because pumping down always keeps the word inside L.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. On a one-letter alphabet the whole argument reduces to arithmetic: pumping adds k letters, and the resulting length must again be a perfect square. The bound |xy| ≤ p is what caps k.

Step by step.

  1. Since |xy| ≤ p and y ≠ ε, we have 1 ≤ k ≤ p.
  2. The next perfect square after p² is (p + 1)² = p² + 2p + 1.
  3. Because k ≤ p < 2p + 1, we get p² < p² + k < (p+1)².
  4. An integer strictly between two consecutive squares is not a square, so ap²+k ∉ L.
  5. But the pumping lemma demands xy²z ∈ L. Contradiction — so L is not regular.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) The lemma guarantees |y| ≥ 1, so k ≥ 1; k = 0 is not allowed.
  • (C) ap² is a perfect-square length, so it is in L.
  • (D) Pumping down gives p² − k, which is also between (p − 1)² and p² only for small k; it is not the step that produces the clean contradiction.

Common misconception. Reaching for the "count the letters in each block" argument, which needs two blocks. On a unary alphabet there are no blocks — only lengths — and the proof is a statement about squares.

Takeaway. For unary languages, translate the pumping lemma into arithmetic on lengths: |w| must survive an addition of at most p.

questions.question: To prove that L = {w ∈ {a, b}* : #a(w) = #b(w)} is not regular by the Myhill–Nerode theorem, one exhibits an infinite set of pairwise inequivalent strings. Which of the following sets works?
questions.question_html: To prove that L = {w ∈ {a, b}* : #a(w) = #b(w)} is not regular by the Myhill–Nerode theorem, one exhibits an infinite set of pairwise inequivalent strings. Which of the following sets works?
options: { aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0 }
{ bⁿaⁿ : n ≥ 0 }
options_html: { (ab)ⁿ : n ≥ 0 }
{ aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0 }
{ bⁿaⁿ : n ≥ 0 }
{ aⁿ : n ≥ 0 }
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Two strings are inequivalent when some suffix separates them: one continuation lands in L and the other does not. The set must therefore contain strings whose imbalance differs, so that a suffix can be tuned to exactly cancel one imbalance and not the other.

Step by step.

  1. Take aⁱ and aʲ with i ≠ j. Use the suffix bⁱ.
  2. aⁱbⁱ has equal counts, so it is in L.
  3. aʲbⁱ has j a's against i b's, so it is in L exactly when j = i. For i ≠ j it is not, and the case j = 0 is covered too, since bⁱ ∉ L for i ≥ 1.
  4. So every pair aⁱ, aʲ is inequivalent: infinitely many classes, so L is not regular.
  5. The other three sets fail for a structural reason: every string in them already has #a = #b, and appending any suffix z changes the difference by #a(z) − #b(z), which is the same for all of them. They all fall into a single class.

Answer: Option (D) — {aⁿ : n ≥ 0}.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A), (B), (C) Each is a set of balanced words. Two balanced words accept exactly the same suffixes, so they are equivalent and contribute one class, not infinitely many.

Common misconception. Choosing a set of words that are all in the language. Inequivalent witnesses usually need to be outside the language, or at least unbalanced, so that a suffix can distinguish them.

Takeaway. For a counting language, witness with the prefixes that build up different imbalances — here aⁿ, separated by bⁿ.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: For L = L((ab)*) over Σ = {a, b}, what is the smallest p ≥ 1 such that every w ∈ L with |w| ≥ p can be written w = xyz with |xy| ≤ p, |y| ≥ 1 and xyⁱz ∈ L for every i ≥ 0?
questions.question_html: For L = L((ab)*) over Σ = {a, b}, what is the smallest p ≥ 1 such that every w ∈ L with |w| ≥ p can be written w = xyz with |xy| ≤ p, |y| ≥ 1 and xyⁱz ∈ L for every i ≥ 0?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The pumping constant is the length below which a word may be exempt. Here the only words of L that are at risk are ε and ab, and both are short.

Step by step.

  1. Words of L are ε, ab, abab, ababab, … — all of even length.
  2. Show p = 2 works. For any w ∈ L with |w| ≥ 2, take x = ε, y = ab (the first two symbols), and z the rest. Then |xy| = 2 ≤ 2 and |y| = 2 ≥ 1.
  3. xyⁱz = (ab)ⁱ z. Since z is itself a sequence of complete ab pairs, (ab)ⁱz ∈ (ab)* for every i ≥ 0, including i = 0.
  4. Show p = 1 fails. The word w = ab has |w| ≥ 1, but |xy| ≤ 1 forces y = a and z = b; then xy⁰z = b ∉ L.
  5. So the smallest valid constant is 2.

Answer: 2.

Common misconception. Quoting the number of states of the minimal complete DFA (3, counting the dead state) as though it were the smallest constant. The state count is an upper bound for p; the smallest value can be smaller, and here it is.

Takeaway. p is bounded above by the number of states, but the question asks for the smallest value, which you find by testing the shortest words of L.

questions.question: Which one of the following is a correct argument, using closure properties, that L = {w ∈ {a, b}* : #a(w) = #b(w)} is not regular?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following is a correct argument, using closure properties, that L = {w ∈ {a, b}* : #a(w) = #b(w)} is not regular?
options: L ∩ a*b* = {aⁿbⁿ}, and the intersection of a non-regular language with a regular one is non-regular, so L is non-regular.
L ∩ a*b* = {aⁿbⁿ}. Since a*b* is regular, L regular would make L ∩ a*b* regular; but {aⁿbⁿ} is not regular, so L is not regular.
L ∪ a*b* = {a, b}* is regular, so L must be regular too.
L* = {a, b}*, and a non-regular language can have a regular Kleene star, so L is non-regular.
options_html: L ∩ a*b* = {aⁿbⁿ}, and the intersection of a non-regular language with a regular one is non-regular, so L is non-regular.
L ∩ a*b* = {aⁿbⁿ}. Since a*b* is regular, L regular would make L ∩ a*b* regular; but {aⁿbⁿ} is not regular, so L is not regular.
L ∪ a*b* = {a, b}* is regular, so L must be regular too.
L* = {a, b}*, and a non-regular language can have a regular Kleene star, so L is non-regular.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Closure properties are used in the contrapositive direction: if L were regular, then so would be anything obtained from L by a regularity-preserving operation. A regular result that is known not to be regular is the contradiction.

Step by step.

  1. Compute the intersection. A word in a*b* is aⁱbʲ; it has equal counts exactly when i = j. So L ∩ a*b* = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0}.
  2. Suppose L is regular. The class of regular languages is closed under intersection, and a*b* is regular, so L ∩ a*b* would be regular.
  3. But {aⁿbⁿ} is not regular — the standard pumping argument applies.
  4. Contradiction, so L is not regular. The direction of the implication is what makes the argument valid.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) The claim "non-regular ∩ regular is non-regular" is false: every non-regular language intersected with ∅ gives ∅, which is regular.
  • (C) A union being regular says nothing about its parts: L ∪ (Σ* \ L) = Σ* for any L at all.
  • (D) A true observation that is not an argument — L* = Σ* holds for this L, and it constrains nothing.

Common misconception. Using closure properties forwards ("a regular language intersected with something gives…"). They only transfer regularity from the parts to the result; to conclude non-regularity you must argue by contradiction from an assumed regular L.

Takeaway. The closure recipe: intersect with a suitable regular set to expose a known non-regular core, then argue by contradiction.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the pumping lemma for regular languages are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about the pumping lemma for regular languages are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Every finite language satisfies the pumping lemma, vacuously, once p exceeds the length of its longest word.
Satisfying the pumping lemma does not prove regularity: it is a necessary but not a sufficient condition.
One word w ∈ L together with one decomposition that fails to pump is enough to prove that L is not regular.
If L satisfies the pumping lemma with constant p = 1, then L is regular.
options_html: Every finite language satisfies the pumping lemma, vacuously, once p exceeds the length of its longest word.
Satisfying the pumping lemma does not prove regularity: it is a necessary but not a sufficient condition.
One word w ∈ L together with one decomposition that fails to pump is enough to prove that L is not regular.
If L satisfies the pumping lemma with constant p = 1, then L is regular.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The pumping lemma is a one-way implication: regular ⇒ pumpable. Its contrapositive, not pumpable ⇒ not regular, is the direction that is actually usable, and it requires defeating every decomposition of a suitably chosen word for every constant.

Step by step.

  1. (A) If p exceeds the longest word, no word of L has length ≥ p, so the condition is quantified over an empty set and holds. TRUE ✓
  2. (B) There are non-regular languages that satisfy the lemma, so satisfaction cannot be used to conclude regularity. TRUE ✓
  3. (C) A single failed decomposition proves nothing: the lemma only promises that some decomposition pumps. To refute it you must show that no decomposition of w pumps, and that this holds for every p. FALSE ✗
  4. (D) The value of the constant carries no structural information. A non-regular language that satisfies the lemma for some p can be re-parameterised, and regularity is a property of the language, not of a numeric constant. FALSE ✗

Answer: Options (A) and (B).

Common misconception. Confusing "there exists a decomposition" with "every decomposition". The quantifier structure — for all p, there exists w, for all decompositions, there exists i — is the whole content of the lemma, and negating it correctly is the examinable skill.

Takeaway. Use the pumping lemma only in the negative direction, and only with a word and a proof that every legal decomposition breaks. For a positive answer, use Myhill–Nerode or exhibit an automaton.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let G be a context-free grammar with no ε-productions, and let T be a complete derivation tree for a string w ∈ L(G). Which one of the following numbers is the same for every complete derivation tree of w?
questions.question_html: Let G be a context-free grammar with no ε-productions, and let T be a complete derivation tree for a string w ∈ L(G). Which one of the following numbers is the same for every complete derivation tree of w?
options: the number of internal nodes
the total number of nodes
the number of leaves
the height of the tree
options_html: the number of internal nodes
the total number of nodes
the number of leaves
the height of the tree
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The leaves of a complete derivation tree, read left to right, spell the yield. With no ε-productions no leaf can contribute the empty string, so leaves and symbols of the yield stand in one-to-one correspondence.

Step by step.

  1. Each leaf contributes exactly one symbol to the yield of the tree.
  2. The yield is w, so every complete derivation tree of w has exactly |w| leaves, whatever its shape.
  3. The internal nodes are the productions applied. Two derivations of the same string may apply different numbers of productions: in S → A | a, A → a the string a has one tree with 1 internal node and another with 2.
  4. The total number of nodes is leaves plus internal nodes, and the height also changes from tree to tree, so only the leaf count is fixed.

Answer: Option (C) — the number of leaves, which equals |w|.

Common misconception. Assuming that all derivation trees of a string have the same shape, and therefore the same node count and height. Ambiguity exists precisely because the shapes differ; what cannot differ is how many symbols the leaves have to spell.

questions.question: Let G be the grammar S → aSb | ε. The complete derivation tree of the string a²b² is drawn with the ε-production shown as a single child labelled ε. How many leaves does that tree have?
questions.question_html: Let G be the grammar S → aSb | ε. The complete derivation tree of the string a²b² is drawn with the ε-production shown as a single child labelled ε. How many leaves does that tree have?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An ε-production gives an internal node a single child labelled ε. That child is a leaf, but it contributes nothing to the yield, so the tree has more leaves than the string has symbols.

Step by step.

  1. Derive the string: S ⇒ aSb ⇒ a(aSb)b ⇒ a(aεb)b = aabb.
  2. The root S has children a, S, b; the middle S again has children a, S, b; the innermost S has the single child ε.
  3. Leaves in left-to-right order: a, a, b, b, ε — five of them.
  4. The four terminal leaves spell aabb; the fifth leaf contributes the empty string.

Answer: Option (D) — 5 leaves.

Common misconception. Counting only the terminal leaves and answering 4. The ε-leaf is a real leaf of the drawn tree; it simply adds nothing to the yield. This is exactly why a tree may have more leaves than |w| once ε-productions are allowed.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let G be the grammar S → aSb | ε. The complete derivation tree of the string a⁵b⁵ is drawn with the ε-production shown as a single child labelled ε. The height of a tree is the number of edges on a longest path from the root to a leaf. What is the height of that tree?
questions.question_html: Let G be the grammar S → aSb | ε. The complete derivation tree of the string a⁵b⁵ is drawn with the ε-production shown as a single child labelled ε. The height of a tree is the number of edges on a longest path from the root to a leaf. What is the height of that tree?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Every application of S → aSb adds one edge to the spine of the tree, and the spine ends at the single ε leaf created by S → ε.

Step by step.

  1. The string a⁵b⁵ needs five applications of S → aSb, one per matched pair, and then one application of S → ε at the innermost S.
  2. The nodes on the spine are S₀, S₁, S₂, S₃, S₄, S₅, where S₅ is the node that expands to ε.
  3. The path from S₀ to the ε-leaf therefore has 5 edges, and no other path is longer because every terminal leaf hangs directly off one of these S nodes.
  4. Height = 5.

Answer: 5

Common misconception. Counting the six nodes on the path and answering 6, or counting the ten terminal symbols and answering 10. Height counts edges, not nodes, and only along the longest single path.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: A complete derivation tree of a string uses 7 productions, and its yield has length 5. How many nodes does the tree have in total, counting internal nodes and leaves together?
questions.question_html: A complete derivation tree of a string uses 7 productions, and its yield has length 5. How many nodes does the tree have in total, counting internal nodes and leaves together?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Each internal node is one application of a production, and each leaf is one symbol of the yield. The two counts are therefore independent of each other and simply add.

Step by step.

  1. Internal nodes = number of productions applied = 7.
  2. Leaves = length of the yield = 5, since each leaf contributes exactly one symbol.
  3. Total nodes = internal nodes + leaves = 7 + 5 = 12.
  4. Check with the edge count: a tree with 12 nodes has 11 edges, and the 7 internal nodes have 7 children in total across the last level plus the internal ones — consistent with a tree of 12 nodes.

Answer: Option (C) — 12 nodes.

Common misconception. Answering 9 by applying the CNF identity 2|w| − 1 without checking that the grammar is in Chomsky Normal Form, or answering 13 by adding an extra node for a phantom root. Only in CNF with no ε-productions is the node count forced to be 2|w| − 1.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let G = (V, T, P, S) be a context-free grammar and let T be a complete derivation tree for a string w ∈ L(G). Select every statement that is TRUE.
questions.question_html: Let G = (V, T, P, S) be a context-free grammar and let T be a complete derivation tree for a string w ∈ L(G). Select every statement that is TRUE.
options: If G contains an ε-production and w ≠ ε, the tree may contain a leaf labelled ε.
If every production of G has a right-hand side of length at most two, then every internal node of the tree has exactly two children.
If G contains a unit production A → B, the tree may contain an internal node labelled A whose only child is labelled B.
The number of internal nodes of the tree equals the number of productions applied in the derivation that the tree represents.
options_html: If G contains an ε-production and w ≠ ε, the tree may contain a leaf labelled ε.
If every production of G has a right-hand side of length at most two, then every internal node of the tree has exactly two children.
If G contains a unit production A → B, the tree may contain an internal node labelled A whose only child is labelled B.
The number of internal nodes of the tree equals the number of productions applied in the derivation that the tree represents.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The children of an internal node are exactly the right-hand side of the production used there. The number of children is therefore the length of that right-hand side — one for a unit production or a terminal production, two for a binary production, and one labelled ε for an ε-production.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true. In S → aSb | ε the tree of aabb contains the leaf ε, even though w ≠ ε.
  2. (B) false. A right-hand side of length one is allowed by the hypothesis, and it gives a node with a single child — a unit production A → B or a terminal production A → a. "At most two" is not "exactly two".
  3. (C) true. Applying A → B creates a node labelled A with the single child B.
  4. (D) true. Each internal node is one application of a production, and each application creates exactly one internal node, so the two counts agree.

Answer: Options (A, C and D).

Common misconception. Reading "at most two" as "exactly two" and concluding that the tree is a full binary tree. Unit productions and terminal productions both have a right-hand side of length one, so a node may have a single child.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let G be the grammar S → SS | a. A derivation tree of the string a⁴ is drawn. How many nodes of that tree are labelled S, and how does the answer depend on which tree is drawn?
questions.question_html: Let G be the grammar S → SS | a. A derivation tree of the string a⁴ is drawn. How many nodes of that tree are labelled S, and how does the answer depend on which tree is drawn?
options: 4, and it is the same for every such tree
3, and it is the same for every such tree
3, but it differs between the five trees of a⁴
5, and it is the same for every such tree
options_html: 4, and it is the same for every such tree
3, and it is the same for every such tree
3, but it differs between the five trees of a⁴
5, and it is the same for every such tree
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. In S → SS | a every internal node has exactly two children, so every derivation tree is a full binary tree whose leaves are the terminals. A full binary tree with n leaves always has exactly n − 1 internal nodes.

Step by step.

  1. The yield a⁴ supplies 4 leaves, one per terminal.
  2. A full binary tree with 4 leaves has 4 − 1 = 3 internal nodes.
  3. Every internal node is labelled S (the only nonterminal) and every leaf is labelled a, so the tree has exactly 3 nodes labelled S.
  4. The shape can vary — there are 5 such trees — but the leaf count and the child count are fixed, so the internal-node count is fixed too.

Answer: Option (B) — 3 nodes labelled S, the same for every tree.

Common misconception. Believing that because there are several trees they must have different sizes. Different shapes with the same leaf count always have the same number of internal nodes; only the arrangement differs.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let G be a context-free grammar in which every production has a right-hand side of length exactly two, and let w ∈ L(G) with |w| = n ≥ 1. Taking height as the number of edges on a longest root-to-leaf path, what is the largest possible height of a derivation tree of w?
questions.question_html: Let G be a context-free grammar in which every production has a right-hand side of length exactly two, and let w ∈ L(G) with |w| = n ≥ 1. Taking height as the number of edges on a longest root-to-leaf path, what is the largest possible height of a derivation tree of w?
options: n
⌈log₂ n⌉
options_html: n
⌈log₂ n⌉
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A right-hand side of length exactly two gives every internal node exactly two children, so every derivation tree is a full binary tree with n leaves.

Step by step.

  1. Write h for the height and n for the number of leaves.
  2. A path of h edges passes through h internal nodes, and each of them has a second child that is not on the path. Those second children are distinct nodes of the tree, and each of them roots at least one leaf, so n ≥ h + 1, that is h ≤ n − 1.
  3. The bound is attained by the "comb" shape, in which each internal node has one terminal child and one internal child; the tree then looks like a path of n − 1 edges.
  4. So the largest possible height is n − 1.

Answer: Option (A) — n − 1.

Common misconception. Answering ⌈log₂ n⌉, which is the smallest possible height (a balanced tree), or 2n − 1, which is the number of nodes rather than the height. Read the question as asking for a maximum and reason about the most lopsided tree.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following grammars is ambiguous?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following grammars is ambiguous?
options: S → SS | (S) | ε
S → aSb | ab
S → aS | bS | ε
options_html: S → (S) | ()
S → SS | (S) | ε
S → aSb | ab
S → aS | bS | ε
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A grammar is ambiguous when some string in its language has two distinct derivation trees. The quickest witness is a string that can be split into two parts of the language in more than one way.

Step by step.

  1. (A) generates exactly (ⁿ)ⁿ: every string is forced, one tree each. Unambiguous.
  2. (C) generates {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1}: the a's must all be produced before the b's. Unambiguous.
  3. (D) is right-linear — each right-hand side has at most one nonterminal, at the extreme right — and every string over {a, b} has exactly one derivation. Unambiguous.
  4. (B) is ambiguous. Take the string ()()(). One tree splits it as () followed by ()() at the root; another splits it as ()() followed by (). Both are legal S → SS derivations, so the string has two distinct derivation trees.

Answer: Option (B) — S → SS | (S) | ε.

Common misconception. Testing only short strings. For grammar (B) the strings () and ()() each have exactly one tree; the ambiguity first shows at length 6. A single unambiguous string never proves a grammar unambiguous, and one ambiguous string is enough to prove it ambiguous.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let G be the grammar S → SS | a | b. Every string in L(G) is a non-empty string over {a, b}. What is the length of the shortest string in L(G) that has two distinct derivation trees?
questions.question_html: Let G be the grammar S → SS | a | b. Every string in L(G) is a non-empty string over {a, b}. What is the length of the shortest string in L(G) that has two distinct derivation trees?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A derivation tree for a string of length n is a full binary tree with n leaves, so the only freedom is how the string is split into two non-empty parts at the root. Two trees exist exactly when the string can be split into two parts of the language in two different ways.

Step by step.

  1. Length 1. The single symbol must be produced by S → a or S → b; there is one tree.
  2. Length 2. The only split is (first symbol)(second symbol), and both halves are single symbols of the language. One tree.
  3. Length 3. Take aab. It splits as a | ab and as aa | b, and all four parts are strings of the language. Two distinct trees.
  4. So the shortest ambiguous string has length 3. (In general the number of trees for a string of length n is the Catalan number C(n−1).)

Answer: 3

Common misconception. Answering 2, usually by imagining that ab can be produced both as S ⇒ SS ⇒ ab and in some other order. There is only one split of a two-symbol string, so only one tree.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let G be the grammar S → S + S | S * S | a. How many distinct derivation trees does G have for the string a + a * a?
questions.question_html: Let G be the grammar S → S + S | S * S | a. How many distinct derivation trees does G have for the string a + a * a?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. In this grammar neither operator is given precedence and neither is given associativity, so each binary parenthesisation of the expression is a separate derivation tree. Counting trees is counting the parenthesisations.

Step by step.

  1. The expression has three operands and two operators, so every tree is a full binary tree with three leaves.
  2. A full binary tree with three leaves has exactly two shapes: the root operator is the first one, or the root operator is the second one.
  3. Shape 1: (a + a) * a — root *, left child a + a.
  4. Shape 2: a + (a * a) — root +, right child a * a.
  5. Both are derivations of G, so there are 2 distinct derivation trees — the classic evidence that the grammar is ambiguous.

Answer: Option (A) — 2 trees.

Common misconception. Answering 1 by silently applying the usual precedence of * over +. Precedence is a property of a particular grammar, not of the expression: this grammar has none, which is exactly why it is ambiguous.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let G have the productions S → A | B, A → aA | a and B → aB | a. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Let G have the productions S → A | B, A → aA | a and B → aB | a. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: G is unambiguous and L(G) = a⁺
G is ambiguous and L(G) = a*
G is unambiguous and L(G) = a*
G is ambiguous and L(G) = a⁺
options_html: G is unambiguous and L(G) = a⁺
G is ambiguous and L(G) = a*
G is unambiguous and L(G) = a*
G is ambiguous and L(G) = a⁺
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A and B are two different nonterminals with identical productions, and S may start with either. Every string therefore has at least two derivation trees, one through A and one through B.

Step by step.

  1. The language. A produces a⁺: each A → aA adds one a and the last step uses A → a. The same holds for B, so L(G) = a⁺ — one or more a's, never the empty string.
  2. Ambiguity. For the string a there are two trees: S ⇒ A ⇒ a and S ⇒ B ⇒ a.
  3. A single string with two distinct derivation trees is enough, so G is ambiguous.
  4. Hence G is ambiguous and L(G) = a⁺.

Answer: Option (D) — ambiguous, with L(G) = a⁺.

Common misconception. Choosing a* because both alternatives look like they could stop immediately. A has no ε-production, so it must emit at least one a; the empty string is not in the language. The ambiguity comes from the two parallel routes, not from the ε.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Select every statement about ambiguous context-free grammars that is TRUE.
questions.question_html: Select every statement about ambiguous context-free grammars that is TRUE.
options: Every finite language has an unambiguous context-free grammar.
If a grammar has an ε-production, then it is ambiguous.
If every string of L(G) has exactly one derivation tree, then no string of L(G) has two distinct leftmost derivations.
If L(G) is regular, then G is unambiguous.
options_html: Every finite language has an unambiguous context-free grammar.
If a grammar has an ε-production, then it is ambiguous.
If every string of L(G) has exactly one derivation tree, then no string of L(G) has two distinct leftmost derivations.
If L(G) is regular, then G is unambiguous.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Ambiguity is a property of a grammar; regularity and finiteness are properties of a language. The bridge between them is that the number of derivation trees of a string equals the number of its leftmost derivations.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true. A finite language {w₁, …, wₖ} is generated unambiguously by S → w₁ | … | wₖ with fresh nonterminals for each symbol, or simply by listing the strings; every string then has exactly one tree.
  2. (B) false. S → aSb | ε is unambiguous and contains an ε-production. ε-productions create ambiguity only in combination with other overlapping alternatives.
  3. (C) true. The number of leftmost derivations of a string equals the number of its derivation trees, so one tree means at most one leftmost derivation — and there is always at least one.
  4. (D) false. The grammar S → A | B, A → a, B → a is ambiguous, yet its language {a} is regular.

Answer: Options (A and C).

Common misconception. Treating ambiguity as a property of the language. A regular — indeed a finite — language always has an unambiguous grammar, but nothing forces the particular grammar in front of you to be that one.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following grammars is ambiguous?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following grammars is ambiguous?
options: S → aSb | ab
S → aSb | ε
S → aSb | aSbb | ε
S → aS | bS | ε
options_html: S → aSb | ab
S → aSb | ε
S → aSb | aSbb | ε
S → aS | bS | ε
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Alternatives whose languages overlap create ambiguity. In S → aSb | aSbb | ε a derivation may add one b or two b's at each level, so the same string can be built with different mixtures of the two alternatives.

Step by step.

  1. (A) generates {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1}. The a's and b's are forced into matched pairs, so each string has exactly one tree. Unambiguous.
  2. (B) generates {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0}, again one tree per string. Unambiguous.
  3. (D) is right-linear and generates every string over {a, b}; each string has one derivation, read off left to right. Unambiguous.
  4. (C) generates aᵏbᵐ with k ≤ m ≤ 2k. Each of the k levels adds either 1 or 2 b's, so the number of trees for a string with m − k "doubling" levels is C(k, m − k). For a²b³ this is C(2, 1) = 2: the levels may add 2 then 1, or 1 then 2. Two trees, so the grammar is ambiguous.

Answer: Option (C) — S → aSb | aSbb | ε.

Common misconception. Assuming that because the alternatives look different they cannot produce the same string. Ambiguity comes from overlap in the languages of the alternatives, not from their appearance; here aSb and aSbb both contribute to strings whose b-count lies strictly between the two extremes.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: A grammar has exactly the productions S → aB | ε and B → b. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html: A grammar has exactly the productions S → aB | ε and B → b. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: It is in Chomsky Normal Form.
It is in Greibach Normal Form, under the standard allowance of S → ε when ε ∈ L(G) and S occurs on the right side of no production.
It is in both normal forms.
It is in neither normal form.
options_html: It is in Chomsky Normal Form.
It is in Greibach Normal Form, under the standard allowance of S → ε when ε ∈ L(G) and S occurs on the right side of no production.
It is in both normal forms.
It is in neither normal form.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Chomsky Normal Form allows only A → BC (two nonterminals) and A → a (one terminal). Greibach Normal Form allows only A → aα with a a terminal and α a string of nonterminals, plus the single exception S → ε.

Step by step.

  1. Not CNF. The production S → aB has a terminal followed by a nonterminal; CNF has no such form.
  2. GNF, first two productions. S → aB is aα with α = B, and B → b is aα with α = ε.
  3. GNF, the ε-production. ε ∈ L(G) and S appears on no right side, so S → ε is exactly the exception that GNF permits.
  4. So the grammar is in Greibach Normal Form and not in Chomsky Normal Form.

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Rejecting the grammar because of S → ε. Greibach Normal Form does allow one ε-production — S → ε, when the language contains ε and S is never used on a right side. Without that exception no GNF grammar could generate a language containing ε.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let G be a grammar in Chomsky Normal Form with no ε-productions, and let T be a complete derivation tree for a string w ∈ L(G) with |w| ≥ 2. How many children does every internal node of T have?
questions.question_html: Let G be a grammar in Chomsky Normal Form with no ε-productions, and let T be a complete derivation tree for a string w ∈ L(G) with |w| ≥ 2. How many children does every internal node of T have?
options: exactly two
at most two
at least two
either one or two
options_html: exactly two
at most two
at least two
either one or two
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Every production of a CNF grammar is either A → BC or A → a. The children of an internal node are the right-hand side of the production used there, so the child count is the length of that right-hand side.

Step by step.

  1. A production A → a ends the branch: the node labelled a is a leaf, not an internal node.
  2. A production A → BC gives the internal node A exactly two children, B and C.
  3. No ε-productions means no node has a single child labelled ε.
  4. Hence every internal node has exactly two children: the tree is a full binary tree.

Answer: Option (A) — exactly two children.

Common misconception. Answering "at most two" by carrying over the CNF definition without applying the two extra hypotheses. "At most two" would be the right answer for a general grammar with short right sides; with CNF and no ε-productions the count is forced to be exactly two.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: A grammar has the productions S → ABCDE, A → a, B → b, C → c, D → d and E → e. It is converted to Chomsky Normal Form by the standard procedure, which replaces a right side of length k ≥ 3 by a chain of productions of length two, introducing one new nonterminal per split. How many new nonterminals does the procedure introduce for the production S → ABCDE?
questions.question_html: A grammar has the productions S → ABCDE, A → a, B → b, C → c, D → d and E → e. It is converted to Chomsky Normal Form by the standard procedure, which replaces a right side of length k ≥ 3 by a chain of productions of length two, introducing one new nonterminal per split. How many new nonterminals does the procedure introduce for the production S → ABCDE?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A right side of length k is broken into k − 1 binary productions, and the first of them can keep the original left side, so k − 2 new nonterminals are needed.

Step by step.

  1. Here k = 5, so k − 2 = 3.
  2. Concretely: S → A X₁, X₁ → B X₂, X₂ → C X₃, X₃ → D E.
  3. The new nonterminals are X₁, X₂, X₃ — three of them.
  4. The other five productions are already of the form A → a, so no terminal needs to be replaced and no further nonterminal is introduced.

Answer: 3

Common misconception. Answering 4 by assuming one new nonterminal per binary production, or 5 by assuming one per symbol. The first split keeps S as the left side and the last group has two symbols, so the count is k − 2.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: A grammar has the productions S → ABC, A → a, B → b and C → c. It is converted to Chomsky Normal Form by the standard procedure: new nonterminals are introduced only where the form requires them, and no production is duplicated. How many productions does the resulting CNF grammar have?
questions.question_html: A grammar has the productions S → ABC, A → a, B → b and C → c. It is converted to Chomsky Normal Form by the standard procedure: new nonterminals are introduced only where the form requires them, and no production is duplicated. How many productions does the resulting CNF grammar have?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Only two things in CNF conversion add productions: splitting a right side longer than two, and replacing a terminal that sits beside a nonterminal. Here the terminals already have nonterminals of their own, so only one split is needed.

Step by step.

  1. The three terminal productions A → a, B → b, C → c already have the CNF form; they are kept unchanged (3 productions).
  2. S → ABC has length 3, so it is split once: S → A X and X → B C, with one new nonterminal X (2 productions).
  3. No right side contains a terminal beside a nonterminal, so no further nonterminal is introduced.
  4. Total: 3 + 2 = 5 productions.

Answer: Option (D) — 5 productions.

Common misconception. Answering 4 by forgetting that S → ABC cannot stay as it is, or 7 by inventing terminal nonterminals for a, b, c that the grammar already provides as A, B, C.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let G be a grammar in Chomsky Normal Form with no ε-productions, and let T be a complete derivation tree for a string w ∈ L(G) with |w| = n ≥ 2. Select every statement that is TRUE.
questions.question_html: Let G be a grammar in Chomsky Normal Form with no ε-productions, and let T be a complete derivation tree for a string w ∈ L(G) with |w| = n ≥ 2. Select every statement that is TRUE.
options: Every internal node of T has exactly two children.
T has exactly n − 1 internal nodes.
The height of T is at least ⌈log₂ n⌉.
The height of T is at most ⌈log₂ n⌉.
options_html: Every internal node of T has exactly two children.
T has exactly n − 1 internal nodes.
The height of T is at least ⌈log₂ n⌉.
The height of T is at most ⌈log₂ n⌉.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A CNF grammar with no ε-productions produces only binary and terminal productions, so every derivation tree is a full binary tree whose n leaves are the terminals of w.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true. A → BC gives two children; A → a creates a leaf, not an internal node.
  2. (B) true. A full binary tree with n leaves has exactly n − 1 internal nodes — equivalently, the derivation uses 2n − 1 productions in all.
  3. (C) true. A tree of height h has at most 2^h leaves, so n ≤ 2^h and h ≥ ⌈log₂ n⌉.
  4. (D) false. The height can be far larger: the comb-shaped tree has height n − 1, which for n = 8 is 7 against ⌈log₂ 8⌉ = 3. ⌈log₂ n⌉ is a lower bound, not an upper one.

Answer: Options (A, B and C).

Common misconception. Confusing a lower bound with an upper bound. ⌈log₂ n⌉ is the smallest height a tree with n leaves can have — the balanced shape — while a lopsided tree of the same string can be much taller.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following statements about Greibach Normal Form is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following statements about Greibach Normal Form is TRUE?
options: A grammar in Greibach Normal Form can derive ε only through a production S → ε, and only when S occurs on the right side of no production.
Every grammar in Greibach Normal Form is unambiguous.
In a grammar in Greibach Normal Form every right-hand side begins with a nonterminal.
A grammar in Greibach Normal Form may contain a unit production A → B.
options_html: A grammar in Greibach Normal Form can derive ε only through a production S → ε, and only when S occurs on the right side of no production.
Every grammar in Greibach Normal Form is unambiguous.
In a grammar in Greibach Normal Form every right-hand side begins with a nonterminal.
A grammar in Greibach Normal Form may contain a unit production A → B.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Greibach Normal Form requires every production to have the shape A → aα, where a is a terminal and α is a possibly empty string of nonterminals. The only permitted exception is S → ε.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true. Every ordinary production consumes at least one terminal, so ε can only come from the single exception S → ε. That exception is allowed only when ε ∈ L(G) and S is never used on a right side — otherwise a derivation could re-enter S and the grammar could derive ε in ways the normal form does not permit.
  2. (B) false. GNF removes left recursion and fixes the first symbol of every right side; it does not remove ambiguity. S → aSB | b, B → b is in GNF and remains a starting point for ambiguous grammars over the same language.
  3. (C) false. Exactly the opposite: every right side begins with a terminal, which is what makes the next input symbol decide the production.
  4. (D) false. A unit production A → B begins with a nonterminal, so it is not of the form aα and is excluded.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Thinking that a normal form also settles ambiguity or determinism. Normal forms constrain the shape of the productions; they say nothing about how many derivation trees a string has.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let L be a context-free language over Σ = {a, b}. Which one of the following is necessarily context-free?
questions.question_html: Let L be a context-free language over Σ = {a, b}. Which one of the following is necessarily context-free?
options: the complement Σ* \ L
L ∩ {ww : w ∈ {a, b}*}
{ww : w ∈ L}
options_html: the complement Σ* \ L
L ∩ {ww : w ∈ {a, b}*}
L ∪ (Σ* \ L)
{ww : w ∈ L}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The context-free languages are closed under union, concatenation and Kleene star, but not under intersection or complementation. A union that swallows the whole alphabet is therefore safe even though the two parts of it are not individually well behaved.

Step by step.

  1. (C) true. L ∪ (Σ* \ L) = Σ* for every language L, and Σ* is regular, hence context-free. No property of L is needed.
  2. (A) false. Complementation does not preserve context-freeness. If it did, closure under union and complementation would give closure under intersection, which fails.
  3. (B) false. Take L = Σ*, which is context-free. Then L ∩ {ww} = {ww}, and {ww : w ∈ {a, b}*} is the standard non-context-free language.
  4. (D) false. With L = Σ* the set {ww : w ∈ L} is again {ww}, which is not context-free.

Answer: Option (C).

Common misconception. Assuming that a set built out of a context-free language by set operations stays context-free. Only the listed operations are safe; complement and intersection are not, and doubling each half of a string is a classic way to destroy context-freeness.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let L₁ = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0} and L₂ = {cⁿdⁿ : n ≥ 0}, both read over the alphabet {a, b, c, d}. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Let L₁ = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0} and L₂ = {cⁿdⁿ : n ≥ 0}, both read over the alphabet {a, b, c, d}. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: only L₁ ∪ L₂ is context-free
only L₁ ∩ L₂ is context-free
both L₁ ∪ L₂ and L₁ ∩ L₂ are context-free
neither L₁ ∪ L₂ nor L₁ ∩ L₂ is context-free
options_html: only L₁ ∪ L₂ is context-free
only L₁ ∩ L₂ is context-free
both L₁ ∪ L₂ and L₁ ∩ L₂ are context-free
neither L₁ ∪ L₂ nor L₁ ∩ L₂ is context-free
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Union of two context-free languages is always context-free. Intersection is not preserved in general, but here the two languages use disjoint alphabets, so their intersection collapses to a single short string.

Step by step.

  1. The union. L₁ and L₂ are each context-free, and the context-free languages are closed under union, so L₁ ∪ L₂ is context-free.
  2. The intersection. Every string of L₁ uses only a and b; every string of L₂ uses only c and d.
  3. The only string in both is ε, so L₁ ∩ L₂ = {ε}, which is finite and therefore regular, hence context-free.
  4. Both languages are context-free.

Answer: Option (C) — both are context-free.

Common misconception. Applying the general fact "context-free languages are not closed under intersection" as if it said every intersection fails. Non-closure only guarantees that some intersection is outside the class; a particular intersection may well be context-free.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let L = {aⁿbⁿcᵐ : n ≥ 0, m ≥ 0} over the alphabet {a, b, c}. How many strings of length 5 belong to L?
questions.question_html: Let L = {aⁿbⁿcᵐ : n ≥ 0, m ≥ 0} over the alphabet {a, b, c}. How many strings of length 5 belong to L?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Every string of L is fixed by its two counts: n a's followed by n b's followed by m c's. Its length is 2n + m, and for a fixed pair (n, m) there is exactly one string.

Step by step.

  1. Set 2n + m = 5 with n, m ≥ 0.
  2. n = 0 gives m = 5: the string ccccc.
  3. n = 1 gives m = 3: the string abccc.
  4. n = 2 gives m = 1: the string aabbc.
  5. n ≥ 3 would need m < 0, which is not allowed. So there are exactly 3 strings.

Answer: 3

Common misconception. Counting arrangements of a's, b's and c's and multiplying by binomial coefficients. The language fixes the order — all a's, then all b's, then all c's — so each legal pair (n, m) gives exactly one string.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Consider these seven languages over the alphabet {a, b, c, d}. How many of them are context-free?(i) {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0}(ii) {aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 0}(iii) {ww : w ∈ {a, b}*}(iv) {aⁱbʲ : i ≠ j, i, j ≥ 0}(v) {aⁿbⁿcᵐ : n, m ≥ 0}(vi) {aⁿbⁿcⁿdⁿ : n ≥ 0}(vii) {aⁿbⁿcᵐdᵐ : n, m ≥ 0}
questions.question_html:
Consider these seven languages over the alphabet {a, b, c, d}. How many of them are context-free?
(i) {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0}
(ii) {aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 0}
(iii) {ww : w ∈ {a, b}*}
(iv) {aⁱbʲ : i ≠ j, i, j ≥ 0}
(v) {aⁿbⁿcᵐ : n, m ≥ 0}
(vi) {aⁿbⁿcⁿdⁿ : n ≥ 0}
(vii) {aⁿbⁿcᵐdᵐ : n, m ≥ 0}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A context-free language may enforce one matched count at a time; the moment two independent counts must agree, the language usually leaves the class. A single stack cannot verify two independent balances.

Step by step.

  1. (i) context-free. S → aSb | ε.
  2. (ii) not context-free. Three matched counts; the pumping lemma on aᵖbᵖcᵖ breaks every decomposition.
  3. (iii) not context-free. The copy language {ww} is the standard example — the machine would have to remember an unbounded prefix.
  4. (iv) context-free. It is the union of {aⁱbʲ : i < j} and {aⁱbʲ : i > j}, each generated by a small grammar; the class is closed under union.
  5. (v) context-free. S → aSb | C, C → cC | ε: the c's are free after the matched block.
  6. (vi) not context-free. Four matched counts, and already three of them would be too many.
  7. (vii) context-free. It is the concatenation of {aⁿbⁿ} and {cᵐdᵐ}, and the class is closed under concatenation: S → XY, X → aXb | ε, Y → cYd | ε. The two balances run one after the other, never at the same time.
  8. Context-free: (i), (iv), (v) and (vii) — 4 of the seven.

Answer: 4

Common misconception. Assuming that any language with two matched pairs is outside the class. What matters is whether the two balances must be checked at the same time. In (vii) the a = b block finishes before the c = d block begins, so one stack suffices; in a language such as {aⁿbᵐcⁿdᵐ} the two balances are interleaved and it does not.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let DCFL denote the class of languages accepted by some deterministic pushdown automaton. Select every statement that is TRUE.
questions.question_html: Let DCFL denote the class of languages accepted by some deterministic pushdown automaton. Select every statement that is TRUE.
options: Every language in DCFL is context-free.
DCFL is closed under complementation.
DCFL is closed under union.
Every language in DCFL has an unambiguous context-free grammar.
options_html: Every language in DCFL is context-free.
DCFL is closed under complementation.
DCFL is closed under union.
Every language in DCFL has an unambiguous context-free grammar.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A deterministic pushdown automaton is a special case of a nondeterministic one, so DCFL sits inside the context-free languages. Determinism buys some closure properties and costs others.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true. Every DPDA is an NPDA, so DCFL ⊆ CFL.
  2. (B) true. DCFL is one of the classes where complementation is preserved — swap the accepting and non-accepting states of a DPDA that never gets stuck. This is a genuine contrast with the context-free languages, which are not closed under complementation.
  3. (C) false. The union of two deterministic context-free languages need not be deterministic: {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1} ∪ {aⁿb²ⁿ : n ≥ 1} is not accepted by any DPDA.
  4. (D) true. A DPDA has at most one run on each input, so a single derivation tree per string can be read off it. Determinism always implies the existence of an unambiguous grammar.

Answer: Options (A, B and D).

Common misconception. Assuming that a class closed under complementation must also be closed under union, or the reverse. Closure properties come in independent pairs; DCFL has complementation but not union, while CFL has union but not complementation.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Select every statement about the closure properties of the context-free languages that is TRUE.
questions.question_html: Select every statement about the closure properties of the context-free languages that is TRUE.
options: They are closed under intersection with a regular language, but not under intersection in general.
If L₁ is context-free and L₂ is not, then L₁ ∩ L₂ is not context-free.
The union of a context-free language with a non-context-free language can be context-free.
If L₁ ⊆ L₂ and L₂ is context-free, then L₁ is context-free.
options_html: They are closed under intersection with a regular language, but not under intersection in general.
If L₁ is context-free and L₂ is not, then L₁ ∩ L₂ is not context-free.
The union of a context-free language with a non-context-free language can be context-free.
If L₁ ⊆ L₂ and L₂ is context-free, then L₁ is context-free.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Closure is a statement about the class as a whole, never about one particular pair of languages. A property can fail for the class and still hold for the pair in front of you.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true. Intersecting with a regular language means running the pushdown automaton and the finite automaton together, which is again a pushdown automaton. Intersecting two context-free languages would need two stacks, and {aⁿbⁿcᵐ} ∩ {aᵐbⁿcⁿ} = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} shows the failure.
  2. (B) false. Take L₁ = Σ*, which is context-free, and any non-context-free L₂. Then L₁ ∩ L₂ = L₂, which is not context-free — but take instead L₁ = {aⁿbⁿ} and L₂ a non-context-free language disjoint from it, and the intersection is ∅, which is context-free. The conclusion does not follow.
  3. (C) true. Let N be any non-context-free language over {a, b}, for instance {ww}, and take L = Σ*. Then L ∪ N = Σ*, which is regular and hence context-free. A union can hide a non-context-free part completely.
  4. (D) false. Subsets of a context-free language are arbitrary. {ww} is a subset of Σ*, which is context-free, yet {ww} is not.

Answer: Options (A and C).

Common misconception. Treating "not closed under intersection" as "every intersection is outside the class", and "closed under union" as "a union tells you what its parts were". Neither is true: closure describes what is guaranteed for all inputs, not what happens in one example.

The conclusion does not follow.(C) true. Let N be any non-context-free language over {a, b}, for instance {ww}, and take L = Σ*. Then L ∪ N = Σ*, which is regular and hence context-free. A union can hide a non-context-free part completely.(D) false. Subsets of a context-free language are arbitrary. {ww} is a subset of Σ*, which is context-free, yet {ww} is not.Answer: Options (A and C).Common misconception. Treating "not closed under intersection" as "every intersection is outside the class", and "closed under union" as "a union tells you what its parts were". Neither is true: closure describes what is guaranteed for all inputs, not what happens in one example.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: A deterministic pushdown automaton (DPDA) has a single stack, and at each step it can inspect only the topmost stack symbol. Which one of the following consequences of that restriction is TRUE?
questions.question_html: A deterministic pushdown automaton (DPDA) has a single stack, and at each step it can inspect only the topmost stack symbol. Which one of the following consequences of that restriction is TRUE?
options: A DPDA can compare the first half of a string with the second half in the same order, so it accepts {ww : w ∈ {a, b}*}.
A DPDA can store the whole input on its stack and later read the stack from the bottom upwards.
A DPDA can compare the second half of a string with the first half in reverse order, so it accepts {w wᴿ : w ∈ {a, b}*}, but it cannot compare the halves in the same order.
A DPDA cannot accept any language that is not regular.
options_html: A DPDA can compare the first half of a string with the second half in the same order, so it accepts {ww : w ∈ {a, b}*}.
A DPDA can store the whole input on its stack and later read the stack from the bottom upwards.
A DPDA can compare the second half of a string with the first half in reverse order, so it accepts {w wᴿ : w ∈ {a, b}*}, but it cannot compare the halves in the same order.
A DPDA cannot accept any language that is not regular.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The stack is a last-in-first-out store: symbols pushed last come back first. A machine that reads a string left to right and pushes it can only replay it in reverse order when it pops.

Step by step.

  1. On w = a₁a₂ … aₙ the DPDA pushes a₁, a₂, …, aₙ; the top is aₙ.
  2. Popping yields aₙ, aₙ₋₁, …, a₁, which is exactly the order in which wᴿ is written. So {w wᴿ} is accepted by a DPDA — guess the middle on the even case, or accept it as the standard palindrome construction does with a deterministic check of the second half.
  3. For {ww} the second half would have to be compared with a₁a₂ … aₙ in the same order, i.e. the stack would have to be read from the bottom; the model forbids it, and in fact {ww} is not even context-free.
  4. Options (B) and (D) are false outright: the stack top is the only accessible cell, and {aⁿbⁿ} is a non-regular language that a DPDA accepts.

Answer: Option (C) — reverse order comparison only.

Common misconception. Believing that "the stack remembers the input" is enough to compare two halves in the same order. It remembers the input, but only in reverse; the LIFO discipline is the whole point of the model.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: A DPDA has state set Q with |Q| = 4, input alphabet Σ = {a, b} and stack alphabet Γ = {Z₀, A}. A transition is written δ(q, σ, X) with σ ∈ Σ ∪ {ε} and X ∈ Γ, and in a DPDA each such triple holds at most one move. What is the largest number of triples (q, σ, X) for which δ can be non-empty?
questions.question_html: A DPDA has state set Q with |Q| = 4, input alphabet Σ = {a, b} and stack alphabet Γ = {Z₀, A}. A transition is written δ(q, σ, X) with σ ∈ Σ ∪ {ε} and X ∈ Γ, and in a DPDA each such triple holds at most one move. What is the largest number of triples (q, σ, X) for which δ can be non-empty?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The transition table of a pushdown automaton is indexed by a state, an input symbol or ε, and a stack symbol. Determinism limits the contents of each cell to one move; it does not reduce the number of cells.

Step by step.

  1. Choices of state: |Q| = 4.
  2. Choices of the second coordinate: the two input symbols together with the empty string, |Σ| + 1 = 3.
  3. Choices of stack symbol: |Γ| = 2.
  4. Total cells = 4 × 3 × 2 = 24. Every cell may be non-empty, as long as the determinism restriction (no input move and an ε-move for the same state and stack symbol) is respected elsewhere in the table.

Answer: 24

Common misconception. Using |Σ| = 2 and forgetting the ε-row, which gives 16; or multiplying by the number of moves per cell, which would be meaningless because a DPDA has at most one.

questions.question: The DPDA M has states {q₀, q₁, q₂}, Σ = {a, b}, Γ = {Z₀, A}, start state q₀, initial stack symbol Z₀, final state q₂, and exactly these moves: δ(q₀,a,Z₀)={(q₀,AZ₀)}, δ(q₀,a,A)={(q₀,AA)}, δ(q₀,b,A)={(q₁,ε)}, δ(q₁,b,A)={(q₁,ε)}, δ(q₁,ε,Z₀)={(q₂,Z₀)}. After M has read the input a⁴b², how many symbols are on its stack, counting the bottom marker Z₀?
questions.question_html: The DPDA M has states {q₀, q₁, q₂}, Σ = {a, b}, Γ = {Z₀, A}, start state q₀, initial stack symbol Z₀, final state q₂, and exactly these moves: δ(q₀,a,Z₀)={(q₀,AZ₀)}, δ(q₀,a,A)={(q₀,AA)}, δ(q₀,b,A)={(q₁,ε)}, δ(q₁,b,A)={(q₁,ε)}, δ(q₁,ε,Z₀)={(q₂,Z₀)}. After M has read the input a⁴b², how many symbols are on its stack, counting the bottom marker Z₀?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A stack configuration is a word over Γ; a push adds one symbol, a pop removes the top one, and the bottom marker is never removed while the machine is still running.

Step by step.

  1. Start: Z₀ — one symbol.
  2. Four a's, each pushing one A: A A A A Z₀ — five symbols.
  3. First b pops one A and moves to q₁: A A A Z₀.
  4. Second b pops one A: A A Z₀ — three symbols. The ε-move on Z₀ then takes the machine to q₂ without changing the height.

Answer: 3

Common misconception. Answering 5 by counting the four A's and forgetting that the two b's pop; or answering 2 by forgetting the bottom marker, which is still on the stack.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let L = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0} ∪ {aⁿb²ⁿ : n ≥ 0}. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Let L = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0} ∪ {aⁿb²ⁿ : n ≥ 0}. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: L is regular.
L is deterministic context-free but not regular.
L is context-free but not deterministic context-free.
L is not context-free.
options_html: L is regular.
L is deterministic context-free but not regular.
L is context-free but not deterministic context-free.
L is not context-free.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A nondeterministic PDA may guess which of two conditions holds; a deterministic one must decide before the evidence arrives. Two families of strings that share a prefix but need different comparisons are exactly what determinism cannot handle.

Step by step.

  1. An NPDA accepts L: on reading the a's it pushes A's and, at the first b, guesses whether to match one A per b or one A per two b's. One of the two guesses is right, so L is context-free.
  2. After reading aⁿ the configuration of any machine is the same whether the string will end in bⁿ or in b²ⁿ: the stack holds AⁿZ₀ in both cases. A DPDA must therefore commit to one comparison ratio at the first b.
  3. If it matches one A per b, then after aⁿbⁿ the stack is empty and the machine has forgotten n; with finitely many states it cannot tell whether the extra b's number exactly n, so it either rejects aⁿb²ⁿ or accepts strings such as aⁿbⁿ⁺¹ that are not in L. The symmetric choice fails on aⁿbⁿ.
  4. L is not regular: intersecting with a*b* gives {aⁿbⁿ} up to the second family, and pumping aⁿbⁿ breaks the equality of the two counts.

Answer: Option (C) — context-free but not deterministic context-free.

Common misconception. Assuming that every context-free language has a deterministic PDA because the familiar examples (aⁿbⁿ, balanced brackets, palindromes) all do. Determinism is an extra requirement and this union of two families is the standard witness that it can fail.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Select every language below that is deterministic context-free.
questions.question_html: Select every language below that is deterministic context-free.
options: {aⁱbʲ : i ≠ j, i, j ≥ 0}
{aⁿbⁿcᵐ : n ≥ 0, m ≥ 0}
{aⁱbʲcᵏ : i = j or j = k}
options_html: {aⁱbʲ : i ≠ j, i, j ≥ 0}
{aⁿbⁿcᵐ : n ≥ 0, m ≥ 0}
{aⁱbʲcᵏ : i = j or j = k}
{w ∈ {a, b}* : nₐ(w) = n_b(w)}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A language is deterministic context-free when some DPDA accepts it. The practical test is whether the machine can decide what to do from the prefix it has read, without guessing which of several conditions the whole string will satisfy.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. Push one A per a and pop one per b. If the stack still holds A's when the input ends then i > j; if the stack empties before the b's end then i < j. The choice is made by the machine as it goes, never guessed.
  2. (B) True. Push on a, pop on b, then read any number of c's in a final state; the c-block is separated from the b-block by the input symbol itself, so no guessing is needed.
  3. (C) False. After aⁱbʲ the machine cannot know whether the c-block will have to match i or j; the two alternatives are indistinguishable until the end, which is the standard non-deterministic case. An NPDA accepts it, a DPDA cannot.
  4. (D) True. Keep the signed difference nₐ − n_b on the stack: push A for a surplus of a's, B for a surplus of b's, and pop when a symbol cancels the top. Accept iff the stack is empty at the end. Every step is determined by the input symbol and the stack top.

Answer: Options (A, B and D)

Common misconception. Treating "needs a stack" as "is nondeterministic". A single stack suffices for all four; what fails in (C) is not memory but the ability to choose the right comparison without lookahead.
