questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: A DPDA contains the single move δ(q, ε, X) = (q, X) for one state q and one stack symbol X, and no other move is defined for the pair (q, X). Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html: A DPDA contains the single move δ(q, ε, X) = (q, X) for one state q and one stack symbol X, and no other move is defined for the pair (q, X). Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: The machine accepts every input string.
The machine is no longer deterministic, because it has two moves for (q, X).
The machine rejects every input string.
The machine can loop for ever without consuming input, so it may fail to halt, but the loop adds no string to its language.
options_html: The machine accepts every input string.
The machine is no longer deterministic, because it has two moves for (q, X).
The machine rejects every input string.
The machine can loop for ever without consuming input, so it may fail to halt, but the loop adds no string to its language.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An ε-move changes state and stack without consuming input. A move that returns the machine to the very configuration it started from is a cycle that consumes nothing, so it can be taken any number of times.

Step by step.

  1. The move (q, X) → (q, X) leaves the state and the stack word unchanged. Repeating it returns to the same configuration, so the machine may spin for ever.
  2. Because the configuration never changes, no new input is read and no new configuration is reachable through the loop. The set of configurations in which the machine can be at the end of the input is exactly what it was without the loop.
  3. Hence the accepted language is unchanged: the loop costs termination, not correctness. Determinism is intact — there is still at most one move for (q, X), so (B) is false.
  4. (A) and (C) are false because the loop neither reaches a final state nor empties the stack by itself.

Answer: Option (D) — it may diverge, but it accepts the same language.

Common misconception. Believing that an ε-loop makes the machine nondeterministic, or that it enlarges the language. It does neither; it is a divergence, and divergence is allowed in the acceptance model.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: The class of deterministic context-free languages is closed under complementation but not under union. Which one of the following follows from these two facts alone?
questions.question_html: The class of deterministic context-free languages is closed under complementation but not under union. Which one of the following follows from these two facts alone?
options: The class is closed under intersection.
The class is not closed under intersection.
The class is closed under concatenation.
The class must be closed under union after all, since complementation is available.
options_html: The class is closed under intersection.
The class is not closed under intersection.
The class is closed under concatenation.
The class must be closed under union after all, since complementation is available.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. De Morgan's laws turn intersection into union once complementation is available: L₁ ∩ L₂ = complement(complement(L₁) ∪ complement(L₂)). A closure property and a failure of closure interact through that identity.

Step by step.

  1. Assume the class were closed under intersection.
  2. Take any two deterministic context-free languages L₁, L₂. Their complements are in the class, by the closure under complementation.
  3. Then complement(L₁) ∩ complement(L₂) is in the class, and so is its complement, which is L₁ ∪ L₂ by De Morgan.
  4. That would make the class closed under union, contradicting the given failure of closure. So closure under intersection cannot hold: the class is not closed under intersection.

Answer: Option (B) — not closed under intersection.

Common misconception. Reading "closed under complement" as "closed under every Boolean operation". Complementation alone gives nothing about union or intersection; it is the combination of the two facts that forces the failure.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following is possible for a nondeterministic PDA but impossible for a deterministic one?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following is possible for a nondeterministic PDA but impossible for a deterministic one?
options: Reading the input exactly once, from left to right.
Pushing a symbol onto the stack.
Making a choice that only input read later can confirm or refute.
Accepting a string by reaching a final state.
options_html: Reading the input exactly once, from left to right.
Pushing a symbol onto the stack.
Making a choice that only input read later can confirm or refute.
Accepting a string by reaching a final state.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Both models read the input once, left to right, and both use a stack. The difference is that an NPDA may follow several computations at once, so it can branch on a decision whose correctness is settled only later in the string.

Step by step.

  1. (A), (B) and (D) are shared by both models — they are part of the definition of a pushdown automaton.
  2. A DPDA has at most one move for a given state, input symbol (or ε) and stack symbol, so its whole computation is a single path fixed by the input.
  3. An NPDA may have several moves in that cell and accepts when some path succeeds, which is exactly how it "guesses" — for instance the middle of a palindrome, or whether a string belongs to {aⁿbⁿ} or to {aⁿb²ⁿ}.

Answer: Option (C) — a guess confirmed only later.

Common misconception. Thinking nondeterminism means "several stacks" or "moving the head backwards". It means several computations from one configuration, nothing more.

questions.question: Let L = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0} ∪ {aⁿb²ⁿ : n ≥ 0}. How many strings of length exactly 6 belong to L?
questions.question_html: Let L = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0} ∪ {aⁿb²ⁿ : n ≥ 0}. How many strings of length exactly 6 belong to L?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A string of the first family has 2n symbols, one of the second family 3n symbols. Enumerate the admissible n for each family and drop duplicates.

Step by step.

  1. First family, 2n = 6 gives n = 3: the string is aaabbb.
  2. Second family, 3n = 6 gives n = 2: the string is aabbbb.
  3. No other n works, and the two strings found are different (three a's against two). So exactly two strings of length 6 are in L.

Answer: 2

Common misconception. Counting aabbbb as a member of the first family with n = 2, which would wrongly require aabb; or forgetting that n = 0 contributes only the empty string, of length 0.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: An NPDA is specified with F = ∅: it has no final states at all. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html: An NPDA is specified with F = ∅: it has no final states at all. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: It can still accept a non-empty language, because acceptance by empty stack needs no final state.
It accepts no string at all.
It accepts the empty string only.
It is not a well-formed pushdown automaton.
options_html: It can still accept a non-empty language, because acceptance by empty stack needs no final state.
It accepts no string at all.
It accepts the empty string only.
It is not a well-formed pushdown automaton.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A PDA has two acceptance modes. Accepting by final state needs F ≠ ∅; accepting by empty stack needs nothing but an empty stack at the end of the input, and an empty set of final states is a perfectly legal component of the tuple.

Step by step.

  1. The formal definition M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q₀, Z₀, F) allows F = ∅; nothing else refers to it.
  2. With empty-stack acceptance the machine accepts w when some computation consumes all of w and leaves the stack empty.
  3. For example, one state that pushes an A per a, pops an A per b and finally pops Z₀ accepts {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1} with F = ∅.

Answer: Option (A) — it can still accept a non-empty language.

Common misconception. Identifying "accepting" with "reaching a final state" so completely that an empty F is read as "accepts nothing". The two modes are independent.
questions.solution_plain: Detailed solutionConcept. A PDA has two acceptance modes. questions.question: Let 𝒞 be the class of languages accepted by nondeterministic pushdown automata. Select every statement that is TRUE.
questions.question_html: Let 𝒞 be the class of languages accepted by nondeterministic pushdown automata. Select every statement that is TRUE.
options: 𝒞 is closed under union.
𝒞 is closed under intersection.
𝒞 is closed under complementation.
Allowing ε-transitions does not enlarge 𝒞.
options_html: 𝒞 is closed under union.
𝒞 is closed under intersection.
𝒞 is closed under complementation.
Allowing ε-transitions does not enlarge 𝒞.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. 𝒞 is exactly the class of context-free languages. Its closure properties are those of the CFLs: union yes, concatenation and star yes, intersection and complementation no.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. Add a new start state with ε-moves into the start configurations of the two machines; whichever machine accepts, the new one accepts.
  2. (B) False. {aⁿbⁿcᵐ : m ≥ 0} and {aᵏbⁿcⁿ : k ≥ 0} are context-free, but their intersection is {aⁿbⁿcⁿ}, which is not.
  3. (C) False. The complement of a CFL need not be a CFL; the standard witness is a context-free language whose complement fails the pumping lemma for CFLs.
  4. (D) True. Any ε-transition can be eliminated: a move that pops on ε after a push is folded into a single move of the composite transition relation, and the class of accepted languages is unchanged.

Answer: Options (A and D)

Common misconception. Carrying the Boolean-closure intuition of regular languages over to context-free ones. The stack makes the machine more powerful, not more closed.

questions.question: Let L be a language over the alphabet {a, b}. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Let L be a language over the alphabet {a, b}. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: If L is closed under reversal then some NPDA accepts L.
If some NPDA accepts L then some NPDA accepts Lᴿ.
Every language accepted by an NPDA is deterministic context-free.
The reversal of a deterministic context-free language need not be context-free.
options_html: If L is closed under reversal then some NPDA accepts L.
If some NPDA accepts L then some NPDA accepts Lᴿ.
Every language accepted by an NPDA is deterministic context-free.
The reversal of a deterministic context-free language need not be context-free.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The class of languages accepted by NPDAs is the class of context-free languages, and that class is closed under reversal: reverse the right-hand side of every production and the grammar generates Lᴿ.

Step by step.

  1. (B) True. From a grammar G for L build Gᴿ whose productions are A → αᴿ for each A → α of G. Every derivation of w in G becomes a derivation of wᴿ in Gᴿ, so L(Gᴿ) = Lᴿ, and an NPDA exists for it.
  2. (A) False. The language {ww : w ∈ {a, b}*} is closed under reversal — the reverse of ww is wᴿwᴿ, again of the form xx — yet it is not context-free, so no NPDA accepts it.
  3. (C) False. {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0} ∪ {aⁿb²ⁿ : n ≥ 0} is accepted by an NPDA but by no DPDA.
  4. (D) False. Deterministic context-free languages are closed under reversal: reverse the machine, swap the roles of push and pop where the construction requires it, and the result is again a DPDA. So the reversal of a DCFL is always a DCFL, hence context-free.

Answer: Option (B) — the reversal of an NPDA language is again one.

Common misconception. Confusing "the class is closed under reversal" with "a language that is closed under reversal belongs to the class". Closure properties move languages inside a class; they do not characterise it.

questions.question: Select every statement about nondeterministic pushdown automata that is TRUE.
questions.question_html: Select every statement about nondeterministic pushdown automata that is TRUE.
options: For one state, one input symbol and one stack symbol the machine may have several moves.
A string is accepted when at least one computation consumes the whole string and ends in a final state (or with an empty stack, in that mode).
The whole input must be consumed before the machine accepts.
The machine may insert a symbol anywhere in the stack, not only at the top.
options_html: For one state, one input symbol and one stack symbol the machine may have several moves.
A string is accepted when at least one computation consumes the whole string and ends in a final state (or with an empty stack, in that mode).
The whole input must be consumed before the machine accepts.
The machine may insert a symbol anywhere in the stack, not only at the top.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Nondeterminism widens the transition relation; it does not change the data structure. The stack stays LIFO and acceptance still requires the input to be finished.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. δ(q, σ, X) is a set of moves in an NPDA, so several successors are possible; that is the definition of nondeterminism.
  2. (B) True. Acceptance is existential: one successful computation suffices, and that computation must have consumed all the input.
  3. (C) True. A machine that stops in a final state with input left over has not accepted; the definition requires the input to be exhausted.
  4. (D) False. Every move reads the top symbol and replaces it by a string; the symbols below it are untouched. Insertion in the middle of the stack is impossible.

Answer: Options (A, B and C)

Common misconception. Believing that a PDA can reach into the stack. Only the top is visible, which is why the LIFO order decides what the machine can compare.

questions.question: Which one of the following languages can be accepted by a deterministic PDA that accepts by empty stack?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following languages can be accepted by a deterministic PDA that accepts by empty stack?
options: {a, ab}
{w ∈ {a, b}* : w ends in b}
{ε, a}
{aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1}
options_html: {a, ab}
{w ∈ {a, b}* : w ends in b}
{ε, a}
{aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1}
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A DPDA that accepts by empty stack stops the moment the stack is empty, and it can never be revived. So no accepted string can be a proper prefix of another accepted string — the prefix property.

Step by step.

  1. {a, ab}: a is a proper prefix of ab, so after reading a the stack would already be empty and the machine could not go on to accept ab.
  2. {w : w ends in b}: ab and abb are both in the language and the first is a proper prefix of the second — same obstruction.
  3. {ε, a}: ε is a proper prefix of a.
  4. {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1}: no member is a proper prefix of another (the lengths 2n are distinct and the shape forbids it), so the empty-stack machine works — push an A per a, pop it on the matching b, and pop Z₀ at the end.

Answer: Option (D) — {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1}.

Common misconception. Thinking that any deterministic context-free language can be given an empty-stack DPDA. Only the prefix-free ones can; the rest need final-state acceptance.

questions.question: A pushdown automaton M accepts the string w by empty stack. Which one of the following is TRUE at the moment M accepts?
questions.question_html: A pushdown automaton M accepts the string w by empty stack. Which one of the following is TRUE at the moment M accepts?
options: M is in one of its final states.
The stack is empty, so even the bottom marker has been popped.
M has read only a proper prefix of w.
The stack still contains exactly the bottom marker.
options_html: M is in one of its final states.
The stack is empty, so even the bottom marker has been popped.
M has read only a proper prefix of w.
The stack still contains exactly the bottom marker.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. "Empty stack" means literally the empty word: the bottom marker Z₀ has been removed. If Z₀ were still there the stack would not be empty.

Step by step.

  1. Acceptance by empty stack requires (q, w, γ) ⊢* (q′, ε, ε) for some state q′: the whole input consumed and the stack word empty.
  2. Since Z₀ is a stack symbol like any other in this mode, it must have been popped.
  3. No final state is involved — (A) is false; the input is fully consumed — (C) is false; and (D) describes the final-state construction, where Z₀ typically survives.

Answer: Option (B) — the stack, including the bottom marker, is empty.

Common misconception. Picturing "empty" as "down to the bottom marker". That is the final-state convention; empty-stack acceptance pops the marker as well.

questions.question: A language has the prefix property when no string of the language is a proper prefix of another string of the language. How many of the following five languages have the prefix property?L₁ = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1}; L₂ = {a, ab}; L₃ = {aⁿbⁿcᵐ : n ≥ 1, m ≥ 1}; L₄ = {w wᴿ : w ∈ {a, b}*}; L₅ = {ε, a}.
questions.question_html:
A language has the prefix property when no string of the language is a proper prefix of another string of the language. How many of the following five languages have the prefix property?
L₁ = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1}; L₂ = {a, ab}; L₃ = {aⁿbⁿcᵐ : n ≥ 1, m ≥ 1}; L₄ = {w wᴿ : w ∈ {a, b}*}; L₅ = {ε, a}.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Test the property by looking for a pair of words of the language where one is a proper prefix of the other. One such pair is enough to destroy the property.

Step by step.

  1. L₁: the words are ab, aabb, aaabbb, …. No word of the language is a prefix of a longer word of the language — a prefix of aⁿbⁿ that ends before the last b is unbalanced. Property holds.
  2. L₂: a is a proper prefix of ab. Fails.
  3. L₃: aabbc and aabbcc are both in the language and the first is a proper prefix of the second. Fails.
  4. L₄: aa (with w = a) is a proper prefix of aaaa (with w = aa), both in the language. Fails.
  5. L₅: ε is a proper prefix of a. Fails.

Exactly one language, L₁, has the property.

Answer: 1

Common misconception. Counting L₄ as prefix-free because palindromes "look closed". They are not: aa and aaaa are both palindromes.

questions.question: Select every statement comparing the two acceptance modes that is TRUE.
questions.question_html: Select every statement comparing the two acceptance modes that is TRUE.
options: For nondeterministic PDAs the two modes accept exactly the same class of languages.
For deterministic PDAs the two modes do not accept the same class of languages.
A language accepted by a DPDA by empty stack has the prefix property.
Every deterministic context-free language is accepted by some DPDA by empty stack.
options_html: For nondeterministic PDAs the two modes accept exactly the same class of languages.
For deterministic PDAs the two modes do not accept the same class of languages.
A language accepted by a DPDA by empty stack has the prefix property.
Every deterministic context-free language is accepted by some DPDA by empty stack.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Nondeterminism makes the two modes interchangeable; determinism does not, because an empty-stack DPDA cannot survive a prefix of an accepted word.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. Both modes characterise the context-free languages when the machine is nondeterministic: a PDA accepting by final state is converted to one accepting by empty stack (new bottom marker plus a state that empties the stack from every final state), and conversely.
  2. (B) True. {a, ab} is accepted by a DPDA by final state but by none by empty stack.
  3. (C) True. If u were a proper prefix of uv with both in the language, the machine would empty its stack at the end of u and could not continue to accept uv.
  4. (D) False. Exactly the deterministic context-free languages that are not prefix-free — such as {a, ab} — have no empty-stack DPDA.

Answer: Options (A, B and C)

Common misconception. Assuming the equivalence proved for NPDAs carries over to DPDAs. The conversion introduces nondeterminism, which a deterministic machine cannot absorb.

questions.question: Let L = {w ∈ {a, b}* : w ends in b}. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Let L = {w ∈ {a, b}* : w ends in b}. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: L is accepted by a DPDA by empty stack.
L is not context-free.
L is accepted by a DPDA by final state, and by no DPDA by empty stack.
L is not accepted by any DPDA.
options_html: L is accepted by a DPDA by empty stack.
L is not context-free.
L is accepted by a DPDA by final state, and by no DPDA by empty stack.
L is not accepted by any DPDA.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The language is regular, hence deterministic context-free, so a DPDA accepts it by final state. Empty-stack acceptance additionally needs the prefix property.

Step by step.

  1. L is described by the regular expression (a + b)*b, so a two-state DFA decides it and a DPDA that ignores its stack accepts it by final state.
  2. The strings ab and abb both belong to L, and ab is a proper prefix of abb. The prefix property fails.
  3. An empty-stack DPDA would have to empty its stack at the end of ab and still be able to read on to accept abb, which the mode forbids.

Answer: Option (C) — final state only.

Common misconception. Believing that "regular, therefore simple" implies every acceptance mode works. The mode, not the language class, is what the prefix property constrains.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements about the two acceptance modes of pushdown automata is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following statements about the two acceptance modes of pushdown automata is TRUE?
options: A language is accepted by some DPDA by empty stack if and only if it has the prefix property and is accepted by some DPDA by final state.
Every deterministic context-free language is accepted by some DPDA by empty stack.
A language accepted by a DPDA by empty stack need not have the prefix property.
If a language is accepted by some DPDA by empty stack then it is regular.
options_html: A language is accepted by some DPDA by empty stack if and only if it has the prefix property and is accepted by some DPDA by final state.
Every deterministic context-free language is accepted by some DPDA by empty stack.
A language accepted by a DPDA by empty stack need not have the prefix property.
If a language is accepted by some DPDA by empty stack then it is regular.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The exact characterisation of empty-stack deterministic acceptance is "deterministic context-free and prefix-free". Each half of the condition is necessary, and together they are sufficient.

Step by step.

  1. Necessity of prefix-freeness. A DPDA that accepts by empty stack stops when the stack empties; it cannot continue reading towards a longer accepted word. So no accepted word is a proper prefix of another.
  2. Necessity of being a DCFL. It is accepted by a DPDA, hence deterministic context-free by definition.
  3. Sufficiency. Given a DPDA accepting L by final state with L prefix-free, add a new bottom marker below Z₀ and a state that pops the stack whenever a final state is reached. Because no accepted word extends another, the added behaviour never turns a rejected word into an accepted one.
  4. (B), (C) and (D) contradict one of these facts: {a, ab} refutes (B); the argument above refutes (C); and {aⁿbⁿ} is a non-regular language accepted by a DPDA by empty stack, refuting (D).

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Remembering only one half of the theorem — usually the prefix condition — and then concluding that any prefix-free language, including some non-context-free ones, is accepted by a DPDA by empty stack.

questions.question: The grammar G has the single production S → aS | b. It is converted into the standard single-state NPDA that accepts by empty stack, with initial stack Z₀S. Consider the read step that consumes the first a of the input aab. What is on the stack immediately after that step, before any further ε-move? (Write the top of the stack first.)

Consider the read step that consumes the first a of the input aab. What is on the stack immediately after that step, before any further ε-move? (Write the top of the stack first.)
options: a S Z₀
Z₀
S a Z₀

options_html: a S Z₀

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The construction replaces the variable on top of the stack by the right-hand side of a production with an ε-move, then reads the terminal that is now on top. The stack therefore holds the unmatched part of the sentential form.

Step by step.

  1. Start: S Z₀ (top S).
  2. ε-move with S → aS: S is replaced by aS, giving a S Z₀.
  3. Read the first a, which pops the a: the stack is S Z₀.
  4. Continuing the same way on the second a leaves S Z₀ again, and the final b is produced by S → b, after which Z₀ is popped and the machine accepts.

Answer: Option (D) — S Z₀.

Common misconception. Answering a S Z₀ by forgetting that the read step pops the terminal, or S a Z₀ by confusing the stack order — the top is on the left.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Read the machine as a recursive description: the outermost a and the last b are matched, and the inside is another accepted word. The base case is the shortest accepted word, ab.

Step by step.

  1. The machine accepts ab: one push, one pop, then the marker. So ab must be generated — the base case.
  2. Wrapping an accepted word w in one more a at the front and one more b at the back is again accepted, which is the production S → aSb.
  3. S → aSb | ab generates aᵏ(ab)bᵏ = aᵏ⁺¹bᵏ⁺¹, that is {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1}, exactly the language of the machine.
  4. The other options fail: S → abS | ε gives (ab)*; S → aSb | ε includes ε, which the machine rejects; the fourth grammar is ambiguous and generates words with the wrong counts.

Answer: Option (A) — S → aSb | ab.

Common misconception. Choosing S → aSb | ε from memory. That grammar generates {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0}; the difference of one word, ε, is exactly the point of the question.

questions.question: The grammar G has the productions S → aSb | c. G is converted into the standard single-state NPDA that accepts by empty stack, with initial stack Z₀S. Just before the machine consumes the terminal c of the input aacbb, how many symbols are on the stack, counting the bottom marker Z₀?
questions.question_html: The grammar G has the productions S → aSb | c. G is converted into the standard single-state NPDA that accepts by empty stack, with initial stack Z₀S. Just before the machine consumes the terminal c of the input aacbb, how many symbols are on the stack, counting the bottom marker Z₀?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The stack holds the part of the sentential form that is still to be matched. Each ε-move expands the variable on top; each read step removes the terminal on top.

Step by step.

  1. Z₀S, top S.
  2. Expand with S → aSb: a S b Z₀. Read the first a: S b Z₀.
  3. Expand with S → aSb: a S b b Z₀. Read the second a: S b b Z₀.
  4. Expand with S → c: c b b Z₀ — four symbols, and the terminal c is on top, about to be read. After reading it the stack is b b Z₀, and the two b's empty it.

Answer: 4

Common misconception. Counting after the c has been read (3) rather than before, or forgetting the bottom marker Z₀ (3 as well, for the wrong reason). Read the question as a snapshot of the configuration immediately before the read step.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Select every statement about the two standard constructions between grammars and pushdown automata that is TRUE.
questions.question_html: Select every statement about the two standard constructions between grammars and pushdown automata that is TRUE.
options: Every context-free grammar has an equivalent NPDA that accepts by empty stack.
Every NPDA has an equivalent context-free grammar.
The single-state construction requires the grammar to be in Chomsky Normal Form.
A grammar in Greibach Normal Form yields a single-state NPDA in which every move reads exactly one input symbol and pushes a string of variables.
options_html: Every context-free grammar has an equivalent NPDA that accepts by empty stack.
Every NPDA has an equivalent context-free grammar.
The single-state construction requires the grammar to be in Chomsky Normal Form.
A grammar in Greibach Normal Form yields a single-state NPDA in which every move reads exactly one input symbol and pushes a string of variables.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The two constructions are the two directions of one theorem: context-free grammars and nondeterministic pushdown automata describe the same class of languages.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. Start the stack with Z₀S; expand the top variable by an ε-move using a production, and read a terminal when it reaches the top. When the stack is empty the input has been derived.
  2. (B) True. The variables of the grammar are triples [q, X, r], one per pair of states and stack symbol, and a production [q, X, r] → a [q₁, Y₁, q₂] … [qₖ, Yₖ, r] mimics one move of the machine.
  3. (C) False. Any grammar works; no normal form is needed for the grammar-to-NPDA direction. Chomsky Normal Form is used for other purposes, such as the CYK algorithm and length arguments.
  4. (D) True. In Greibach Normal Form every production is A → aα with a a terminal, so no ε-move is needed: each step reads one input symbol and replaces one variable by a string of variables.

Answer: Options (A, B and D)

Common misconception. Believing that the construction needs a normal form. The plain construction works on any grammar; normal forms are a convenience, not a precondition.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: A grammar is in Greibach Normal Form: every production is A → aα, where a is a terminal and α is a (possibly empty) string of variables. In the single-state NPDA built from it, which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html: A grammar is in Greibach Normal Form: every production is A → aα, where a is a terminal and α is a (possibly empty) string of variables. In the single-state NPDA built from it, which one of the following is TRUE?
options: The machine needs ε-moves to expand the productions.
The stack alphabet must contain every terminal of the grammar.
Every move reads exactly one input symbol and pushes a string of variables.
The machine has one final state and accepts by final state.
options_html: The machine needs ε-moves to expand the productions.
The stack alphabet must contain every terminal of the grammar.
Every move reads exactly one input symbol and pushes a string of variables.
The machine has one final state and accepts by final state.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Greibach Normal Form is exactly the shape that lets one move of the machine do both jobs at once: consume the next input symbol and replace the variable by the rest of the right-hand side.

Step by step.

  1. With A → aα on top of the stack and a as the next input symbol, the machine reads a and pushes α in one move.
  2. No move is made on ε alone, so (A) is false.
  3. Only variables ever sit on the stack, so the stack alphabet is the set of variables together with the bottom marker — terminals need not appear, and (B) is false.
  4. The construction is the single-state, empty-stack one, so (D) is false: the machine has no final state at all.

Answer: Option (C).

Common misconception. Confusing the two constructions. The general grammar-to-NPDA construction does use ε-moves and keeps terminals on the stack; the Greibach version eliminates both.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following problems about a context-free grammar G is decidable?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following problems about a context-free grammar G is decidable?
options: Is G ambiguous?
Is L(G) finite?
Is L(G) regular?
Is L(G) = L(G′) for another context-free grammar G′?
options_html: Is G ambiguous?
Is L(G) finite?
Is L(G) regular?
Is L(G) = L(G′) for another context-free grammar G′?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The decidable questions about a context-free grammar are the "small" ones — emptiness, finiteness and membership. The questions that quantify over all strings, or compare two grammars, are undecidable.

Step by step.

  1. (B) Decidable. Remove useless symbols, then test whether the remaining grammar has a cycle — a variable that can derive a sentential form containing itself. With no cycle only finitely many strings are derivable, and that is exactly when L(G) is finite.
  2. (A) Undecidable. Deciding ambiguity of a context-free grammar is a classical undecidable problem, and there exist inherently ambiguous context-free languages.
  3. (C) Undecidable. Whether a context-free language is regular cannot be decided from a grammar for it.
  4. (D) Undecidable. Equivalence of two context-free grammars is undecidable, even though equivalence of two deterministic ones is decidable.

Answer: Option (B) — finiteness is decidable.

Common misconception. Expecting the whole "regular-language toolkit" to apply, or assuming that because membership is decidable, equivalence is too. Only emptiness, finiteness and membership survive.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: The Church–Turing thesis identifies the informal notion of an effective procedure with computation by a Turing machine. Which one of the following statements about the thesis is TRUE?
questions.question_html: The Church–Turing thesis identifies the informal notion of an effective procedure with computation by a Turing machine. Which one of the following statements about the thesis is TRUE?
options: It is a theorem of mathematics, proved by Turing in 1936 from the axioms of set theory.
It is false, because a random-access machine with unit-cost arithmetic computes functions that no Turing machine can compute.
It asserts that every Turing machine halts on every input, so that every language is decidable.

It cannot be proved, because it equates an informal notion with a formal one; it is supported instead by the fact that every reasonable model proposed since — multitape machines, register machines, the λ-calculus, cellular automata — accepts exactly the same class of languages.
options_html: It is a theorem of mathematics, proved by Turing in 1936 from the axioms of set theory.
It is false, because a random-access machine with unit-cost arithmetic computes functions that no Turing machine can compute.
It asserts that every Turing machine halts on every input, so that every language is decidable.

It cannot be proved, because it equates an informal notion with a formal one; it is supported instead by the fact that every reasonable model proposed since — multitape machines, register machines, the λ-calculus, cellular automata — accepts exactly the same class of languages.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The thesis is a definition, not a statement inside a formal system. It says: a function is computable by an effective procedure exactly when some Turing machine computes it. Because “effective procedure” is an informal notion, no proof in the mathematical sense is possible — there is nothing to prove from.

Step by step.

  1. One half of the thesis is a theorem: every Turing machine is an effective procedure, since its moves can be carried out mechanically. That direction is provable and is not in doubt.
  2. The other half — every effective procedure is a Turing machine — quantifies over an informal class, so it cannot be derived. It is accepted as a working hypothesis.
  3. The evidence is convergence: every model of computation proposed independently (multitape and nondeterministic machines, RAM and register machines, the λ-calculus, Markov algorithms, cellular automata) has turned out to accept exactly the recursively enumerable languages. No model has ever been found that computes more.
  4. Hence (D). Option (A) is wrong because no such proof exists; (B) is wrong because a RAM is simulated by a Turing machine and so has no extra power; (C) is wrong because halting is undecidable.

Answer: Option (D).

Common misconception. Treating the thesis as something Turing proved. What Turing proved in 1936 was that his machine model captures the λ-definable functions; the identification with all effective procedures is the hypothesis that carries his name.

questions.question: A two-dimensional tape machine is a Turing machine whose tape is the infinite grid ℤ × ℤ: the head stands on one cell and may move up, down, left or right, reading and writing one symbol per step. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.question_html: A two-dimensional tape machine is a Turing machine whose tape is the infinite grid ℤ × ℤ: the head stands on one cell and may move up, down, left or right, reading and writing one symbol per step. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: It accepts strictly more languages than an ordinary Turing machine, because it can store a whole matrix of data at once.

It accepts exactly the recursively enumerable languages: the cells of the grid can be listed in a spiral order, and the two-dimensional machine is then simulated on a one-dimensional tape with at most a polynomial slowdown.
It accepts exactly the context-sensitive languages, because the grid bounds the amount of memory available.
It is equivalent to a finite automaton, because each cell still holds only one symbol.
options_html: It accepts strictly more languages than an ordinary Turing machine, because it can store a whole matrix of data at once.

It accepts exactly the recursively enumerable languages: the cells of the grid can be listed in a spiral order, and the two-dimensional machine is then simulated on a one-dimensional tape with at most a polynomial slowdown.
It accepts exactly the context-sensitive languages, because the grid bounds the amount of memory available.
It is equivalent to a finite automaton, because each cell still holds only one symbol.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A simulation argument. Any finite object can be encoded as a finite string, and a grid with finitely many non-blank cells is a finite object. The whole content of the grid can therefore be flattened onto a one-dimensional tape.

Step by step.

  1. Order the cells of ℤ × ℤ by a spiral that starts at the origin: (0,0), (1,0), (1,1), (0,1), (−1,1), …. This is a bijection with ℕ, so each grid cell has a finite index.
  2. Keep the whole grid on one tape, storing cell k of the spiral at tape position k, with the blank symbol for the cells never written.
  3. To move the head up, down, left or right the simulating machine computes the new spiral index from the old one. The index of a neighbour is at most a constant factor larger than the current index, so the head walks there in time proportional to the index — polynomial in the number of cells the 2-D machine has visited.
  4. Every 2-D machine is therefore simulated by a 1-D machine, and the converse is immediate (ignore the second coordinate). The two models accept the same class, the recursively enumerable languages, which is (B).

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Reading “more memory per step” as “more computing power”. Extra dimensions change the running time, never the class of languages; only an unbounded number of independent stores, or unbounded nondeterminism with an oracle, changes that.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following statements comparing the random-access machine (RAM) model with the Turing machine is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following statements comparing the random-access machine (RAM) model with the Turing machine is TRUE?
options: A RAM program can compute functions that no Turing machine can compute, because it can address any memory cell in one step.

Every RAM program can be simulated by a Turing machine, so both models accept the same class of languages; the RAM is used because its instruction set matches real machines, not because it is more powerful.
A RAM is strictly weaker than a Turing machine, because it has no tape head that it can move.
A RAM can decide the halting problem, because it reaches any part of its memory immediately.
options_html: A RAM program can compute functions that no Turing machine can compute, because it can address any memory cell in one step.

Every RAM program can be simulated by a Turing machine, so both models accept the same class of languages; the RAM is used because its instruction set matches real machines, not because it is more powerful.
A RAM is strictly weaker than a Turing machine, because it has no tape head that it can move.
A RAM can decide the halting problem, because it reaches any part of its memory immediately.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A RAM has finitely many registers, an unbounded array of memory cells, and instructions such as LOAD, STORE, ADD, JUMP. Every such instruction touches finitely many cells, so the whole machine can be simulated step by step on a Turing tape.

Step by step.

  1. Store the registers and the used prefix of memory as one encoded block on the tape.
  2. Simulating one RAM instruction means scanning the block to find the addressed cell, changing it, and scanning back: a polynomial amount of tape work per instruction.
  3. So every RAM computation is a Turing computation, and since a Turing machine is trivially a RAM (ignore the addressing), the two models are equivalent.
  4. What differs is time: the RAM charges one unit for an addition on machine words, which is why it is the model of choice for algorithm analysis. That is a modelling convenience, not extra power, so (B) is correct. (A) and (D) claim power that no effective model has; (C) reverses the relation.

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Believing that random access — reaching cell i in one step — is a computational primitive a Turing machine lacks. A Turing machine lacks the speed, not the ability: it can walk to cell i and the walk is finite.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let N be a nondeterministic Turing machine. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Let N be a nondeterministic Turing machine. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: N accepts a string w exactly when at least one branch of its computation tree on w reaches an accepting state.
If N decides a language L, then every branch of its computation must halt on every input.
Every language decided by a nondeterministic Turing machine is also decided by some deterministic Turing machine.
A nondeterministic machine with two work tapes is strictly more powerful than a nondeterministic machine with one work tape.
options_html: N accepts a string w exactly when at least one branch of its computation tree on w reaches an accepting state.
If N decides a language L, then every branch of its computation must halt on every input.
Every language decided by a nondeterministic Turing machine is also decided by some deterministic Turing machine.
A nondeterministic machine with two work tapes is strictly more powerful than a nondeterministic machine with one work tape.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A nondeterministic machine is a tree of configurations. Acceptance is existential — one successful branch is enough — but deciding also demands that the answer be delivered in finite time, which is a statement about every branch.

Step by step.

  1. (A) By definition the machine accepts when some branch halts in an accepting state. TRUE ✓
  2. (B) A decider must halt on every input with a definite answer. If one branch looped forever the machine could not be said to have rejected, so every branch must halt. TRUE ✓
  3. (C) Breadth-first search of the computation tree simulates all branches; the tree of depth t(n) has at most b^(t(n)) nodes, so the deterministic simulation halts, at exponential cost. The class decided is unchanged. TRUE ✓
  4. (D) Extra work tapes are simulated by one tape with a quadratic slowdown, exactly as in the deterministic case, so no extra languages. FALSE ✗

Answer: Options (A, B and C).

Common misconception. Reading (B) as too strong — “a recogniser may loop on a rejected string, so a nondeterministic decider may too”. A recogniser may; a decider may not. The word decides is what forces all branches to terminate.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: A two-tape Turing machine has |Q| = 4 states and tape alphabet Γ with |Γ| = 3 (the blank is included). Its transition function is the partial function δ : Q × Γ × Γ → Q × Γ × Γ × {L, R} × {L, R}: it reads the symbol under each of the two heads and, in one step, writes on both tapes and moves both heads. What is the largest number of entries the transition table can have?
questions.question_html: A two-tape Turing machine has |Q| = 4 states and tape alphabet Γ with |Γ| = 3 (the blank is included). Its transition function is the partial function δ : Q × Γ × Γ → Q × Γ × Γ × {L, R} × {L, R}: it reads the symbol under each of the two heads and, in one step, writes on both tapes and moves both heads. What is the largest number of entries the transition table can have?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The transition table is a partial function, so its largest possible size is the size of its domain: the number of distinct arguments it can be called with. For a k-tape machine that is |Q| · |Γ|^k.

Step by step.

  1. An argument is a triple (q, X₁, X₂) with q ∈ Q and each Xᵢ ∈ Γ.
  2. Number of choices: |Q| = 4 for the state, and |Γ| = 3 independently for each of the two tape symbols.
  3. Domain size = 4 × 3 × 3 = 36.
  4. The value side — next state, two written symbols, two directions — does not affect the count of entries; it only fixes how much each entry stores.

Answer: 36.

Common misconception. Counting values instead of arguments: multiplying by 4 for the directions and 3 for the written symbols gives 36 × 4 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 3888, which counts possible transitions, not entries of the table. For a one-tape machine the same reasoning gives the familiar |Q| · |Γ|.

Counting values instead of arguments: multiplying by 4 for the directions and 3 for the written symbols gives 36 × 4 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 3888, which counts possible transitions, not entries of the table. For a one-tape machine the same reasoning gives the familiar |Q| · |Γ|.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following statements about the class of recursive (decidable) languages is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following statements about the class of recursive (decidable) languages is TRUE?
options: It is closed under union and intersection but not under complementation.
It is closed under complementation but not under intersection.
It is closed under union, intersection and complementation, and also under concatenation and Kleene star.
It contains exactly those languages that have a recogniser, that is, a machine that halts on every string it accepts.
options_html: It is closed under union and intersection but not under complementation.
It is closed under complementation but not under intersection.
It is closed under union, intersection and complementation, and also under concatenation and Kleene star.
It contains exactly those languages that have a recogniser, that is, a machine that halts on every string it accepts.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Closure of a class means: combine languages that have deciders and the result again has a decider. Deciders always halt, so they can be run one after another and their answers combined with a truth table.

Step by step.

  1. Given deciders D₁ for L₁ and D₂ for L₂, run both on the input; both halt.
  2. Union: accept if either accepts. Intersection: accept if both accept. Complement: swap accept and reject in D₁. All three are deciders, so all three sets are recursive.
  3. Concatenation: on input w try every split w = uv; there are |w| + 1 of them and each test halts, so the whole procedure halts.
  4. Kleene star: decide w ∈ L* by dynamic programming over the prefixes of w, again a finite halting computation.
  5. So (C) holds, and (A), (B) fail on the parts they deny. (D) describes the recursively enumerable languages, which are strictly larger: K has a recogniser but no decider.

Answer: Option (C).

Common misconception. Assuming that because the recursive languages are closed under complementation, so are the r.e. languages. They are not: a recogniser can certify acceptance but never non-acceptance, and that asymmetry is exactly what the complement destroys.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let A be a recursive language and let B be a recursively enumerable language, both over the same alphabet. Which one of the following is TRUE for every such pair?
questions.question_html: Let A be a recursive language and let B be a recursively enumerable language, both over the same alphabet. Which one of the following is TRUE for every such pair?
options: A ∪ B is recursive and A ∩ B is recursive.
A \ B is recursive.
A ∩ B is recursively enumerable.
A ∪ B is recursive.
options_html: A ∪ B is recursive and A ∩ B is recursive.
A \ B is recursive.
A ∩ B is recursively enumerable.
A ∪ B is recursive.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The recursive languages sit inside the r.e. languages, and the r.e. class is closed under union and intersection. A subset of a recursive language inherits nothing, so a recursive A cannot be used to bound A ∩ B.

Step by step.

  1. (C) Both A and B are r.e., and the r.e. languages are closed under intersection: run the two recognisers in parallel and accept when both have accepted. TRUE
  2. (A) The first half is true, the second is not. Take A = Σ* and B = K; then A ∩ B = K, which is r.e. but not recursive. FALSE
  3. (B) A \ B = A ∩ B̄, and B̄ need not even be r.e.; with A = Σ* and B = K the difference is K̄, not r.e. FALSE
  4. (D) Σ* ∪ K = Σ* is recursive, but with A = {ε} and B = K the union {ε} ∪ K is r.e. and not recursive. FALSE

Answer: Option (C).

Common misconception. Believing that intersecting with a recursive set makes the result decidable. It does not: A ∩ B ⊆ A, but a subset of a recursive set can be as badly undecidable as any r.e. set, because membership in it still depends on B.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which one of the following statements is TRUE for all languages over a finite alphabet Σ?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following statements is TRUE for all languages over a finite alphabet Σ?
options: If L is recursively enumerable and Σ* \ L is finite, then L is recursive.
If L is recursively enumerable and infinite, then L is recursive.
If L is recursively enumerable and L ⊆ K for some recursively enumerable K, then L is recursive.
If L and its complement are both infinite, then L is recursively enumerable.
options_html: If L is recursively enumerable and Σ* \ L is finite, then L is recursive.
If L is recursively enumerable and infinite, then L is recursive.
If L is recursively enumerable and L ⊆ K for some recursively enumerable K, then L is recursive.
If L and its complement are both infinite, then L is recursively enumerable.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A co-finite set — one whose complement is finite — is the union of a finite set and a set that is trivially decidable. Recognisability plus a decidable complement gives decidability.

Step by step.

  1. Let F = Σ* \ L, finite. Then F is recursive: hard-wire its finitely many members into a lookup table.
  2. L = Σ* \ F = F̄ is the complement of a recursive set, hence recursive by closure under complementation. (A) is TRUE and needs no use of the r.e. hypothesis.
  3. (B) fails for K, which is r.e. and infinite but not recursive.
  4. (C) fails with K = L: an r.e. set is a subset of itself.
  5. (D) fails for L = K̄: both K̄ and its complement K are infinite, yet K̄ is not r.e.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Thinking that “almost everything is in L” makes membership easy. It does not by itself — what makes it easy is that the exceptions form a finite, hence decidable, set. Replace “finite” by “r.e.” in (A) and the statement becomes false.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let A and B be languages over a finite alphabet and let ≤m denote mapping (many-one) reducibility. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Let A and B be languages over a finite alphabet and let ≤m denote mapping (many-one) reducibility. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: If A ≤m B and B is recursively enumerable, then A is recursively enumerable.
If A ≤m B and A is undecidable, then B is undecidable.
If A ≤m B then Ā ≤m B̄, using the same reduction function.
If A ≤m B and B is recursive, then A is recursively enumerable but need not be recursive.
options_html: If A ≤m B and B is recursively enumerable, then A is recursively enumerable.
If A ≤m B and A is undecidable, then B is undecidable.
If A ≤m B then Ā ≤m B̄, using the same reduction function.
If A ≤m B and B is recursive, then A is recursively enumerable but need not be recursive.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A reduction f with w ∈ A ⇔ f(w) ∈ B lets a decider or recogniser for B answer questions about A. Difficulty therefore flows backwards along ≤m: from B to A.

Step by step.

  1. (A) On input w, compute f(w) and run the recogniser for B; accept exactly when it does. TRUE ✓
  2. (B) If B were decidable, (A) with a decider would decide A, contradicting undecidability. TRUE ✓
  3. (C) w ∈ Ā ⇔ w ∉ A ⇔ f(w) ∉ B ⇔ f(w) ∈ B̄, so the very same f reduces Ā to B̄. TRUE ✓
  4. (D) If B is recursive then composing f with a decider for B decides A outright, so A is recursive, not merely r.e. FALSE ✗

Answer: Options (A, B and C).

Common misconception. Reversing the arrow: concluding that B is undecidable whenever A is, without the reduction. The useful form is “hard on the left, therefore hard on the right” — that is, reduce a known-hard problem to the problem you are attacking.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let L be a recursively enumerable language over a finite alphabet and let f be a total computable function. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Let L be a recursively enumerable language over a finite alphabet and let f be a total computable function. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: f(L) is recursive.
f(L) is recursively enumerable only if f is injective.
f(L) is recursively enumerable.
f⁻¹(L) is always recursive.
options_html: f(L) is recursive.
f(L) is recursively enumerable only if f is injective.
f(L) is recursively enumerable.
f⁻¹(L) is always recursive.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The image of an r.e. set under a computable map is r.e.: to enumerate the image, enumerate the source and print f of each element. No decidability survives, because the enumeration never says “and nothing else”.

Step by step.

  1. Let E enumerate L. The machine that runs E and prints f(x) for each output x enumerates exactly f(L) — every element is hit at least once. So f(L) is r.e. (C) is TRUE.
  2. (A) fails: with L = K and f the identity, f(L) = K is not recursive.
  3. (B) fails for the same reason: the identity is injective and its image is still just r.e.
  4. (D) fails: f⁻¹(K) for f the identity is K, not recursive.

Answer: Option (C).

Common misconception. Expecting the preimage and the image to behave alike. The preimage of a decidable set under a computable map is decidable (compute f(w), then test), and the image of a decidable set need not be — r.e.-ness is what both directions preserve.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: A Turing machine M has states {q₀, q₁}, tape alphabet {␣, 0, 1} and the transition table below, where ␣ is the blank. A pair that is not listed has no move, and the machine halts as soon as it enters a configuration whose pair has no move. Which one of the following statements about the input 01 is TRUE? | 0 | 1 | ␣ q₀ | q₀,0,R | q₁,1,R | q₁,␣,L q₁ | — | q₀,1,R | q₁,␣,L
questions.question_html:
A Turing machine M has states {q₀, q₁}, tape alphabet {␣, 0, 1} and the transition table below, where ␣ is the blank. A pair that is not listed has no move, and the machine halts as soon as it enters a configuration whose pair has no move. Which one of the following statements about the input 01 is TRUE?

| 0 | 1 | ␣ q₀ | q₀,0,R | q₁,1,R | q₁,␣,L q₁ | — | q₀,1,R | q₁,␣,L
options: M halts and accepts after 3 moves.
M halts and rejects, because the pair (q₁, 0) is undefined.
M never halts on 01: the head oscillates between the final 1 and the blank cell to its right.
M halts after 4 moves.
options_html: M halts and accepts after 3 moves.
M halts and rejects, because the pair (q₁, 0) is undefined.
M never halts on 01: the head oscillates between the final 1 and the blank cell to its right.
M halts after 4 moves.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Halting is decided by the run, not by the table. A machine loops exactly when its configuration repeats; here the repeated configuration is easy to spot because the machine has only two states and never writes anything new.

Step by step. Input 01, head on the leftmost cell.

  1. (q₀, 0) → write 0, move right: head on the 1.
  2. (q₀, 1) → write 1, move right: head on the blank cell just after the input.
  3. (q₁, ␣) → write ␣, move left: head back on the 1.
  4. (q₁, 1) → write 1, move right: head on the blank again, now in state q₀.
  5. From here steps 2–4 repeat forever, since nothing is ever rewritten. The configuration (q₀, head on the blank) recurs, so M never halts on 01. (C)
  6. On the input 00, by contrast, the run is (q₀,0) → (q₀,0) → (q₁,␣) and stops, because (q₁, 0) is undefined: the machine halts, so it does not loop on every input.

Answer: Option (C).

Common misconception. Counting moves and stopping at the first missing entry. The table is only half the story: the head position is part of the configuration, and a machine can keep re-entering the same pair forever without ever leaving the defined part of the table.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let A = {⟨M, w⟩ : M accepts w} and H = {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w}. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Let A = {⟨M, w⟩ : M accepts w} and H = {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w}. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: A is recursive, because acceptance is a finite event that a simulator eventually observes.
Both A and H are recursively enumerable, and neither is recursive.
H is recursively enumerable while A is not.
Both A and H are recursive.
options_html: A is recursive, because acceptance is a finite event that a simulator eventually observes.
Both A and H are recursively enumerable, and neither is recursive.
H is recursively enumerable while A is not.
Both A and H are recursive.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Acceptance is a positive event: run the machine and accept the moment it enters an accepting state. Halting is also positive: run it and accept the moment it stops. Neither event can be certified absent, which is why neither set is decidable.

Step by step.

  1. A is r.e. The universal machine simulates M on w step by step and accepts as soon as M does.
  2. H is r.e. Simulate; accept as soon as the simulation stops, whether it stopped accepting or rejecting.
  3. A is not recursive. A decider for A would decide K, the halting problem on the diagonal, which is undecidable.
  4. H is not recursive for the same reason — and note that a machine which never halts and one which halts rejecting look identical from outside until the run stops.
  5. (A) confuses “eventually observed” with “decided”: if M never accepts, the simulator waits forever and never answers. (C) reverses the inclusion, since A ⊆ H: a machine that accepts must halt. (D) contradicts undecidability.

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Believing that acceptance is decidable while halting is not, or the reverse. The two are inter-reducible: from a decider for A one builds a decider for H by modifying M to enter an accepting state on every halting configuration.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: For a fixed machine M₀, the set {w : M₀ halts on w} is decidable.
For a fixed string w₀, the set {⟨M⟩ : M halts on w₀} is undecidable.
The set {⟨M⟩ : M halts on ε within 10 steps} is decidable.
If a language L is undecidable, then its complement is undecidable.
options_html: For a fixed machine M₀, the set {w : M₀ halts on w} is decidable.
For a fixed string w₀, the set {⟨M⟩ : M halts on w₀} is undecidable.
The set {⟨M⟩ : M halts on ε within 10 steps} is decidable.
If a language L is undecidable, then its complement is undecidable.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Fixing one of the two arguments of the halting problem matters. Fixing the machine leaves a question about one run each; fixing the input leaves the problem as hard as before. Bounding the number of steps always decides.

Step by step.

  1. (A) False. Take M₀ a universal machine: {w : M₀ halts on w} then encodes the halting problem. Even for a fixed ordinary machine the set can be undecidable, because M₀ may itself simulate arbitrary machines. FALSE ✗
  2. (B) True: this is the halting problem with the second argument fixed, still undecidable by the standard reduction from HALT. TRUE ✓
  3. (C) True: simulate exactly 10 steps and look at the result. The bound is a constant, so the simulation always terminates. TRUE ✓
  4. (D) True: if L̄ were decidable, swapping accept and reject in its decider would decide L. TRUE ✓

Answer: Options (B, C and D).

Common misconception. Reading (A) as the harmless case because the machine is fixed. What matters is the number of parameters left free, not which one was fixed: a universal machine over a fixed input is still an undecidable question.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: On the input 1ⁿ the machine M below starts with its head on the leftmost 1. A pair that is not listed has no move and the machine then halts; q_a is its only accepting state and ␣ is the blank. How many moves (transitions taken) does M make on the input 1111 before it halts? | 0 | 1 | ␣ q₀ | — | q₁,0,R | — q₁ | — | q₁,1,R | q₂,1,L q₂ | q_a,0,R | q₂,1,L | —
questions.question_html:
On the input 1ⁿ the machine M below starts with its head on the leftmost 1. A pair that is not listed has no move and the machine then halts; q_a is its only accepting state and ␣ is the blank. How many moves (transitions taken) does M make on the input 1111 before it halts?

| 0 | 1 | ␣ q₀ | — | q₁,0,R | — q₁ | — | q₁,1,R | q₂,1,L q₂ | q_a,0,R | q₂,1,L | —
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Count moves by splitting the run into phases, then add. Here the phases are: mark the first 1, sweep right, write at the blank, sweep left, enter q_a.

Step by step. Input 1111.

  1. Mark. (q₀,1) → (q₁,0,R): one move. The tape reads 0111 and the head is on the second cell.
  2. Sweep right. The three remaining 1s are crossed in three moves, leaving the head on the blank: 0111␣.
  3. Write. (q₁,␣) → (q₂,1,L): one move. The tape now reads 01111 and the head moves left.
  4. Sweep left. The three 1s in cells 4, 3 and 2 are crossed in three moves, ending with the head on the leading 0.
  5. Accept. (q₂,0) → (q_a,0,R): one move, and the machine halts.
  6. Total. 1 + 3 + 1 + 3 + 1 = 9 moves.

The same four phases give 1 + (n − 1) + 1 + (n − 1) + 1 = 2n + 1 moves for a general input 1ⁿ — one mark, n − 1 rightward, one write, n − 1 leftward, one accept — which at n = 4 is 9. The write already places the head on the fourth 1, so the return sweep needs only three further moves.

Answer: 9.

Common misconception. Counting the written cell twice, once when the head arrives and once when it leaves. A move is one transition; the head lands on the new cell within that move, so the return sweep starts already on the last written cell.

The tape reads 0111 and the head is on the second cell.Sweep right. The three remaining 1s are crossed in three moves, leaving the head on the blank: 0111␣.Write. (q₁,␣) → (q₂,1,L): one move. The tape now reads 01111 and the head moves left.Sweep left. The three 1s in cells 4, 3 and 2 are crossed in three moves, ending with the head on the leading 0.Accept. (q₂,0) → (q_a,0,R): one move, and the machine halts.Total. 1 + 3 + 1 + 3 + 1 = 9 moves.The same four phases give 1 + (n − 1) + 1 + (n − 1) + 1 = 2n + 1 moves for a general input 1ⁿ — one mark, n − 1 rightward, one write, n − 1 leftward, one accept — which at n = 4 is 9. The write already places the head on the fourth 1, so the return sweep needs only three further moves.Answer: 9.Common misconception. Counting the written cell twice, once when the head arrives and once when it leaves. A move is one transition; the head lands on the new cell within that move, so the return sweep starts already on the last written cell.

questions.question: A Turing machine M₁ has a single state q₀, tape alphabet {␣, 1}, and exactly one transition, δ(q₀, 1) = (q₀, 1, R). It halts as soon as it enters a configuration with no move. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html: A Turing machine M₁ has a single state q₀, tape alphabet {␣, 1}, and exactly one transition, δ(q₀, 1) = (q₀, 1, R). It halts as soon as it enters a configuration with no move. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: M₁ halts on every input: the head crosses the run of 1s and then reads a blank, for which no move is defined.
M₁ never halts on any input, because its state never changes.
M₁ halts only on the empty string.
M₁ halts exactly on those inputs whose length is even.
options_html: M₁ halts on every input: the head crosses the run of 1s and then reads a blank, for which no move is defined.
M₁ never halts on any input, because its state never changes.
M₁ halts only on the empty string.
M₁ halts exactly on those inputs whose length is even.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A machine halts when the pair (state, symbol read) is outside the domain of δ. A run that merely looks repetitive may still terminate, because the head is moving into new territory.

Step by step.

  1. On the empty input the head already reads a blank, (q₀, ␣) is undefined, so the machine halts in 0 moves.
  2. On 1ⁿ each move crosses one 1: after exactly n moves the head reads the blank cell just past the input.
  3. (q₀, ␣) has no move, so the machine halts after n moves. It halts on every input, so (A) is correct.
  4. The configuration never repeats — the head position is new each time — which is exactly why “the state never changes” (B) is not evidence of looping.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Equating “the state does not change” with “the machine loops”. A loop needs the whole configuration — state, head position and tape content — to repeat. Here the tape grows under the head and the run always ends at the first blank.

questions.question: The machine M below halts as soon as it enters a configuration with no move; q₂ is its only accepting state, ␣ is the blank, and the input is placed on the tape with the head on its leftmost symbol. How many strings over {0, 1} of length at most 4 does M accept? | 0 | 1 | ␣ q₀ | q₁,0,R | q₀,1,R | — q₁ | q₂,0,R | q₀,1,R | — q₂ | q₂,0,R | q₂,1,R | —
questions.question_html:
The machine M below halts as soon as it enters a configuration with no move; q₂ is its only accepting state, ␣ is the blank, and the input is placed on the tape with the head on its leftmost symbol. How many strings over {0, 1} of length at most 4 does M accept?

| 0 | 1 | ␣ q₀ | q₁,0,R | q₀,1,R | — q₁ | q₂,0,R | q₀,1,R | — q₂ | q₂,0,R | q₂,1,R | —
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The table never writes anything and only moves right, so the machine is a finite automaton in disguise: q₀ means “no 0 seen yet”, q₁ means “the last symbol was a 0”, and q₂ means “two consecutive 0s have been seen”. Acceptance therefore means: the input contains 00.

Step by step. Count the strings of each length that contain 00.

  1. Length 0 and 1: none, so 0 strings.
  2. Length 2: only 00, so 1.
  3. Length 3: 000, 001, 100, so 3.
  4. Length 4: count the complement instead. A binary string with no two consecutive 0s is built by appending 1 to a good string, or 01 to a good string of length two less: f(n) = f(n−1) + f(n−2) with f(0) = 1, f(1) = 2, giving f(4) = 8. Hence 16 − 8 = 8 strings contain 00.
  5. Total 0 + 0 + 1 + 3 + 8 = 12.
  6. The machine itself checks out: it halts on every input of length at most 4 because it only moves right and reaches the blank in at most four moves, and a run that has reached q₂ stays there, so the blank is read in an accepting state.

Answer: 12.

Common misconception. Forgetting the strings of length 4 that begin with 00 and then diverge, such as 0010 and 0011, or counting 00 itself twice because it is a prefix of longer accepted strings. Enumerate by length, once each.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let L = {⟨M⟩ : M accepts at least 100 distinct strings}. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Let L = {⟨M⟩ : M accepts at least 100 distinct strings}. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: L is recursively enumerable but not recursive.
L is not recursively enumerable, because the hundredth acceptance may come after an arbitrarily long run.
L is recursive, because 100 is a fixed finite number.
L is recursive but its complement is not recursively enumerable.
options_html: L is recursively enumerable but not recursive.
L is not recursively enumerable, because the hundredth acceptance may come after an arbitrarily long run.
L is recursive, because 100 is a fixed finite number.
L is recursive but its complement is not recursively enumerable.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. “At least k distinct strings” is a non-trivial property of L(M), so Rice’s theorem makes it undecidable. The existential shape of the property — finitely many witnesses — makes it recognisable.

Step by step.

  1. Recogniser. Enumerate the strings w₀, w₁, w₂, … in order and run M on each for an increasing number of steps, interleaved (dovetail). Every acceptance is eventually seen.
  2. Keep a list of the strings accepted so far; when the list reaches 100 distinct strings, accept. Since L(M) is infinite or finite, either 100 acceptances occur — and then they occur in finite time — or they never do.
  3. Not recursive. Some r.e. languages have at least 100 strings and some have fewer, so the property is non-trivial and Rice’s theorem applies. (If it were recursive, so would be {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = ∅}, by the same style of reduction.)
  4. (B) mistakes “unbounded time” for “no recogniser”: the dovetail never needs to know that the hundredth string will never come. (C) confuses a finite threshold with decidability. (D) is false since L is not recursive.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Thinking that “at least 100” is decidable because 100 is finite. The threshold is finite; the language is not. Contrast “at most 100”, which is not even r.e.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let L = {⟨M⟩ : |L(M)| ≤ 100}. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Let L = {⟨M⟩ : |L(M)| ≤ 100}. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: L is recursively enumerable but not recursive.
L is recursive, because the bound 100 is finite.
L is neither recursively enumerable nor co-recursively enumerable.
L is co-recursively enumerable but not recursively enumerable.
options_html: L is recursively enumerable but not recursive.
L is recursive, because the bound 100 is finite.
L is neither recursively enumerable nor co-recursively enumerable.
L is co-recursively enumerable but not recursively enumerable.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An upper bound on the size of L(M) is a universal statement: “no 101st string is ever accepted”. Universal statements can be refuted in finite time but never confirmed, so the set is co-r.e. and not r.e.

Step by step.

  1. Complement. L̄ = {⟨M⟩ : |L(M)| ≥ 101}, which is r.e. by the same dovetail argument as before: wait for 101 distinct acceptances.
  2. Hence L is co-r.e. — its complement is r.e.
  3. Not r.e. Suppose a recogniser R for L existed. Reduce K̄ to L: given ⟨M⟩, build M′ that on any input simulates M on ⟨M⟩ and, if that run ever halts, accepts every input. Then M diverges on ⟨M⟩ gives L(M′) = ∅, while halting gives L(M′) = Σ*. So R would decide K̄, which is impossible.
  4. So L is co-r.e. and not r.e., which is (D). (B) ignores that the machine may keep accepting forever; (A) and (C) contradict steps 1 and 3.

Answer: Option (D).

Common misconception. Assuming that “at most” and “at least” swap roles symmetrically. They do not: an existential property yields an r.e. set, a universal one yields a co-r.e. set, and the two meet only at the decidable sets.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Let L = {⟨M⟩ : L(M) is not recursively enumerable}. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Let L = {⟨M⟩ : L(M) is not recursively enumerable}. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: L is undecidable by Rice’s theorem.
L is recursively enumerable but not recursive.
L is the set of all strings, Σ*.
L = ∅, so L is recursive.
options_html: L is undecidable by Rice’s theorem.
L is recursively enumerable but not recursive.
L is the set of all strings, Σ*.
L = ∅, so L is recursive.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Read the property before reaching for Rice. Every L(M) is, by definition, accepted by the machine M — so every L(M) is recursively enumerable. A property that no r.e. language has is trivial (it holds for nothing), and Rice’s theorem says nothing about trivial properties.

Step by step.

  1. For any machine M, the set L(M) is the language accepted by M, so it is r.e. by definition.
  2. Hence the condition “L(M) is not recursively enumerable” is false for every M, and L = ∅.
  3. ∅ is decidable: a machine that always rejects decides it. So L is recursive, and (D) holds.
  4. (A) fails because Rice requires a non-trivial property; here the property holds for no r.e. language. (B) and (C) are false because the set is empty, not infinite.

Answer: Option (D).

Common misconception. Applying Rice’s theorem mechanically to every property phrased over L(M). The theorem has two hypotheses — semantic and non-trivial — and this property fails the second, since it is unsatisfiable by construction. A useful reflex: ask whether any machine can have the property. If none can, the set is ∅; if all can, it is Σ*.

questions.question: Rice’s theorem states that every non-trivial property of the language L(M) yields an undecidable set of machine descriptions. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Rice’s theorem states that every non-trivial property of the language L(M) yields an undecidable set of machine descriptions. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: If a property P of r.e. languages satisfies P(∅) ≠ P(Σ*), then P is non-trivial.
If a property P of r.e. languages is non-trivial, then P(∅) ≠ P(Σ*).
The property “M has at least one unreachable state” lies outside the scope of Rice’s theorem, because it describes the machine rather than L(M).
Every undecidable language is of the form {⟨M⟩ : P(L(M))} for some property P.
options_html: If a property P of r.e. languages satisfies P(∅) ≠ P(Σ*), then P is non-trivial.
If a property P of r.e. languages is non-trivial, then P(∅) ≠ P(Σ*).
The property “M has at least one unreachable state” lies outside the scope of Rice’s theorem, because it describes the machine rather than L(M).
Every undecidable language is of the form {⟨M⟩ : P(L(M))} for some property P.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Non-trivial means: true for at least one r.e. language and false for at least one. ∅ and Σ* are the two convenient extremes, and a disagreement there is a quick certificate of non-triviality — but not the only one.

Step by step.

  1. (A) If P(∅) ≠ P(Σ*) then P holds for one of them and fails for the other, so both a true case and a false case exist. TRUE ✓
  2. (B) False: take P(L) = “L is ∅ or L = Σ*”. It is non-trivial, yet P(∅) = P(Σ*) = true. FALSE ✗
  3. (C) Reachability of a state is read off the transition table, so two machines with the same language can differ on it. It is a syntactic property and Rice does not apply (in fact it is decidable). TRUE ✓
  4. (D) False: K̄ is undecidable but not an index set of this form, and in fact not even r.e. FALSE ✗

Answer: Options (A and C).

Common misconception. Using P(∅) ≠ P(Σ*) as a definition of non-triviality. It is a sufficient test, not a necessary one — exactly what (B) gets wrong.

questions.question: How many of the following five sets are decidable?(i) {⟨M⟩ : M has exactly 5 states}(ii) {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = {ε}}(iii) {⟨M⟩ : M accepts ε within 5 steps}(iv) {⟨M⟩ : L(M) is infinite}(v) {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = L(M₀)}, where M₀ is a fixed machine
questions.question_html:
How many of the following five sets are decidable?
(i) {⟨M⟩ : M has exactly 5 states}
(ii) {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = {ε}}
(iii) {⟨M⟩ : M accepts ε within 5 steps}
(iv) {⟨M⟩ : L(M) is infinite}
(v) {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = L(M₀)}, where M₀ is a fixed machine
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Two different sources of decidability: reading a finite description, and bounding the length of a run. Everything else that speaks about L(M) non-trivially falls to Rice’s theorem.

Step by step.

  1. (i) decidable. Count the states in the description ⟨M⟩; no simulation is involved.
  2. (ii) undecidable. “L(M) = {ε}” is a non-trivial property of L(M): {ε} has it and ∅ does not.
  3. (iii) decidable. Simulate exactly 5 steps from the start configuration and look at the result. The bound is a constant.
  4. (iv) undecidable. Non-trivial: Σ* is infinite, ∅ is not. Rice applies.
  5. (v) undecidable. Equivalence with a fixed machine is a non-trivial property of L(M) — true for M₀ itself and false for a machine accepting nothing extra — so Rice applies.
  6. Decidable: (i) and (iii), that is 2 of the five.

Answer: 2.

Common misconception. Marking (v) decidable because M₀ is fixed. Fixing one side does not help: deciding L(M) = L(M₀) would decide L(M) = ∅ by taking M₀ to accept nothing, and that is undecidable.
