questions.question: Which one of the following statements about the deterministic context-free languages (DCFLs) is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following statements about the deterministic context-free languages (DCFLs) is TRUE?
options: The DCFLs coincide with the context-free languages.
The DCFLs form a proper subclass of the context-free languages, and they are closed under complementation but not under union or intersection.
The DCFLs form a proper subclass of the context-free languages, and they are closed under union, intersection and complementation.
Every DCFL is regular.
options_html: The DCFLs coincide with the context-free languages.
The DCFLs form a proper subclass of the context-free languages, and they are closed under complementation but not under union or intersection.
The DCFLs form a proper subclass of the context-free languages, and they are closed under union, intersection and complementation.
Every DCFL is regular.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Determinism removes the machine’s ability to guess, so some context-free languages are lost; but it also gives a unique run, which makes complementation easy. Closure under union is lost because the union of two DCFLs may need a guess.

Step by step.

  1. Proper subclass. {aⁿbⁿ} is a DCFL, and {w wᴿ} is too, so DCFLs are not all regular. Conversely {aⁱbʲcᵏ : i = j or j = k} is context-free but needs a nondeterministic guess, so it is not a DCFL. Hence REG ⊊ DCFL ⊊ CFL.
  2. Complement. Take a DPDA accepting by final state, make every state accepting that was not, and add a sink: because the run is unique and (after the standard normalisation) always consumes the whole input, the complement is accepted by another DPDA. So DCFLs are closed under complementation.
  3. Union fails. {aⁱbʲ : i ≠ j} is the union of two DCFLs but is not itself deterministic; intersection fails for the same reason.
  4. That is exactly (B). (A), (C) and (D) contradict steps 1–3.

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Carrying the CFL closure table over to the deterministic subclass. The two tables differ in exactly one entry: CFLs are closed under union and intersection but not complementation; DCFLs are closed under complementation but not union or intersection.

REG ⊊ DCFL ⊊ CFL ⊊ R ⊊ CSL ⊊ RE
DCFL ⊊ REG ⊊ CFL ⊊ CSL ⊊ R ⊊ RE
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Each level of the hierarchy adds one resource: finite memory, one stack used deterministically, one stack with guessing, a tape bounded by the input, an unbounded tape that must halt, and finally an unbounded tape that need not halt.

Step by step. A witness for each strict inclusion:

  1. REG ⊊ DCFL: {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1} is accepted by a DPDA and is not regular.
  2. DCFL ⊊ CFL: {w wᴿ} is a DCFL; {aⁱbʲcᵏ : i = j or j = k} is context-free and not deterministic.
  3. CFL ⊊ CSL: {aⁿbⁿcⁿ : n ≥ 1} is context-sensitive and not context-free (pump it: the pumped block breaks the three-way equality).
  4. CSL ⊆ R: a linear-bounded automaton has finitely many configurations for a fixed input, so simulation with a repetition check decides membership. The inclusion is strict by diagonalisation: enumerate the LBAs, and let D = {⟨A⟩ : A is an LBA and A does not accept ⟨A⟩}. LBA acceptance is decidable, so D is decidable; but D differs from the language of every LBA on that LBA’s own code, so D ∉ CSL. Hence CSL ⊊ R.
  5. R ⊊ RE: K is r.e. and undecidable.
  6. Only (A) puts DCFL between REG and CFL, and only (A) keeps CSL below R.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Placing CSL above R (option C) because “context-sensitive sounds stronger”. It is not: a linear-bounded automaton has a tape bounded by the input, so it has finitely many configurations and always halts. The class that escapes decidability is RE.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: Which of the following statements about decision problems for the classes of the Chomsky hierarchy are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about decision problems for the classes of the Chomsky hierarchy are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Membership is decidable for every class in the hierarchy, including the recursively enumerable languages.
Emptiness is decidable for context-free grammars but undecidable for context-sensitive grammars.
Equivalence is decidable for regular languages and undecidable for context-free languages.
Every context-sensitive language is recursive.
options_html: Membership is decidable for every class in the hierarchy, including the recursively enumerable languages.
Emptiness is decidable for context-free grammars but undecidable for context-sensitive grammars.
Equivalence is decidable for regular languages and undecidable for context-free languages.
Every context-sensitive language is recursive.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Each level has its own decidability profile, and the profiles are not monotone in an obvious way: emptiness survives up to the context-free level and then dies, while membership survives one level further.

Step by step.

  1. (A) False. Membership for an r.e. language is the acceptance problem, undecidable in general: the machine may run forever on a string it does not accept. FALSE ✗
  2. (B) True. For a CFG, mark the productive non-terminals; the language is empty exactly when the start symbol is unproductive. For a context-sensitive grammar the question is undecidable. TRUE ✓
  3. (C) True. Two DFAs are compared by minimising and checking isomorphism (or by testing emptiness of the symmetric difference); for CFGs equivalence is undecidable. TRUE ✓
  4. (D) True: a linear-bounded automaton has finitely many configurations for a fixed input, so a simulation with a repetition check decides membership and therefore every CSL is recursive. TRUE ✓

Answer: Options (B, C and D).

Common misconception. Assuming decidability improves monotonically as the class shrinks. It does for membership (decidable up to CSL) but not for emptiness or equivalence, which are decidable for regular languages, only partly for CFGs, and undecidable beyond.

questions.subject: theory-of-computation
questions.question: For how many of the four classes — regular, context-free, context-sensitive and recursively enumerable — is the membership problem (given a grammar or machine of that class and a string w, decide whether w belongs to its language) decidable?
questions.question_html: For how many of the four classes — regular, context-free, context-sensitive and recursively enumerable — is the membership problem (given a grammar or machine of that class and a string w, decide whether w belongs to its language) decidable?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Membership asks one question about one string. It is decidable whenever the computation that answers it is bounded — by the input length, or by a bound computable from the input.

Step by step.

  1. Regular: run the DFA on w, at most |w| transitions. Decidable.
  2. Context-free: CYK on Chomsky normal form takes O(|w|³ · |G|). Decidable.
  3. Context-sensitive: a linear-bounded automaton has at most |Q| · |w| · |Γ|^|w| configurations, so simulate that many steps and stop if no accepting configuration is reached. Decidable.
  4. Recursively enumerable: no such bound exists. The simulation of an arbitrary machine on w may run forever, so a “no” answer can never be delivered. Undecidable — this is the acceptance problem.
  5. Decidable for three of the four classes, so the answer is 3.

Answer: 3.

Common misconception. Answering 4 on the grounds that a universal machine can always “just simulate”. Simulation decides acceptance only when it halts; on a string outside the language it may never halt, and a decision procedure must answer every input.
